Know that He, glorified is He, has decreed the attainment of success (al-falah) for whoever possesses seven attributes. Before delving into the explanation of these attributes, two investigations are necessary:

The first investigation: ﴿qad﴾ is the opposite of (ma) in its function, for (qad) affirms what is expected, while (lamma) negates it. And there is no doubt that the believers were expecting such good news, namely the announcement of the establishment of success for them, so they were addressed with something that indicates the establishment of what they had expected.

The second investigation: al-falah means attaining the desired goal; it is also said to mean remaining in goodness. (Aflaha) means he entered into success, like (abshara), he entered into good news. It is also said (aflahahu) means he made him reach success. On this basis is the reading of Talhah ibn Musarrif, "uflihа" in the passive voice. And from him (aflahu) according to the dialect of "akaluni al-baraghith" (the fleas ate me), or on the basis of vagueness and explanation.

Page 68
The first attribute: His saying: ﴿the believers﴾, and the discussion of faith has already been presented in Surat al-Baqarah.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿those who are humble in their prayer﴾. The scholars differed concerning khushu'. Some of them made it one of the actions of the heart, such as fear and awe; others made it one of the actions of the limbs, such as stillness and refraining from looking around; and others combined both matters, and this is the preferable view. So the one who is humble in his prayer must have, from what relates to the heart, actions of utmost submission and humility before the One worshipped, and from the abstentions, that his mind is not turned toward anything other than glorification; and from what relates to the limbs, that he is still, lowering his gaze, looking at the place of his prostration, and from the abstentions, that he does not turn right or left. But the khushu' that is seen in a person is nothing except what relates to the limbs, for what relates to the heart is not seen. Al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin said: "The Muslims used to raise their eyes to the sky during their prayer, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to do so too. When this verse was revealed, he lowered his head, and his gaze did not go beyond his place of prayer." If it is said: Do you say that this is obligatory in prayer? We say: It is obligatory according to us, and there are matters that indicate it.

The first of them: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muhammad: 24], and reflection (tadabbur) cannot be conceived without standing upon the meaning. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 4], meaning: pause upon its wonders and meanings.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14], and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation, and heedlessness is contrary to remembrance; so whoever is heedless throughout his entire prayer, how can he be establishing prayer for His remembrance?

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not be among the heedless﴾ [al-A'raf: 205], and the apparent meaning of a prohibition is prohibition (tahrim).

The fourth: His saying: ﴿until you know what you are saying﴾ [an-Nisa: 43], which is the reason given for prohibiting the intoxicated, and it applies consistently to the heedless one who is absorbed and preoccupied with the worldly life.

The fifth: His saying, peace be upon him: "Humility (khushu') is only for the one who is meek and humbles himself," where the word (innama) indicates restriction; and His saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever his prayer does not restrain him from indecency and wrongdoing, he increases from Allah only in distance." The prayer of the heedless does not prevent indecency. And he, peace be upon him, said: "How many a standing worshipper has from his standing only fatigue and exhaustion," and he meant by it none but the heedless. And he also said: "The servant does not have from his prayer except what he understood."

The sixth: Al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The one who prays is conversing intimately with his Lord, as the report has stated, and speech with heedlessness is not intimate conversation at all. Its explanation is that when a person pays zakat in a state of heedlessness, the purpose of it has been achieved in some respects, namely breaking greed and enriching the poor. Likewise, fasting subdues the faculties and breaks the force of desire, which is the enemy of Allah, exalted is He. So it is not far-fetched that its purpose may be achieved with heedlessness. Likewise the Hajj consists of arduous acts, and in it there is such striving through which trial is achieved, whether the heart is present or not. As for the prayer, there is nothing in it except remembrance, recitation, bowing, prostration, standing and sitting. As for remembrance, it is intimate conversation with Allah, exalted is He. Then either its purpose is that it be intimate conversation, or the purpose is merely the letters and sounds. There is no doubt in the corruption of this latter category, for moving the tongue with babble has no valid purpose. So it is established that its purpose is intimate conversation, and that is not realized except when the tongue expresses what is in the heart of supplications. So what question is there in His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6], while the heart was heedless of it? Rather, I say: If a person swears and says: "By Allah, I will thank so-and-so, praise him, and ask him for a need," then the words indicating these meanings flow on his tongue during the day, he will not have fulfilled his oath; and if they flow on his tongue in the darkness of night while that person is present and he does not know his presence and does not see him, he does not become truthful in his oath, and his speech is not addressed to him, as long as he is not present with his heart. And if these words flow on his tongue while he is present in the brightness of day, but the speaker is heedless because he is absorbed in worry with some thought, and he had no intention to direct the address to him at the time of his utterance, he does not become truthful in his oath. And there is no doubt that the purpose of recitation is remembrances, praise, glorification, supplication and invocation, and the one addressed is Allah, exalted is He. So when the heart is veiled by the veil of heedlessness and is unaware of the majesty and greatness of Allah, and then his tongue moves by force of habit, how far is that from acceptance.

As for bowing and prostration, their purpose is glorification. If it were permissible for them to be glorification of Allah, exalted is He, while he is heedless of Him, it would be permissible for them to be glorification of the idol placed before him while he is heedless of it. Also, when glorification is not realized, nothing remains but mere movement of the back and head, and there is in it no hardship by which it becomes a pillar of religion and a dividing line between disbelief and faith, and by which one undertakes the Hajj, zakat, jihad and the rest of the arduous acts of obedience, and by which killing is specifically made obligatory. In sum, every intelligent person is certain that witnessing the great special qualities is not merely its outward acts, unless there is added to them the purpose of this intimate conversation. So these considerations indicate that prayer must necessarily include presence (hudur).

The seventh: The jurists differed about what one intends with the salam (greeting of peace at the end of prayer), in congregation and when alone: whether he intends addressing those present, or both absence and presence together. If reflection on the meaning of the salam, which is the end of prayer, is necessary, then reflection on the meaning of the takbir and tasbih, which are the things intended in prayer, is all the more necessary by way of priority. The opponent argued that making humility and khushu' a condition is contrary to the consensus of the jurists, so it should not be paid attention to. The answer is in several respects.

The first: that presence (hudur) according to us is not a condition for validity (ijza'), but a condition for acceptance (qabul). By validity is meant that the obligation of repetition does not arise, and by acceptance is meant the ruling of reward. The jurists only investigate the ruling of validity, not the ruling of reward, and our purpose in this context is this. Its example in what is witnessed is one who borrows a garment from you and returns it in the best manner: he has discharged the obligation and deserves praise; and one who throws it back to you with contempt has discharged the obligation but deserves blame. Likewise, whoever magnifies Allah, exalted is He, while performing the worship becomes one who establishes the obligation and deserves reward, and whoever treats it with contempt becomes one who apparently establishes the obligation but deserves blame.

The second: we deny this consensus. As for the theologians (mutakallimun), they have agreed that presence and khushu' are necessary, and they argued for it by saying that prostration to Allah, exalted is He, is obedience, while prostration to an idol is disbelief, and each of the two is identical to the other in its essence and its necessary features; so there must be a factor because of which prostration in one of the two forms becomes obedience and in the other disobedience. They said: and that is nothing but intention and will, and by intention is meant performing those acts out of the motive of obedience, and this motive cannot be realized except in presence. Hence they agreed that presence is necessary. As for the jurists, the jurist Abu al-Layth, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in Tanbih al-Ghafilin that the completion of recitation is that one recites without error in grammar and recites with reflection.

As for al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, he transmitted from Abu Talib al-Makki, from Bishr al-Hafi, that he said: "Whoever does not have khushu', his prayer is corrupt." And from al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him: "Every prayer in which the heart is not present, it hastens toward punishment." And from Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "Whoever knows who is on his right and left deliberately while he is in prayer, there is no prayer for him." It is also narrated with a chain traced to the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Indeed the servant prays a prayer of which there is not written for him a sixth or a tenth; rather there is written for the servant from his prayer only what he understood of it." And 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Zayd said: The scholars have agreed that the servant has from his prayer only what he understood, and he claimed consensus on it. When this is established, we say: Suppose that all the jurists ruled that it is permissible; did not the usulis and the people of piety make the matter strict regarding it? So why not take the path of caution? For some of the scholars chose to lead the prayer, and he was asked about that, and he said: "I fear that if I leave out the Fatihah, al-Shafi'i will reproach me, and if I recite it behind the imam, Abu Hanifa will reproach me, so I chose to lead the prayer seeking to escape this disagreement." And Allah knows best.

* * *

The third attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and those who turn away from idle talk﴾. And regarding idle talk (laghw) there are several opinions.

The first: that it includes everything that is prohibited or disliked, or that is permissible but for which a person has no necessity or need.

The second: that it refers only to everything that is prohibited, and this explanation is more specific than the first.

The third: that it refers only to disobedience in speech and utterance, and this is more specific than the second.

**Fourth:** It is what is permissible and of no need, and the one who holds this view argues from His words, exalted be He: ﴿Allah will not hold you to account for what is idle in your oaths﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:225]. How, then, can that be applied to sins, for which there must be accountability? The earlier scholars argued that *laghw* (idle talk) is so called because it is "annulled" (*yulgha*), and whatever the religion requires to be annulled deserves the name *laghw* more. Therefore every forbidden act must be *laghw*. Moreover, *laghw* may be disbelief, as in His words: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and talk idly during it﴾ [Fussilat 41:26]. It may also be falsehood, as in His words: ﴿You will not hear in it any idle talk﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 88:11], and His words: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk or sinful utterance﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:25]. Then, He praised them for turning away from this *laghw*, and turning away from it means not doing it, not approving of it, and not associating with those who engage in it. On this sense He said: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan 25:72]. Know that when He described them as humble in prayer, He followed it with the description of turning away from *laghw*, so that He would combine for them two burdensome acts of self-discipline, doing and abstaining, which are the two foundations upon which obligation is built. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The fifth attribute:** His words, exalted be He: ﴿And who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy﴾. Regarding this there are several questions.

**First question:** Why did He not say *"except from (ʿan) their wives"*? The answer: al-Farra' said the meaning is "except from (min) their wives." The author of *al-Kashshaf* mentioned three possibilities.

The first: it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: "except while being in authority over their wives or managing them." This is from your saying: "So-and-so was over so-and-so," and a parallel is: "Ziyad was over Basra," meaning he was its governor. From this comes the saying: "So-and-so is under so-and-so," and for this reason the wife was called a "bed" (*firash*). The meaning is that they guard their private parts in all circumstances, except in the circumstance of marrying or taking concubines.

The second: it is connected to an omitted element indicated by ﴿not blameworthy﴾, as if it were said: "They are blamed, except regarding their wives," meaning: they are blamed for every intercourse except that which has been permitted to them, for they are not blameworthy for it. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: you make it a complement (*silah*) of ﴿guard﴾.

**Second question:** Why was it not said *"man malakat"* (who), rather than *"ma malakat"* (what)? The answer: because the concubine combines two attributes: first, femaleness, which is a cause of deficiency in intellect; second, that she is of a kind that is sold and bought like other goods. Because these two attributes are combined in her, she was treated as if she were not among rational beings.

**Third question:** Does this verse indicate the prohibition of *mut'ah* (temporary marriage), as is reported from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad? The answer: Yes. Its explanation is that she is not his wife, so she must not be permissible for him. We say she is not his wife because they do not inherit from one another by consensus, and had she been his wife, inheritance would have occurred, by His words: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:12]. Since it is established that she is not his wife, it follows that she is not permissible to him, by His words: ﴿except from their wives or those their right hands possess﴾. And Allah knows best.

**Fourth question:** Is it not the case that sexual enjoyment with a wife and with a slave-woman is impermissible in certain circumstances, such as menstruation and the waiting period (*iddah*), and with a slave-woman when she is married to another or during her waiting period? Likewise, the male slave is included in the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿or those their right hands possess﴾. The answer is in two parts.

The first: the position of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, is that an exception from a negation does not produce an affirmation. He argued for this with the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "There is no prayer without purification, and no marriage without a guardian." This does not imply that prayer occurs merely by the presence of purification, nor that marriage occurs merely by the presence of a guardian. The benefit of the exception is to restrict the ruling, not to restrict what the ruling is applied to. So His words: ﴿And who guard their private parts﴾ ﴿except from their wives﴾ mean that guarding the private parts from everyone is obligatory, except in these two cases, for I have mentioned the ruling for them neither by negation nor by affirmation.

The second: even if we grant that an exception from a negation is an affirmation, its maximum effect is that it is a general statement which has been specified by evidence, and so it remains a proof for what lies beyond it.

As for His words: ﴿Those are the transgressors﴾, meaning: those who are complete in transgression and who go to its extremes.

* * *

**The sixth attribute:** His words, exalted be He: ﴿And who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾. Qara' Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read *li-amanatihim* (singular). Know that the thing entrusted and the thing covenanted is called *amanah* (trust) and *ʿahd* (covenant). From this is His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:58], and He said: ﴿and betray your trusts﴾ [al-Anfal 8:27]. Only the outward forms are rendered back, not the meanings, so what is entrusted is the trust itself. A *ʿahd* is what one binds upon oneself in matters that bring one closer to one's Lord; it also applies to what Allah has commanded, as in His words: ﴿Those who said: "Indeed, Allah has taken a covenant with us"﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:183]. A *rāʿī* is one who stands over a thing for preservation and improvement, like a shepherd of sheep or a shepherd of a flock. It is said: "Who is the *rāʿī* of this matter?" meaning: who is in charge of it.

Know that trust encompasses everything whose abandonment would fall under betrayal, and He, exalted be He, has said: ﴿O you who believe, do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts﴾ [al-Anfal 8:27]. Among that are the acts of worship for which a person is entrusted, and all acts of worship enter into this, because they are either hidden entirely, like fasting, the ritual bath from major impurity, and performing ablution thoroughly, or the manner of performing them is hidden. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The greatest of people in betrayal is one who does not complete his prayer." And it is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The first of your religion that you will lose is trustworthiness, and the last you will lose is prayer."

Among that is what a person binds himself to by an action or a statement, so he is obliged to fulfil it, such as deposits, contracts, and what is connected to them. Among that are the statements by which slaves and women are freed, for he is trusted in that. Among that is that he should protect his trust and not spoil it by usurpation or otherwise. As for the covenant, it includes contracts, oaths, and vows. Thus Allah, exalted be He, has made clear that observing these matters and standing by them is a condition for attaining success.

* * *

**The seventh attribute:** His words: ﴿And who are attentive to their prayers﴾. He repeated its mention because humility (*khushu'*) and attentiveness (*muhafazah*) are distinct and not necessarily linked. Humility is a quality of the one praying while performing his prayer, whereas attentiveness is valid when he has not yet performed it in its completeness. Rather, what is meant by attentiveness is taking care of its conditions, such as the time and purification and other things, and standing over its pillars and completing them, until this becomes his habit at all times. Then, when Allah, exalted be He, mentioned all these matters together, He said: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws; therein they will abide forever﴾. Here there are questions.

**First question:** Why did He call what they obtain of reward and Paradise an *inheritance*, even though He has decreed that Paradise is their due in His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for Paradise﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:111]? The answer is in several respects.

The first: what is reported from the Messenger, peace be upon him, and it is the clearest of what is said about it: that there is no accountable person except that Allah has prepared for him in the Fire what he deserves if he disobeys, and in Paradise what he deserves if he obeys, and He has made for that a sign. So when some of them believe and some do not, the place of the one who did not believe is transferred to the believers, and his destiny becomes the Fire, with which there must be deprivation of reward, like their death. So this is called an inheritance for this reason. The jurists have said that there is no difference between what the deceased owned and what the owner is assigned in terms of its being inherited from him. Likewise they said of blood money due for killing that it is inherited, even though he did not truly own it, and this supports what we have mentioned. If it is said that He, exalted be He, described all that they are entitled to as inheritance, and according to what you have said, what someone else would have deserved had he obeyed would enter into the inheritance, we say: it is not impossible that He, exalted be He, assigned to this particular believer the station which that disbeliever would have had had he obeyed, because at that time the stations were increasing, and when this one believed, He transferred that to him.

The second: the transfer of Paradise to them without reckoning and without knowing its measures resembles the transfer of wealth to an heir.

The third: Paradise was the dwelling of our father Adam, peace be upon him. When it passes to his offspring, this resembles inheritance.

**Second question:** How did He pass judgment that those described by the seven attributes are successful, even though He did not complete the mention of obligatory acts of worship, such as fasting, pilgrimage, and purification? The answer: His words ﴿And who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾ encompass all obligations, both of acts and of abstentions, as we have previously stated, and purifications are included in the attentiveness to the five prayers, because they are among its conditions.

**Third question:** Does His words ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ indicate that no one else enters it? The answer: His words ﴿they are the inheritors﴾ imply restriction, but it is obligatory to abandon acting upon it, because it is established that children, the insane, young boys, and the dark-eyed maidens (*hur ʿin*) enter Paradise, and sinners among the People of the Qiblah also enter it after pardon, by His words: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:48].

**Fourth question:** Is all of Paradise *al-Firdaws*? The answer: *al-Firdaws* is the Paradise in the language of Abyssinia, and it is said in the language of the Romans. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari narrated from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: "al-Firdaws is the enclosure of the Most Merciful; in it are rivers and trees." Abu Umamah narrated from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Ask Allah for al-Firdaws, for it is the highest of the gardens, and the people of al-Firdaws hear the creaking of the Throne."

**Question 5:** Does the verse indicate that these attributes are what make them believers, and that they are believers because of them, or not? **Answer:** Al-Qadi (ʿAbd al-Jabbar) claimed that this is the case, on the basis of his school's view that *īmān* (faith) is a *ism sharʿī* (a term of religious law) applied to the performance of all the obligations. In our view, the verse does not indicate this, because His saying ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾ ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ is like saying "Certainly the intelligent, upright people have succeeded." This does not indicate that almsgiving and uprightness are included in the meaning of "people," so the same holds here.

**Question 6:** It is narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "When God Most High created the Garden of ʿAdn, He said to it: 'Speak.' It said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded.﴾" Kaʿb said: "God created Adam with His own hand, wrote the Torah with His own hand, and planted the tree of Ṭūbā with His own hand. Then He said to it: 'Speak.' It said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded.﴾" It is also narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "When a servant performs wuḍūʾ (ablution) well, prays the prayer at its proper time, and maintains its bowings, prostrations, and appointed times, the prayer says: 'May God preserve you as you have preserved me,' and it intercedes for its companion. But if he neglects it, it says: 'May God neglect you as you neglected me,' and it is wrapped up like a worn-out garment and struck against the face of its companion." **Answer:** As for the speech of the Garden, the meaning is that it was prepared for the believers, so this became like a statement from it. This is like His saying, Most High: ﴿They said: "We come willingly."﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 11]. As for His creating the Garden "with His hand," the meaning is that He Himself undertook its creation, not that He delegated it to another. As for the claim that prayer praises whoever fulfils its rights, this is even further from being permissible than the speech of the Garden, because prayer consists of movements and stillnesses, and it is not possible for it to form an image or speak. Therefore the meaning is a figure of speech, as when someone says to a benefactor: "Your kindness to me speaks in gratitude."

**Question 7:** Does the verse indicate that Paradise (al-Firdaws) is created? **Answer:** Al-Qadi said: His saying, Most High, ﴿its fruit is perpetual﴾ [al-Raʿd: 35] indicates that it is not created, so this verse must be interpreted. It is as if He Most High said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, God will create the Garden as an inheritance for the believers," or: "When He creates it, it will speak," following the same pattern by which we interpreted His saying, Most High: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 50]. This is weak, because the supposition of what he mentioned in this verse is no more preferable than supposing it in His saying: ﴿its fruit is perpetual.﴾ Moreover, its fruit is perpetual on the Day of Resurrection. When these two apparent meanings conflict, we rely, in holding that the Garden is created, on His saying, Most High: ﴿It has been prepared for the God-fearing﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 133].

Know that He, glorified is He, has decreed the attainment of success (al-falah) for whoever possesses seven attributes. Before delving into the explanation of these attributes, two investigations are necessary:

The first investigation: ﴿qad﴾ is the opposite of (ma) in its function, for (qad) affirms what is expected, while (lamma) negates it. And there is no doubt that the believers were expecting such good news, namely the announcement of the establishment of success for them, so they were addressed with something that indicates the establishment of what they had expected.

The second investigation: al-falah means attaining the desired goal; it is also said to mean remaining in goodness. (Aflaha) means he entered into success, like (abshara), he entered into good news. It is also said (aflahahu) means he made him reach success. On this basis is the reading of Talhah ibn Musarrif, "uflihа" in the passive voice. And from him (aflahu) according to the dialect of "akaluni al-baraghith" (the fleas ate me), or on the basis of vagueness and explanation.

Page 68
The first attribute: His saying: ﴿the believers﴾, and the discussion of faith has already been presented in Surat al-Baqarah.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿those who are humble in their prayer﴾. The scholars differed concerning khushu'. Some of them made it one of the actions of the heart, such as fear and awe; others made it one of the actions of the limbs, such as stillness and refraining from looking around; and others combined both matters, and this is the preferable view. So the one who is humble in his prayer must have, from what relates to the heart, actions of utmost submission and humility before the One worshipped, and from the abstentions, that his mind is not turned toward anything other than glorification; and from what relates to the limbs, that he is still, lowering his gaze, looking at the place of his prostration, and from the abstentions, that he does not turn right or left. But the khushu' that is seen in a person is nothing except what relates to the limbs, for what relates to the heart is not seen. Al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin said: "The Muslims used to raise their eyes to the sky during their prayer, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to do so too. When this verse was revealed, he lowered his head, and his gaze did not go beyond his place of prayer." If it is said: Do you say that this is obligatory in prayer? We say: It is obligatory according to us, and there are matters that indicate it.

The first of them: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ [Muhammad: 24], and reflection (tadabbur) cannot be conceived without standing upon the meaning. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 4], meaning: pause upon its wonders and meanings.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14], and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation, and heedlessness is contrary to remembrance; so whoever is heedless throughout his entire prayer, how can he be establishing prayer for His remembrance?

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not be among the heedless﴾ [al-A'raf: 205], and the apparent meaning of a prohibition is prohibition (tahrim).

The fourth: His saying: ﴿until you know what you are saying﴾ [an-Nisa: 43], which is the reason given for prohibiting the intoxicated, and it applies consistently to the heedless one who is absorbed and preoccupied with the worldly life.

The fifth: His saying, peace be upon him: "Humility (khushu') is only for the one who is meek and humbles himself," where the word (innama) indicates restriction; and His saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever his prayer does not restrain him from indecency and wrongdoing, he increases from Allah only in distance." The prayer of the heedless does not prevent indecency. And he, peace be upon him, said: "How many a standing worshipper has from his standing only fatigue and exhaustion," and he meant by it none but the heedless. And he also said: "The servant does not have from his prayer except what he understood."

The sixth: Al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The one who prays is conversing intimately with his Lord, as the report has stated, and speech with heedlessness is not intimate conversation at all. Its explanation is that when a person pays zakat in a state of heedlessness, the purpose of it has been achieved in some respects, namely breaking greed and enriching the poor. Likewise, fasting subdues the faculties and breaks the force of desire, which is the enemy of Allah, exalted is He. So it is not far-fetched that its purpose may be achieved with heedlessness. Likewise the Hajj consists of arduous acts, and in it there is such striving through which trial is achieved, whether the heart is present or not. As for the prayer, there is nothing in it except remembrance, recitation, bowing, prostration, standing and sitting. As for remembrance, it is intimate conversation with Allah, exalted is He. Then either its purpose is that it be intimate conversation, or the purpose is merely the letters and sounds. There is no doubt in the corruption of this latter category, for moving the tongue with babble has no valid purpose. So it is established that its purpose is intimate conversation, and that is not realized except when the tongue expresses what is in the heart of supplications. So what question is there in His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6], while the heart was heedless of it? Rather, I say: If a person swears and says: "By Allah, I will thank so-and-so, praise him, and ask him for a need," then the words indicating these meanings flow on his tongue during the day, he will not have fulfilled his oath; and if they flow on his tongue in the darkness of night while that person is present and he does not know his presence and does not see him, he does not become truthful in his oath, and his speech is not addressed to him, as long as he is not present with his heart. And if these words flow on his tongue while he is present in the brightness of day, but the speaker is heedless because he is absorbed in worry with some thought, and he had no intention to direct the address to him at the time of his utterance, he does not become truthful in his oath. And there is no doubt that the purpose of recitation is remembrances, praise, glorification, supplication and invocation, and the one addressed is Allah, exalted is He. So when the heart is veiled by the veil of heedlessness and is unaware of the majesty and greatness of Allah, and then his tongue moves by force of habit, how far is that from acceptance.

As for bowing and prostration, their purpose is glorification. If it were permissible for them to be glorification of Allah, exalted is He, while he is heedless of Him, it would be permissible for them to be glorification of the idol placed before him while he is heedless of it. Also, when glorification is not realized, nothing remains but mere movement of the back and head, and there is in it no hardship by which it becomes a pillar of religion and a dividing line between disbelief and faith, and by which one undertakes the Hajj, zakat, jihad and the rest of the arduous acts of obedience, and by which killing is specifically made obligatory. In sum, every intelligent person is certain that witnessing the great special qualities is not merely its outward acts, unless there is added to them the purpose of this intimate conversation. So these considerations indicate that prayer must necessarily include presence (hudur).

The seventh: The jurists differed about what one intends with the salam (greeting of peace at the end of prayer), in congregation and when alone: whether he intends addressing those present, or both absence and presence together. If reflection on the meaning of the salam, which is the end of prayer, is necessary, then reflection on the meaning of the takbir and tasbih, which are the things intended in prayer, is all the more necessary by way of priority. The opponent argued that making humility and khushu' a condition is contrary to the consensus of the jurists, so it should not be paid attention to. The answer is in several respects.

The first: that presence (hudur) according to us is not a condition for validity (ijza'), but a condition for acceptance (qabul). By validity is meant that the obligation of repetition does not arise, and by acceptance is meant the ruling of reward. The jurists only investigate the ruling of validity, not the ruling of reward, and our purpose in this context is this. Its example in what is witnessed is one who borrows a garment from you and returns it in the best manner: he has discharged the obligation and deserves praise; and one who throws it back to you with contempt has discharged the obligation but deserves blame. Likewise, whoever magnifies Allah, exalted is He, while performing the worship becomes one who establishes the obligation and deserves reward, and whoever treats it with contempt becomes one who apparently establishes the obligation but deserves blame.

The second: we deny this consensus. As for the theologians (mutakallimun), they have agreed that presence and khushu' are necessary, and they argued for it by saying that prostration to Allah, exalted is He, is obedience, while prostration to an idol is disbelief, and each of the two is identical to the other in its essence and its necessary features; so there must be a factor because of which prostration in one of the two forms becomes obedience and in the other disobedience. They said: and that is nothing but intention and will, and by intention is meant performing those acts out of the motive of obedience, and this motive cannot be realized except in presence. Hence they agreed that presence is necessary. As for the jurists, the jurist Abu al-Layth, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in Tanbih al-Ghafilin that the completion of recitation is that one recites without error in grammar and recites with reflection.

As for al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, he transmitted from Abu Talib al-Makki, from Bishr al-Hafi, that he said: "Whoever does not have khushu', his prayer is corrupt." And from al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him: "Every prayer in which the heart is not present, it hastens toward punishment." And from Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "Whoever knows who is on his right and left deliberately while he is in prayer, there is no prayer for him." It is also narrated with a chain traced to the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Indeed the servant prays a prayer of which there is not written for him a sixth or a tenth; rather there is written for the servant from his prayer only what he understood of it." And 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Zayd said: The scholars have agreed that the servant has from his prayer only what he understood, and he claimed consensus on it. When this is established, we say: Suppose that all the jurists ruled that it is permissible; did not the usulis and the people of piety make the matter strict regarding it? So why not take the path of caution? For some of the scholars chose to lead the prayer, and he was asked about that, and he said: "I fear that if I leave out the Fatihah, al-Shafi'i will reproach me, and if I recite it behind the imam, Abu Hanifa will reproach me, so I chose to lead the prayer seeking to escape this disagreement." And Allah knows best.

* * *

The third attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and those who turn away from idle talk﴾. And regarding idle talk (laghw) there are several opinions.

The first: that it includes everything that is prohibited or disliked, or that is permissible but for which a person has no necessity or need.

The second: that it refers only to everything that is prohibited, and this explanation is more specific than the first.

The third: that it refers only to disobedience in speech and utterance, and this is more specific than the second.

**Fourth:** It is what is permissible and of no need, and the one who holds this view argues from His words, exalted be He: ﴿Allah will not hold you to account for what is idle in your oaths﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:225]. How, then, can that be applied to sins, for which there must be accountability? The earlier scholars argued that *laghw* (idle talk) is so called because it is "annulled" (*yulgha*), and whatever the religion requires to be annulled deserves the name *laghw* more. Therefore every forbidden act must be *laghw*. Moreover, *laghw* may be disbelief, as in His words: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and talk idly during it﴾ [Fussilat 41:26]. It may also be falsehood, as in His words: ﴿You will not hear in it any idle talk﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 88:11], and His words: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk or sinful utterance﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:25]. Then, He praised them for turning away from this *laghw*, and turning away from it means not doing it, not approving of it, and not associating with those who engage in it. On this sense He said: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan 25:72]. Know that when He described them as humble in prayer, He followed it with the description of turning away from *laghw*, so that He would combine for them two burdensome acts of self-discipline, doing and abstaining, which are the two foundations upon which obligation is built. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The fifth attribute:** His words, exalted be He: ﴿And who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy﴾. Regarding this there are several questions.

**First question:** Why did He not say *"except from (ʿan) their wives"*? The answer: al-Farra' said the meaning is "except from (min) their wives." The author of *al-Kashshaf* mentioned three possibilities.

The first: it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: "except while being in authority over their wives or managing them." This is from your saying: "So-and-so was over so-and-so," and a parallel is: "Ziyad was over Basra," meaning he was its governor. From this comes the saying: "So-and-so is under so-and-so," and for this reason the wife was called a "bed" (*firash*). The meaning is that they guard their private parts in all circumstances, except in the circumstance of marrying or taking concubines.

The second: it is connected to an omitted element indicated by ﴿not blameworthy﴾, as if it were said: "They are blamed, except regarding their wives," meaning: they are blamed for every intercourse except that which has been permitted to them, for they are not blameworthy for it. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: you make it a complement (*silah*) of ﴿guard﴾.

**Second question:** Why was it not said *"man malakat"* (who), rather than *"ma malakat"* (what)? The answer: because the concubine combines two attributes: first, femaleness, which is a cause of deficiency in intellect; second, that she is of a kind that is sold and bought like other goods. Because these two attributes are combined in her, she was treated as if she were not among rational beings.

**Third question:** Does this verse indicate the prohibition of *mut'ah* (temporary marriage), as is reported from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad? The answer: Yes. Its explanation is that she is not his wife, so she must not be permissible for him. We say she is not his wife because they do not inherit from one another by consensus, and had she been his wife, inheritance would have occurred, by His words: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:12]. Since it is established that she is not his wife, it follows that she is not permissible to him, by His words: ﴿except from their wives or those their right hands possess﴾. And Allah knows best.

**Fourth question:** Is it not the case that sexual enjoyment with a wife and with a slave-woman is impermissible in certain circumstances, such as menstruation and the waiting period (*iddah*), and with a slave-woman when she is married to another or during her waiting period? Likewise, the male slave is included in the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿or those their right hands possess﴾. The answer is in two parts.

The first: the position of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, is that an exception from a negation does not produce an affirmation. He argued for this with the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "There is no prayer without purification, and no marriage without a guardian." This does not imply that prayer occurs merely by the presence of purification, nor that marriage occurs merely by the presence of a guardian. The benefit of the exception is to restrict the ruling, not to restrict what the ruling is applied to. So His words: ﴿And who guard their private parts﴾ ﴿except from their wives﴾ mean that guarding the private parts from everyone is obligatory, except in these two cases, for I have mentioned the ruling for them neither by negation nor by affirmation.

The second: even if we grant that an exception from a negation is an affirmation, its maximum effect is that it is a general statement which has been specified by evidence, and so it remains a proof for what lies beyond it.

As for His words: ﴿Those are the transgressors﴾, meaning: those who are complete in transgression and who go to its extremes.

* * *

**The sixth attribute:** His words, exalted be He: ﴿And who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾. Qara' Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read *li-amanatihim* (singular). Know that the thing entrusted and the thing covenanted is called *amanah* (trust) and *ʿahd* (covenant). From this is His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:58], and He said: ﴿and betray your trusts﴾ [al-Anfal 8:27]. Only the outward forms are rendered back, not the meanings, so what is entrusted is the trust itself. A *ʿahd* is what one binds upon oneself in matters that bring one closer to one's Lord; it also applies to what Allah has commanded, as in His words: ﴿Those who said: "Indeed, Allah has taken a covenant with us"﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:183]. A *rāʿī* is one who stands over a thing for preservation and improvement, like a shepherd of sheep or a shepherd of a flock. It is said: "Who is the *rāʿī* of this matter?" meaning: who is in charge of it.

Know that trust encompasses everything whose abandonment would fall under betrayal, and He, exalted be He, has said: ﴿O you who believe, do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts﴾ [al-Anfal 8:27]. Among that are the acts of worship for which a person is entrusted, and all acts of worship enter into this, because they are either hidden entirely, like fasting, the ritual bath from major impurity, and performing ablution thoroughly, or the manner of performing them is hidden. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The greatest of people in betrayal is one who does not complete his prayer." And it is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The first of your religion that you will lose is trustworthiness, and the last you will lose is prayer."

Among that is what a person binds himself to by an action or a statement, so he is obliged to fulfil it, such as deposits, contracts, and what is connected to them. Among that are the statements by which slaves and women are freed, for he is trusted in that. Among that is that he should protect his trust and not spoil it by usurpation or otherwise. As for the covenant, it includes contracts, oaths, and vows. Thus Allah, exalted be He, has made clear that observing these matters and standing by them is a condition for attaining success.

* * *

**The seventh attribute:** His words: ﴿And who are attentive to their prayers﴾. He repeated its mention because humility (*khushu'*) and attentiveness (*muhafazah*) are distinct and not necessarily linked. Humility is a quality of the one praying while performing his prayer, whereas attentiveness is valid when he has not yet performed it in its completeness. Rather, what is meant by attentiveness is taking care of its conditions, such as the time and purification and other things, and standing over its pillars and completing them, until this becomes his habit at all times. Then, when Allah, exalted be He, mentioned all these matters together, He said: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws; therein they will abide forever﴾. Here there are questions.

**First question:** Why did He call what they obtain of reward and Paradise an *inheritance*, even though He has decreed that Paradise is their due in His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for Paradise﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:111]? The answer is in several respects.

The first: what is reported from the Messenger, peace be upon him, and it is the clearest of what is said about it: that there is no accountable person except that Allah has prepared for him in the Fire what he deserves if he disobeys, and in Paradise what he deserves if he obeys, and He has made for that a sign. So when some of them believe and some do not, the place of the one who did not believe is transferred to the believers, and his destiny becomes the Fire, with which there must be deprivation of reward, like their death. So this is called an inheritance for this reason. The jurists have said that there is no difference between what the deceased owned and what the owner is assigned in terms of its being inherited from him. Likewise they said of blood money due for killing that it is inherited, even though he did not truly own it, and this supports what we have mentioned. If it is said that He, exalted be He, described all that they are entitled to as inheritance, and according to what you have said, what someone else would have deserved had he obeyed would enter into the inheritance, we say: it is not impossible that He, exalted be He, assigned to this particular believer the station which that disbeliever would have had had he obeyed, because at that time the stations were increasing, and when this one believed, He transferred that to him.

The second: the transfer of Paradise to them without reckoning and without knowing its measures resembles the transfer of wealth to an heir.

The third: Paradise was the dwelling of our father Adam, peace be upon him. When it passes to his offspring, this resembles inheritance.

**Second question:** How did He pass judgment that those described by the seven attributes are successful, even though He did not complete the mention of obligatory acts of worship, such as fasting, pilgrimage, and purification? The answer: His words ﴿And who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾ encompass all obligations, both of acts and of abstentions, as we have previously stated, and purifications are included in the attentiveness to the five prayers, because they are among its conditions.

**Third question:** Does His words ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ indicate that no one else enters it? The answer: His words ﴿they are the inheritors﴾ imply restriction, but it is obligatory to abandon acting upon it, because it is established that children, the insane, young boys, and the dark-eyed maidens (*hur ʿin*) enter Paradise, and sinners among the People of the Qiblah also enter it after pardon, by His words: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:48].

**Fourth question:** Is all of Paradise *al-Firdaws*? The answer: *al-Firdaws* is the Paradise in the language of Abyssinia, and it is said in the language of the Romans. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari narrated from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: "al-Firdaws is the enclosure of the Most Merciful; in it are rivers and trees." Abu Umamah narrated from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Ask Allah for al-Firdaws, for it is the highest of the gardens, and the people of al-Firdaws hear the creaking of the Throne."

**Question 5:** Does the verse indicate that these attributes are what make them believers, and that they are believers because of them, or not? **Answer:** Al-Qadi (ʿAbd al-Jabbar) claimed that this is the case, on the basis of his school's view that *īmān* (faith) is a *ism sharʿī* (a term of religious law) applied to the performance of all the obligations. In our view, the verse does not indicate this, because His saying ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾ ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ is like saying "Certainly the intelligent, upright people have succeeded." This does not indicate that almsgiving and uprightness are included in the meaning of "people," so the same holds here.

**Question 6:** It is narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "When God Most High created the Garden of ʿAdn, He said to it: 'Speak.' It said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded.﴾" Kaʿb said: "God created Adam with His own hand, wrote the Torah with His own hand, and planted the tree of Ṭūbā with His own hand. Then He said to it: 'Speak.' It said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded.﴾" It is also narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "When a servant performs wuḍūʾ (ablution) well, prays the prayer at its proper time, and maintains its bowings, prostrations, and appointed times, the prayer says: 'May God preserve you as you have preserved me,' and it intercedes for its companion. But if he neglects it, it says: 'May God neglect you as you neglected me,' and it is wrapped up like a worn-out garment and struck against the face of its companion." **Answer:** As for the speech of the Garden, the meaning is that it was prepared for the believers, so this became like a statement from it. This is like His saying, Most High: ﴿They said: "We come willingly."﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 11]. As for His creating the Garden "with His hand," the meaning is that He Himself undertook its creation, not that He delegated it to another. As for the claim that prayer praises whoever fulfils its rights, this is even further from being permissible than the speech of the Garden, because prayer consists of movements and stillnesses, and it is not possible for it to form an image or speak. Therefore the meaning is a figure of speech, as when someone says to a benefactor: "Your kindness to me speaks in gratitude."

**Question 7:** Does the verse indicate that Paradise (al-Firdaws) is created? **Answer:** Al-Qadi said: His saying, Most High, ﴿its fruit is perpetual﴾ [al-Raʿd: 35] indicates that it is not created, so this verse must be interpreted. It is as if He Most High said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, God will create the Garden as an inheritance for the believers," or: "When He creates it, it will speak," following the same pattern by which we interpreted His saying, Most High: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 50]. This is weak, because the supposition of what he mentioned in this verse is no more preferable than supposing it in His saying: ﴿its fruit is perpetual.﴾ Moreover, its fruit is perpetual on the Day of Resurrection. When these two apparent meanings conflict, we rely, in holding that the Garden is created, on His saying, Most High: ﴿It has been prepared for the God-fearing﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 133].
