The third attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and those who turn away from idle talk﴾. And regarding idle talk (laghw) there are several opinions.

The first: that it includes everything that is prohibited or disliked, or that is permissible but for which a person has no necessity or need.

The second: that it refers only to everything that is prohibited, and this explanation is more specific than the first.

The third: that it refers only to disobedience in speech and utterance, and this is more specific than the second.

**Fourth:** It is what is permissible and of no need, and the one who holds this view argues from His words, exalted be He: ﴿Allah will not hold you to account for what is idle in your oaths﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:225]. How, then, can that be applied to sins, for which there must be accountability? The earlier scholars argued that *laghw* (idle talk) is so called because it is "annulled" (*yulgha*), and whatever the religion requires to be annulled deserves the name *laghw* more. Therefore every forbidden act must be *laghw*. Moreover, *laghw* may be disbelief, as in His words: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and talk idly during it﴾ [Fussilat 41:26]. It may also be falsehood, as in His words: ﴿You will not hear in it any idle talk﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 88:11], and His words: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk or sinful utterance﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:25]. Then, He praised them for turning away from this *laghw*, and turning away from it means not doing it, not approving of it, and not associating with those who engage in it. On this sense He said: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan 25:72]. Know that when He described them as humble in prayer, He followed it with the description of turning away from *laghw*, so that He would combine for them two burdensome acts of self-discipline, doing and abstaining, which are the two foundations upon which obligation is built. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The fifth attribute:** His words, exalted be He: ﴿And who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy﴾. Regarding this there are several questions.

**First question:** Why did He not say *"except from (ʿan) their wives"*? The answer: al-Farra' said the meaning is "except from (min) their wives." The author of *al-Kashshaf* mentioned three possibilities.

The first: it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: "except while being in authority over their wives or managing them." This is from your saying: "So-and-so was over so-and-so," and a parallel is: "Ziyad was over Basra," meaning he was its governor. From this comes the saying: "So-and-so is under so-and-so," and for this reason the wife was called a "bed" (*firash*). The meaning is that they guard their private parts in all circumstances, except in the circumstance of marrying or taking concubines.

The second: it is connected to an omitted element indicated by ﴿not blameworthy﴾, as if it were said: "They are blamed, except regarding their wives," meaning: they are blamed for every intercourse except that which has been permitted to them, for they are not blameworthy for it. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: you make it a complement (*silah*) of ﴿guard﴾.

**Second question:** Why was it not said *"man malakat"* (who), rather than *"ma malakat"* (what)? The answer: because the concubine combines two attributes: first, femaleness, which is a cause of deficiency in intellect; second, that she is of a kind that is sold and bought like other goods. Because these two attributes are combined in her, she was treated as if she were not among rational beings.

**Third question:** Does this verse indicate the prohibition of *mut'ah* (temporary marriage), as is reported from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad? The answer: Yes. Its explanation is that she is not his wife, so she must not be permissible for him. We say she is not his wife because they do not inherit from one another by consensus, and had she been his wife, inheritance would have occurred, by His words: ﴿And for you is half of what your wives leave﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:12]. Since it is established that she is not his wife, it follows that she is not permissible to him, by His words: ﴿except from their wives or those their right hands possess﴾. And Allah knows best.

**Fourth question:** Is it not the case that sexual enjoyment with a wife and with a slave-woman is impermissible in certain circumstances, such as menstruation and the waiting period (*iddah*), and with a slave-woman when she is married to another or during her waiting period? Likewise, the male slave is included in the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿or those their right hands possess﴾. The answer is in two parts.

The first: the position of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, is that an exception from a negation does not produce an affirmation. He argued for this with the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "There is no prayer without purification, and no marriage without a guardian." This does not imply that prayer occurs merely by the presence of purification, nor that marriage occurs merely by the presence of a guardian. The benefit of the exception is to restrict the ruling, not to restrict what the ruling is applied to. So His words: ﴿And who guard their private parts﴾ ﴿except from their wives﴾ mean that guarding the private parts from everyone is obligatory, except in these two cases, for I have mentioned the ruling for them neither by negation nor by affirmation.

The second: even if we grant that an exception from a negation is an affirmation, its maximum effect is that it is a general statement which has been specified by evidence, and so it remains a proof for what lies beyond it.

As for His words: ﴿Those are the transgressors﴾, meaning: those who are complete in transgression and who go to its extremes.

* * *

**The sixth attribute:** His words, exalted be He: ﴿And who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾. Qara' Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read *li-amanatihim* (singular). Know that the thing entrusted and the thing covenanted is called *amanah* (trust) and *ʿahd* (covenant). From this is His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:58], and He said: ﴿and betray your trusts﴾ [al-Anfal 8:27]. Only the outward forms are rendered back, not the meanings, so what is entrusted is the trust itself. A *ʿahd* is what one binds upon oneself in matters that bring one closer to one's Lord; it also applies to what Allah has commanded, as in His words: ﴿Those who said: "Indeed, Allah has taken a covenant with us"﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:183]. A *rāʿī* is one who stands over a thing for preservation and improvement, like a shepherd of sheep or a shepherd of a flock. It is said: "Who is the *rāʿī* of this matter?" meaning: who is in charge of it.

Know that trust encompasses everything whose abandonment would fall under betrayal, and He, exalted be He, has said: ﴿O you who believe, do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts﴾ [al-Anfal 8:27]. Among that are the acts of worship for which a person is entrusted, and all acts of worship enter into this, because they are either hidden entirely, like fasting, the ritual bath from major impurity, and performing ablution thoroughly, or the manner of performing them is hidden. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The greatest of people in betrayal is one who does not complete his prayer." And it is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The first of your religion that you will lose is trustworthiness, and the last you will lose is prayer."

Among that is what a person binds himself to by an action or a statement, so he is obliged to fulfil it, such as deposits, contracts, and what is connected to them. Among that are the statements by which slaves and women are freed, for he is trusted in that. Among that is that he should protect his trust and not spoil it by usurpation or otherwise. As for the covenant, it includes contracts, oaths, and vows. Thus Allah, exalted be He, has made clear that observing these matters and standing by them is a condition for attaining success.

* * *

**The seventh attribute:** His words: ﴿And who are attentive to their prayers﴾. He repeated its mention because humility (*khushu'*) and attentiveness (*muhafazah*) are distinct and not necessarily linked. Humility is a quality of the one praying while performing his prayer, whereas attentiveness is valid when he has not yet performed it in its completeness. Rather, what is meant by attentiveness is taking care of its conditions, such as the time and purification and other things, and standing over its pillars and completing them, until this becomes his habit at all times. Then, when Allah, exalted be He, mentioned all these matters together, He said: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ ﴿who will inherit al-Firdaws; therein they will abide forever﴾. Here there are questions.

**First question:** Why did He call what they obtain of reward and Paradise an *inheritance*, even though He has decreed that Paradise is their due in His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for Paradise﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:111]? The answer is in several respects.

The first: what is reported from the Messenger, peace be upon him, and it is the clearest of what is said about it: that there is no accountable person except that Allah has prepared for him in the Fire what he deserves if he disobeys, and in Paradise what he deserves if he obeys, and He has made for that a sign. So when some of them believe and some do not, the place of the one who did not believe is transferred to the believers, and his destiny becomes the Fire, with which there must be deprivation of reward, like their death. So this is called an inheritance for this reason. The jurists have said that there is no difference between what the deceased owned and what the owner is assigned in terms of its being inherited from him. Likewise they said of blood money due for killing that it is inherited, even though he did not truly own it, and this supports what we have mentioned. If it is said that He, exalted be He, described all that they are entitled to as inheritance, and according to what you have said, what someone else would have deserved had he obeyed would enter into the inheritance, we say: it is not impossible that He, exalted be He, assigned to this particular believer the station which that disbeliever would have had had he obeyed, because at that time the stations were increasing, and when this one believed, He transferred that to him.

The second: the transfer of Paradise to them without reckoning and without knowing its measures resembles the transfer of wealth to an heir.

The third: Paradise was the dwelling of our father Adam, peace be upon him. When it passes to his offspring, this resembles inheritance.

**Second question:** How did He pass judgment that those described by the seven attributes are successful, even though He did not complete the mention of obligatory acts of worship, such as fasting, pilgrimage, and purification? The answer: His words ﴿And who are faithful to their trusts and their covenant﴾ encompass all obligations, both of acts and of abstentions, as we have previously stated, and purifications are included in the attentiveness to the five prayers, because they are among its conditions.

**Third question:** Does His words ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ indicate that no one else enters it? The answer: His words ﴿they are the inheritors﴾ imply restriction, but it is obligatory to abandon acting upon it, because it is established that children, the insane, young boys, and the dark-eyed maidens (*hur ʿin*) enter Paradise, and sinners among the People of the Qiblah also enter it after pardon, by His words: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:48].

**Fourth question:** Is all of Paradise *al-Firdaws*? The answer: *al-Firdaws* is the Paradise in the language of Abyssinia, and it is said in the language of the Romans. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari narrated from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he said: "al-Firdaws is the enclosure of the Most Merciful; in it are rivers and trees." Abu Umamah narrated from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Ask Allah for al-Firdaws, for it is the highest of the gardens, and the people of al-Firdaws hear the creaking of the Throne."

**Question 5:** Does the verse indicate that these attributes are what make them believers, and that they are believers because of them, or not? **Answer:** Al-Qadi (ʿAbd al-Jabbar) claimed that this is the case, on the basis of his school's view that *īmān* (faith) is a *ism sharʿī* (a term of religious law) applied to the performance of all the obligations. In our view, the verse does not indicate this, because His saying ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾ ﴿who are humbly submissive in their prayer﴾ is like saying "Certainly the intelligent, upright people have succeeded." This does not indicate that almsgiving and uprightness are included in the meaning of "people," so the same holds here.

**Question 6:** It is narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "When God Most High created the Garden of ʿAdn, He said to it: 'Speak.' It said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded.﴾" Kaʿb said: "God created Adam with His own hand, wrote the Torah with His own hand, and planted the tree of Ṭūbā with His own hand. Then He said to it: 'Speak.' It said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded.﴾" It is also narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "When a servant performs wuḍūʾ (ablution) well, prays the prayer at its proper time, and maintains its bowings, prostrations, and appointed times, the prayer says: 'May God preserve you as you have preserved me,' and it intercedes for its companion. But if he neglects it, it says: 'May God neglect you as you neglected me,' and it is wrapped up like a worn-out garment and struck against the face of its companion." **Answer:** As for the speech of the Garden, the meaning is that it was prepared for the believers, so this became like a statement from it. This is like His saying, Most High: ﴿They said: "We come willingly."﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 11]. As for His creating the Garden "with His hand," the meaning is that He Himself undertook its creation, not that He delegated it to another. As for the claim that prayer praises whoever fulfils its rights, this is even further from being permissible than the speech of the Garden, because prayer consists of movements and stillnesses, and it is not possible for it to form an image or speak. Therefore the meaning is a figure of speech, as when someone says to a benefactor: "Your kindness to me speaks in gratitude."

**Question 7:** Does the verse indicate that Paradise (al-Firdaws) is created? **Answer:** Al-Qadi said: His saying, Most High, ﴿its fruit is perpetual﴾ [al-Raʿd: 35] indicates that it is not created, so this verse must be interpreted. It is as if He Most High said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, God will create the Garden as an inheritance for the believers," or: "When He creates it, it will speak," following the same pattern by which we interpreted His saying, Most High: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 50]. This is weak, because the supposition of what he mentioned in this verse is no more preferable than supposing it in His saying: ﴿its fruit is perpetual.﴾ Moreover, its fruit is perpetual on the Day of Resurrection. When these two apparent meanings conflict, we rely, in holding that the Garden is created, on His saying, Most High: ﴿It has been prepared for the God-fearing﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 133].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 23, verse 12–16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay.﴾ ﴿Then We made him a sperm-drop in a firm lodging.﴾ ﴿Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot, then We made the clot into a lump of flesh, then We made the lump into bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is God, the best of creators.﴾ ﴿Then indeed you, after that, are to die.﴾ ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be raised up.﴾

Page 74

Know that when He, glory be to Him, commanded acts of worship in the preceding verse, and devotion to God is not valid except after knowing the Creator God, He therefore followed it with mention of that which indicates His existence and His being described by the attributes of majesty and oneness. He mentioned several kinds of proofs:

The first kind: the argument from the changing of man through the stages of creation and the states of nature, and these are nine.

The first stage: His saying, glorified and exalted: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay.﴾ The sulalah (extract) is the essence, because it is extracted from among the turbidity; it is fu'alah, a pattern indicating smallness, like qulamah and qumamah (parings and sweepings). The exegetes differed concerning "man" (al-insan). Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah and Muqatil said: what is meant is Adam, peace be upon him. Adam was extracted from clay, and his offspring were created from a despised fluid. Then the pronoun is taken to refer to "man" who is the son of Adam, and "man" includes Adam, peace be upon him, and his offspring. Others said: "man" here is the son of Adam, and "clay" here is the name of Adam, peace be upon him, and the sulalah is the clay-parts scattered in his limbs which, when they gathered and came to be in the vessels of semen, became semen. This interpretation agrees with His saying, exalted: ﴿And He began the creation of man from clay. Then He made his offspring from an extract of a despised fluid.﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7, 8]. There is another aspect to it: that man is only generated from the sperm-drop, and the sperm-drop is only generated from the surplus of the fourth digestion; that comes only from foods, which are either animal or vegetable; animal food ends in vegetable food, and vegetation is only generated from the purest of the earth and water. So man is in reality generated from an extract of clay. Then that extract, after passing through the stages of creation and the states of nature, becomes semen. This interpretation agrees with the wording and does not require far-fetched assumptions.

The second stage: His saying, exalted: ﴿Then We made him a sperm-drop in a firm lodging.﴾ The meaning of making man a sperm-drop is that He created the substance of man first as clay, then after that made his substance a sperm-drop in the loins of fathers; then the loins ejected it through intercourse into the womb of the woman, and the womb became a firm lodging for this sperm-drop. By qarar (lodging) is meant the place of rest, the settled place; He named it by the verbal noun, then described the womb with the firmness which is the attribute of what settles in it, as in your saying "a traveled road" (ṭarīq sā'ir); or because of its firmness in itself, since it is firm in its own right and secured.

The third stage: His saying, exalted: ﴿Then We made the sperm-drop into a clinging clot﴾, meaning: We transformed the sperm-drop from its attributes into the attributes of the clot, which is congealed blood.

Then the pronoun is taken to refer to "man" who is the son of Adam, and "man" includes Adam, peace be upon him, and his offspring. Others said: "man" here is the son of Adam, and "clay" here is the name of Adam, peace be upon him, and the sulalah is the clay-parts scattered in his limbs which, when they gathered and came to be in the vessels of semen, became semen. When he reached His saying: ﴿another creation﴾ he marveled at it and said: "So blessed is God, the best of creators." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Write, for thus was it revealed." ʿAbd Allah then doubted and said: "If Muhammad is truthful in what he says, then it is revealed to me as it is revealed to him; and if he is lying, then there is no good in his religion," so he fled to Mecca. It was said: he died upon disbelief. It was said: he embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest. Saʿid ibn Jubayr related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: when this verse was revealed, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "So blessed is God, the best of creators." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Thus was it revealed, O ʿUmar." ʿUmar used to say: "My Lord agreed with me in four matters: regarding prayer behind the maqam, regarding the veiling of the wives, my saying to them: 'Desist, or else God will substitute for them better than you,' and then there was revealed His saying: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will substitute for him wives better than you﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5]; and the fourth: I said: ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators,﴾ and he said: 'Thus was it revealed.'" The knowers said: this incident was the cause of happiness for ʿUmar and the cause of wretchedness for ʿAbd Allah, as He, exalted, said: ﴿He leads many astray by it and guides many by it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]. If it is said: in all the reports, humans have spoken at the outset with the like of the Qur'anic composition, and that impairs its being miraculous, as ʿAbd Allah supposed. The answer: this is not improbable when the amount is of the degree at which the miraculous quality does not appear in it, so the doubt of ʿAbd Allah falls away.

Fourth stage: His saying: ﴿Then indeed you, after that, are to die.﴾ Ibn Abi ʿAblah and Ibn Muhaysin read lamā'itūn. The difference between mayyit and mā'it is that mayyit, like ḥayy (living), is a stable attribute, whereas mā'it indicates occurrence: you say "Zayd is mayyit now" and "mā'it tomorrow," and like your saying yamūtu (he dies) and similar; ḍayyiq and ḍā'iq in His saying: ﴿and your breast is constrained by it﴾ [Hud: 12].

Ninth stage: His saying: ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be raised up.﴾ So God, glory be to Him, made the causing to die, which is the annihilation of life, and the resurrection, which is the restoration of what annihilates and destroys it, two further proofs of great power after the initiation and origination.

* * *

Here are some questions:

First question: What is the wisdom in death? Why did He not connect the bliss of the Hereafter and its reward with the bliss of this world, so that it would be more complete as a favor? The answer: this is like a corruption with respect to those who are obligated, for whenever reward is hastened to a person for what he bears of hardship in acts of obedience, his performing the acts of obedience becomes for the sake of those benefits and not for the sake of obeying God. This is shown by the fact that if it were said to one who prays and fasts: "If you do that, we will admit you to Paradise immediately," he would perform that act only seeking Paradise. Therefore God, exalted, deferred it and delayed it through causing to die and then restoring, so that the servant may worship his Lord through obedience to Him and not for the sake of seeking benefit.

Second question: This verse indicates the negation of the punishment of the grave, for He said: ﴿Then indeed you, after that, are to die﴾ and ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be raised up,﴾ and did not mention between the two matters the revival in the grave. The answer is in two respects.

First: in mentioning the two lives there is no negation of a third.

Second: the purpose is to mention the three kinds: origination, causing to die, and restoration, and what was left out of mention is the kind of restoration [in the grave].

**The second type of evidence: reasoning from the creation of the heavens.** This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have created above you seven paths, and We were never unaware of creation.﴾

His saying ﴿seven paths﴾ means seven heavens. They are called *tara'iq* (paths) because they are layered (*tatariquha*), meaning that some of them are above others.

Page 77

It is said: *tarraqa al-rajul na'layhi* (the man placed one sandal over the other) when he fits one sandal on top of another, and *tarraqa bayna thawbayn* (he layered between two garments) when he wears one garment over another. This is the view of al-Khalil (Ibn Ahmad), al-Zajjaj and al-Farra'. Al-Zajjaj said: it is like His saying, ﴿seven heavens in layers﴾ (al-Mulk: 3). Ali ibn Isa said: they were named so because they are paths for the angels in their ascent, descent and flight. Others said: because they are the paths of the stars, where the stars travel. As for the manner in which this is a blessing upon us, it is that He made them a place for our provision, by sending down water from them, made them a dwelling for the angels, because they are the place of reward, and because they are the place from which prophets are sent and revelation descends.

As for His saying, ﴿and We were never unaware of creation﴾, there are several interpretations.

First: "We were not unaware, rather We were guarding the creation from the seven paths falling upon them and destroying them." This is the view of Sufyan ibn Uyayna, and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ (Fatir: 41).

Second: "We created them above them only so that We might send down provision and blessings upon them from them." This is from al-Hasan.

Third: "We created these things, and our creating them indicates the perfection of Our power. Then He explained the perfection of knowledge by His saying, ﴿and We were never unaware of creation﴾, meaning, of their deeds, their words and their hearts, and this conveys the utmost deterrence."

Fourth: "And We were never unaware of the creation of the heavens, rather We are their guardians, so that they do not depart from the measure We intended for them," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no imperfection﴾ (al-Mulk: 3).

Know that this verse indicates many matters.

The first: it indicates the existence of the Creator. The transformation of these bodies from one attribute to another that is opposed to the first, while it was possible for them to remain in that former attribute, indicates that there must be a transformer and changer.

The second: it indicates the invalidity of the claim that things come about by nature (*tabi'a*). If any of those attributes came about by nature, it would be necessary for them to persist and not change. And if you say that those attributes changed because that nature changed, then that nature requires a creator and originator.

The third: it indicates that the Governor is powerful and knowing, because these wonderful acts do not proceed from a being that acts by necessity (*mujib*) or from an ignorant one.

The fourth: it indicates that He is knowing of all that is known and powerful over all that is possible.

The fifth: it indicates the possibility of resurrection and gathering, both by the explicit wording of the verse and by the reasoning that, since the Agent is powerful over all that is possible and knowing of all that is known, it is necessary that He be able to reassemble the components into their former composition.

The sixth: the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, must be attained through reasoning and not through blind imitation (*taqlid*); otherwise, the mention of these proofs would be pointless.

**The third type: reasoning from the descent of rain and the manner of its effect on plants.**

[Page 78]

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And We sent down water from the sky in measure, and We caused it to settle in the earth; and indeed, We are able to take it away.﴾ ﴿Then We produced for you thereby gardens of palm trees and grapevines; for you therein are abundant fruits, and from them you eat.﴾ ﴿And a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai, which grows with oil and a condiment for those who eat.﴾

Know that water in itself is a blessing, and that, in addition to this, it is a cause for the attainment of other blessings. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, mentioned it first, and then mentioned what is attained through it of blessings.

As for His words, ﴿And We sent down water from the sky in measure﴾, the commentators differ concerning "the sky." Most of the exegetes said: Allah, the Exalted, truly sends down the water from the sky, and this is the apparent meaning of the wording. This is confirmed by His words: ﴿And in the sky is your provision and what you are promised﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 22]. Others said: the intended meaning is the clouds, and it was called "sky" because of its height. The meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, raised the watery particles from the depths of the earth to the seas, and from the seas to the sky, until they became sweet and pure because of that elevation. Then those particles come together and form (clouds), and then Allah, the Exalted, sends them down in proportion to the need for them. Had it not been for this, those waters would not have been benefited from, because they would be scattered in the depths of the earth, nor would the water of the seas (be benefited from), because of its saltiness, and because there is no means of channeling the waters of the seas over the surface of the earth, since the seas are the lowest point in depth. Know that these explanations are only contrived by one who denies the Chooser who acts by choice. As for one who affirms Him, he has no need for any of them.

As for His words, ﴿in measure﴾, its meaning is: in a measure by which they are safe from harm and reach benefit in planting, sowing, and drinking; or in the quantity We know to be their needs and their interests.

As for His words, ﴿and We caused it to settle in the earth﴾, it was said: its meaning is: We made it firm in the earth. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: Allah, the Exalted, sent down from Paradise five rivers: Sayhun, Jayhun, the Tigris (Dijlah), the Euphrates (al-Furat), and the Nile, and then He will lift them up at the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, and He will also lift up the Qur'an.

As for His words, ﴿and indeed, We are able to take it away﴾, that is: just as We were able to send it down, so too We are able to lift it up and remove it. The author of al-Kashshaf said: His words ﴿to take it away﴾ — the indefinite nouns (nakirat) were placed first and delayed for emphasis. The meaning is: in one of the ways of taking it away and one of its routes. In this there is an indication of the perfect power of the One who takes it away, and that nothing is difficult for Him, and it is more eloquent in warning than His words: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, then who will bring you flowing water?﴾ [al-Mulk: 30]. Then, when He, glory be to Him, drew attention to the great blessing of creating water, He mentioned after it the blessings that come from water, saying: ﴿Then We produced for you thereby gardens of palm trees and grapevines﴾. Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the palm trees and grapevines only because of the abundance of their benefits, for they stand in the place of food, in the place of condiment, and in the place of fruits, fresh and dried. As for His words, ﴿for you therein are abundant fruits﴾, that is: in the gardens. Just as in them are palm trees and grapevines, so in them are abundant fruits. As for His words, ﴿and from them you eat﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: It is possible that this is from their saying: "So-and-so eats from a trade he practices and from a craft he works," meaning that this is his sustenance and his direction from which he obtains his provision. It is as if He said: These gardens are the means of your provision and your livelihood; from them you make your living.

As for His words, ﴿and a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai﴾, it is coordinated with (gardens) and was also read in the nominative case as a beginning (mubtada', the grammatical subject), meaning: and among what We produced for you is a tree. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Tur Sinai" and "Tur Sinin": the word "tur" in it either is attached to a place called Sina'/Sinin, or it is the name of a mountain composed of a construct (mudaf) and a second term (mudaf ilayhi), like Imru' al-Qays and Ba'labakk according to those who make it an idafa. Whoever pronounces the sin of Sina' with a kasra has made it not take tanwin, due to definiteness and foreignness or the feminine, because it is a place, and fa'la' does not have its alif as a feminine marker, like 'ulba' and harba'. Whoever pronounces it with a fatha has not made it take tanwin, because its alif is a feminine marker like sahra'. It was said: it is the mountain of Palestine. It was said: it is between Egypt and Aylah, and from it Musa, peace be upon him, was called. Al-A'mash read it as (Sina) with qasr (short vowel).

As for His words, ﴿grows with oil﴾, it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: it grows while in it is oil, just as one says: "The commander rode with his army," meaning: with him was the army. It was read as (tunbitu), and in this there are two possibilities.

One: that anbata has the meaning of nabata, as Zuhayr said:

"I saw those in need around their dwellings, settled there, until the herbage sprouted."

The second: its object is omitted, meaning: it produces its olives, and in it is the oil. The exegetes said: Allah, the Exalted, attributed it to this mountain because from it (the tree) spread and dispersed throughout the lands, and because most of it is there. As for His words, ﴿and a condiment for those who eat﴾, it is coordinated with "oil," meaning: a condiment for those who eat. Ṣibgh and ṣibāgh are that in which something is dipped, meaning: bread is dipped in it. The summary of the matter is that He, glory be to Him and exalted, drew attention to His kindness through this tree, because it produces this fruit which is widely benefited from, both when it is fresh and when it is stored, and by being pressed so that the oil appears from it, and the ways of benefiting from it are greatly multiplied.

The fourth type: reasoning from the states of animals.

﴿And indeed in livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink of what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat﴾ ﴿and upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And indeed in livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink of what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat﴾ ﴿and upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾

Know that He, glorified and exalted, mentioned that there is a lesson in them in summary, then followed it with detail from four aspects.

The first: His saying, ﴿We give you to drink of what is in their bellies﴾. What is meant by it is all the ways of benefiting from their milk. The aspect of lesson in it is that it gathers in the udders and is separated from between the digesta and the blood by God's permission, and it turns into purity, into a color and taste agreeable to appetite, and becomes nourishment. So whoever reasons from this to the power and wisdom of God, this is counted among the religious blessings, and whoever benefits from it is in the blessing of this world. Also, these milks that pass from their bellies to their udders, you find them a good drink, and when you slaughter them you find no trace of them, and that indicates the great power of God, exalted. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it was also read as "tusqīkum" with an open tā', meaning: the livestock give you to drink.

The second: His saying, ﴿and for you in them are many benefits﴾, and that is by selling them, benefiting from their prices, and what goes in that direction.

The third: His saying, ﴿and from them you eat﴾, meaning: just as you benefit from them while they are alive, you also benefit from them after slaughter by eating.

The fourth: His saying, ﴿and upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾, because the aspect of benefit from camels in carrying loads on land is like the benefit from the ship at sea. For this reason He combined the two aspects in His bounty, so that He may be thanked for it and that it may be reasoned from.

The fourth type: reasoning from the states of animals.

﴿And indeed in livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink of what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat﴾ ﴿and upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And indeed in livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink of what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat﴾ ﴿and upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾

Know that He, glorified and exalted, mentioned that there is a lesson in them in summary, then followed it with detail from four aspects.

The first: His saying, ﴿We give you to drink of what is in their bellies﴾. What is meant by it is all the ways of benefiting from their milk. The aspect of lesson in it is that it gathers in the udders and is separated from between the digesta and the blood by God's permission, and it turns into purity, into a color and taste agreeable to appetite, and becomes nourishment. So whoever reasons from this to the power and wisdom of God, this is counted among the religious blessings, and whoever benefits from it is in the blessing of this world. Also, these milks that pass from their bellies to their udders, you find them a good drink, and when you slaughter them you find no trace of them, and that indicates the great power of God, exalted. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it was also read as "tusqīkum" with an open tā', meaning: the livestock give you to drink.

The second: His saying, ﴿and for you in them are many benefits﴾, and that is by selling them, benefiting from their prices, and what goes in that direction.

The third: His saying, ﴿and from them you eat﴾, meaning: just as you benefit from them while they are alive, you also benefit from them after slaughter by eating.

The fourth: His saying, ﴿and upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾, because the aspect of benefit from camels in carrying loads on land is like the benefit from the ship at sea. For this reason He combined the two aspects in His bounty, so that He may be thanked for it and that it may be reasoned from.

**The first story: the story of Nuh (Noah), peace be upon him**

﴿And We indeed sent Nuh to his people, and he said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?" So the chiefs who disbelieved among his people said, "This is none but a man like you who wants to make himself superior over you. And if Allah had willed, He would have sent down angels. We never heard of this among our forefathers of old." "He is but a man in whom there is madness, so wait for him for a while."﴾

So the chiefs who disbelieved among his people said, "This is none but a man like you who wants to make himself superior over you. And if Allah had willed, He would have sent down angels. We never heard of this among our forefathers of old." "He is but a man in whom there is madness, so wait for him for a while."﴾

Some people said: Nuh's name was Yashkur, and then he was named Nuh for several reasons:

The first: because of how much he wailed (naha) over himself when he prayed against his people for destruction, and Allah destroyed them with the flood, and he regretted that.

The second: because of his returning to his Lord (muraja'a) concerning his son.

The third: that he passed by a mangy dog and said to it, "Begone, you ugly one!" He was rebuked for this, and Allah said to him, "Did you find fault with Me when I created it, or did you find fault with the dog?"

These reasons are problematic, because it is established that proper names do not convey a description of the one named.

As for His saying ﴿worship Allah﴾, the meaning is that He, glorified is He, sent him to call people to worship Allah, the Exalted, alone. It is not permissible for him to call them to this unless he had first called them to knowing Him, because worship of one who is not known is not permissible; it is permissible and obligatory only after knowledge.

As for His saying ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾, the meaning is that worship of other than Allah is not permissible, since there is no god besides Him. It is part of the due of worship that it be offered to the One who has bestowed creation, life and what follows them. So if these things are not possible except from Him, the Exalted, how could one worship what neither harms nor benefits? The word ﴿ghayruhu﴾ ("other than Him") has been read in the nominative (raf') according to its position (mahall), and in the genitive (jarr) according to its wording (lafz).

Then, when this call did not benefit them and they persisted in worshipping other than Allah, the Exalted, He warned them with His saying ﴿Will you not then fear Him?﴾, because this is a deterrent and a threat, urging them to guard against punishment so that they would turn away from what they were upon.

Then He, glorified is He, related their doubts concerning their denial of the prophethood of Nuh, peace be upon him.

**The first doubt:** their saying ﴿This is none but a man like you﴾. This doubt may bear two meanings:

One of them: it may be said that since he was equal to the rest of people in strength, understanding, knowledge, wealth and poverty, health and sickness, it was impossible for him to be a messenger of Allah, because a messenger must be great in the sight of Allah, the Exalted, and beloved to Him, and the beloved must be distinguished from other than the beloved by greater rank and honour. So when these qualities were absent, we know that prophethood is negated.

The second: it may be said that this man shares all matters with you, but he loved leadership and being followed, and he found no way to them except by claiming prophethood. So this became a doubt for them in disparaging his prophethood. This meaning is confirmed by the Exalted's report about them: ﴿who wants to make himself superior over you﴾, that is, he wants to seek superiority over you and to lead you, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and that you two may have grandeur in the land﴾ [Yunus: 78].

[p. 81]

**The second doubt:** their saying ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾. Its explanation: if Allah, the Exalted, had willed to guide mankind, He would have had to take the way that leads more directly to the goal. It is known that sending angels leads more directly to this goal than sending humans, because angels, due to their elevated station, their great might and their abundant knowledge, would be obeyed by creation, and people would not doubt their messengership. Since He did not do that, we know that He never sent a messenger at all.

**The third doubt:** their saying ﴿We never heard of this among our forefathers of old﴾. The word ﴿this﴾ refers either to Nuh, peace be upon him, or to what he spoke to them of urging the worship of Allah, the Exalted; that is, "We never heard of such speech, or of such a thing as this man claims, being a human being, that he is the messenger of Allah." The explanation of this doubt is that they were peoples who relied, in nothing of their doctrines, except on imitation (taqlid) and on returning to the sayings of their fathers. So when they did not find in the prophethood of Nuh, peace be upon him, this path, they judged it to be false. Al-Qadi said: It may be that they meant by this his being a sent messenger, because it is not impossible that in the times of their fathers there was a period without prophets (fatra), and it may be that they meant by this his calling them to worship Allah alone, because their fathers were worshipping idols.

**The fourth doubt:** their saying ﴿He is but a man in whom there is madness﴾. The word jinnah means either madness or jinn. The ignorant common people say of a madman: his mind has departed by the action of jinn. This doubt is a means of deceiving the common people, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to do deeds contrary to their customs, so those chiefs would say to the common people: he is mad, and one who is mad, how could he be a messenger?

**The fifth doubt:** their saying ﴿so wait for him for a while﴾. This may be connected to what precedes it, meaning: he is mad, so be patient with him until a time when the outcome of his affair becomes clear; if he regains his reason, well and good, otherwise you will kill him. It may also be an independent statement, that they say to their people: be patient, for if he is truly a prophet, Allah will support him and strengthen his cause, and then we will follow him; and if he is a liar, Allah will forsake him and nullify his affair, and then we will be relieved of him.

These are the sum of the doubts which Allah, the Exalted, related from them.

Know that He, glorified is He, did not mention the answers to them, because of their weakness and the clarity of their falsity. This is because every intelligent person knows that a messenger does not become a messenger by being of the same kind as an angel; he becomes so only by being distinguished from others by miracles. So whether he is of the angelic kind or of the human kind, when a miracle appears through him, he must be a messenger. Rather, making the messenger one of mankind is better, for the reason already explained in the earlier surahs, namely that kinship is the source of familiarity and companionship.

As for their saying ﴿who wants to make himself superior over you﴾: if they meant by it his desire to show his excellence so that they would be bound to obey him, this is obligatory upon a messenger. If they meant by it that he would rise above them by way of tyranny and arrogance, and that they should submit, then the prophets are free of that.

As for their saying "We never heard of this": it is an argument from the absence of taqlid to the absence of the thing itself, and it is extremely weak, because the absence of taqlid does not indicate the non-existence of a thing; so how could its non-existence indicate its non-existence?

As for their saying "he has jinnah": they lied, because they knew by necessity his perfect intellect.

As for their saying "so wait for him": it is weak, because if the proof of his prophethood appeared, which is the miracle, it would be obligatory upon them to accept his word immediately, and it is not permissible to delay that until his state of power (dawlah) appears, because power does not indicate truth. And if the miracle did not appear, it would not be permissible to accept his word, whether his power appeared or not.

Since these answers are wholly evident, Allah, glorified is He, has indeed left them out.

His saying, ﴿He said, "My Lord, help me, for they have denied me."﴾ ﴿So We revealed to him, "Build the ark under Our eyes and by Our revelation. When Our command comes and the oven boils over, load into it a pair of every kind, two, and your family, except those against whom the word has already gone forth. And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned."﴾ ﴿So when you and those with you have settled upon the ark, say, "Praise be to Allah, who has delivered us from the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."﴾ ﴿Indeed in that are signs, and indeed We were ever testing.﴾

As for His saying, ﴿"My Lord, help me, for they have denied me,"﴾ there are several interpretations:

The first: in His helping him is their destruction, as if he had said, "Destroy them because of their denial of me."

The second: "Help me in place of what they denied me," as you say, "This is in place of that," meaning, "This is a substitute for that and in its stead." The meaning is: "Replace for me the grief of their denial with the consolation of victory over them."

The third: "Help me by fulfilling what You promised them of punishment, which is what they denied when he said to them, ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ [al-A'raf: 59]." When Allah answered his supplication, He said, ﴿So We revealed to him, "Build the ark under Our eyes,"﴾ meaning under Our protection and watch, as if he had with him from Allah a guardian who keeps him under his eye, so that no one would confront him or spoil his work. From this is their saying, "He is under a sleepless watch from Allah." This verse also refutes the view of the anthropomorphists (al-Mushabbihah) who cling to His, peace be upon him, saying: "Indeed Allah created Adam in His image," because the affirmation of eyes prevents that. They differed about how he, peace be upon him, built the ark. It was said: he was a carpenter and knew how to make it. It was also said: Jibril, peace be upon him, taught him the work of the ship and described to him how to build it. This is the closer view, because of His saying, ﴿under Our eyes and Our revelation.﴾

As for His saying, ﴿When Our command comes,﴾ know that the word "command" (amr), just as it is literally used for requesting an action by speech in a position of authority, is also literally used for a great matter. The proof of this is that when you say, "This is an amr," the mind keeps vacillating between the two meanings, which indicates that it is literal in both. The full argument is mentioned in the book al-Mahsul fi al-Usul (The Harvest in the Principles of Jurisprudence). Some people said: he called it "amr" only for the sake of glorification and magnification, like His saying, ﴿So He said to it and to the earth, "Come, willingly or unwillingly"﴾ [Fussilat: 11].

As for His saying, ﴿and the oven boiled over,﴾ they differed about the tannur (oven). Most hold that it is the well-known oven. It is narrated that it was said to Nuh: "When you see the water gushing out of the oven, board the ship, you and those with you." He commanded him to supplicate for himself, saying, ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing place."﴾ It was read as "manzalan" (with a fatha on the mim), meaning inzalan (a causing to land), or the place of landing, like His saying: ﴿He will surely admit them to an entrance with which they will be pleased﴾ [al-Hajj: 59]. As for the manner of the call, it is as was mentioned earlier in the story of Noah, peace be upon him. Here there are several questions.

**The first question:** The verb *arsala* ("to send") should take *ila* ("to"), like its counterparts *wajjaha* ("to direct"), *anfadha* ("to dispatch") and *ba'atha* ("to send forth"). Why, then, is it construed in the Qur'an sometimes with *ila* and sometimes with *fi* ("in"), as in His saying: ﴿Thus We sent you to a community﴾ [al-Ra'd: 30], ﴿We did not send into any town﴾ [al-A'raf: 94], ﴿So We sent among them a messenger﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 32], meaning among 'Ad, and in another place: ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud﴾ [al-A'raf: 65]?

The answer: it was not construed with *fi* in the same way it was construed with *ila*. Rather, the community or the town was made the place of the sending. On this meaning *ba'atha* came in His saying: ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised in every town a warner﴾ [al-Furqan: 51].

**The second question:** Is it correct what some of them said, that His saying: ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾ is not connected to the first statement, and that he only said it to them after they had denied him, and had rejected him after the proof had been established against them? Then at that point he said to them, warning them about what they were engaged in: ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾ [meaning] this way, for fear of the punishment with which I have warned you?

The answer: it is possible that it is connected to the first statement, in that he saw them turning away from the worship of Allah and occupied with the worship of idols, so he called them to the worship of Allah and warned them of punishment because of their devotion to the worship of idols.

Then know that Allah, exalted is He, related the attributes of those people and related their speech. As for the attributes, they are three, and they are the worst of attributes:
- The first is disbelief in the Creator, glorified is He, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿who disbelieved﴾.
- The second is disbelief in the Day of Resurrection, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and denied the meeting of the Hereafter﴾.
- The third is immersion in love of this world and its desires, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and to whom We had granted luxury in the life of this world﴾, that is: We made them prosperous.

If it is said: Allah mentioned the saying of the people of Hud in response to him in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Hud without a *wa* (conjunction): ﴿The chiefs of those who disbelieved among his people said: "Indeed, we see you in folly"﴾ [al-A'raf: 66], and ﴿We do not see you except as a human being like us﴾ [Hud: 27]. And here it is with the *wa*. So what is the difference between them?

We say: the one without *wa* is on the assumption of a questioner who said: "What did his people say?" and it was answered: "Such and such." As for the one with *wa*, it is a conjunction of what they said to what he said, and its meaning is that in this event there gathered this true statement and this false statement.

As for the doubts of the people, there are two:

The first is their saying: ﴿This is none but a human being like you. He eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾, and the explanation of this doubt has already passed in the first story. His saying: ﴿of what you drink﴾, that is: of your drink; or it is elided from it because what precedes it indicates it, which is His saying: ﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves, then you would indeed be losers.﴾ So they made following the messenger a loss, but they did not make worshipping idols a loss. That is: if you have given him obedience without there being any benefit for you in return, then that is the loss.

The second: they criticized the soundness of the gathering (*hashr*) and the resurrection (*nashr*), and then they criticized his prophethood because of his bringing that. As for their criticism of the soundness of the gathering, it is their saying: ﴿Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ — meaning, you will be returned alive for recompense. Then they did not limit themselves to this degree, until they combined with it a great astonishment, which is their saying: ﴿Far, far is what you are promised!﴾ Then they reinforced the doubt with their saying: ﴿There is only our life of this world: we die and we live﴾. They did not mean by their saying "we die and we live" a single person, but rather they meant that some die and some live, and that there is no return and no gathering. Therefore they said: ﴿and we will not be resurrected.﴾ When they had finished criticizing the soundness of the gathering, they built upon it a criticism of his prophethood. They said: since he has brought this falsehood, he has invented a lie against Allah. Then, when they had established the doubt that criticized his prophethood, they said: ﴿and we are not going to believe him﴾, because the people were like followers to them.

Know that Allah, exalted is He, did not answer these two doubts, because their corruption is evident. As for the first doubt, its weakness has already been explained. As for the second, they considered the gathering improbable, and the gathering is not improbable, for two reasons.

The first: since He, glorified is He, is able over all possibilities and knows all knowables, it is necessary that He be able to gather and resurrect.

The second: if there were no return, then the subjugation of the strong over the weak in this world would be injustice, and this is not fitting for the Wise, as He established, glorified is He, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15].

Here are some issues:

**First issue:** *Inna* is repeated (*innakum*) for emphasis, and the separation between the first and the second by the adverbial phrase made it good. *Mukhrajun* ("brought forth") is the predicate of the first. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and you were dust and bones, brought forth."

**Second issue:** *Hayhat* ("far") is read with *fath* and *kasr*, all with and without tanwin, and with sukun following the pause form.

**Third issue:** In His saying: ﴿There is only our life of this world﴾, *hiya* is a pronoun whose referent is not known except through what follows it as an explanation. Its original form is: "*in al-hayatu illa hayatuna al-dunya*" (there is no life but our life of this world). Then *hiya* was placed in the position of *al-hayat* ("life") because the predicate indicates it. From this is the saying of the poet:
"She is the soul; whatever you load upon her, she bears."
The meaning is: there is no life but this life. And because the negating *in* entered upon *hiya*, which has the meaning of "life" and indicates the genus, it negated it, and so it matched *la* ("no"), which negates what follows it as a negation of the genus.

Know that when that messenger despaired of acceptance from the eminent and the humble, he turned to his Lord and said: ﴿My Lord, support me, for they have denied me.﴾ Its explanation has already passed. Allah answered him in what he asked, and said: ﴿In a little while they will surely become regretful.﴾ The closest view is that what is meant is that the signs of their destruction would appear to them; at that point regret and remorse for not accepting would arise in them, and the time would be the time of the faith of despair, so they would not benefit from the regret. Allah, exalted is He, explained the destruction He sent down upon them with His saying: ﴿So the Blast seized them in truth.﴾ And they mentioned several views about the Blast:

First: Gabriel, peace be upon him, cried out at them, and the cry was so great that they died at it.

Second: the Blast is the earthquake, according to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both.

Third: the Blast is the very punishment and death, as is said of one who dies: "He was called and he answered." This is from al-Hasan.

Fourth: it is the annihilating punishment. The poet said:

(Page 87)

"Time cried out at the family of Barmak with a cry; they fell prostrate on their chins from its severity."

The first view is the better, because it is the literal meaning.

As for His saying: ﴿in truth﴾, its meaning is that He destroyed them with justice, from your saying: "So-and-so judges with truth," when he is just in his judgments. Al-Mufaddal said: "in truth" means: with what cannot be repelled, like His saying: ﴿And the agony of death came in truth﴾ [Qaf: 19].

As for His saying: ﴿So We made them debris﴾, *ghuthaʾ* is the debris carried by the torrent of what has decayed and turned black of leaves and sticks, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He made it dark-brown debris﴾ [al-A'la: 5].

Why, then, is it construed in the Qur'an sometimes with *ila* and sometimes with *fi* ("in"), as in His saying: ﴿Thus We sent you to a community﴾ [al-Ra'd: 30], ﴿We did not send into any town﴾ [al-A'raf: 94], ﴿So We sent among them a messenger﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 32], meaning among 'Ad, and in another place: ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud﴾ [al-A'raf: 65]?

The answer: it was not construed with *fi* in the same way it was construed with *ila*. Rather, the community or the town was made the place of the sending. On this meaning *ba'atha* came in His saying: ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised in every town a warner﴾ [al-Furqan: 51].

Then at that point he said to them, warning them about what they were engaged in: ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾ [meaning] this way, for fear of the punishment with which I have warned you?

The answer: it is possible that it is connected to the first statement, in that he saw them turning away from the worship of Allah and occupied with the worship of idols, so he called them to the worship of Allah and warned them of punishment because of their devotion to the worship of idols.

Then know that Allah, exalted is He, related the attributes of those people and related their speech. As for the attributes, they are three, and they are the worst of attributes:
- The first is disbelief in the Creator, glorified is He, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿who disbelieved﴾.
- The second is disbelief in the Day of Resurrection, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and denied the meeting of the Hereafter﴾.
- The third is immersion in love of this world and its desires, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and to whom We had granted luxury in the life of this world﴾, that is: We made them prosperous.

If it is said: Allah mentioned the saying of the people of Hud in response to him in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Hud without a *wa* (conjunction): ﴿The chiefs of those who disbelieved among his people said: "Indeed, we see you in folly"﴾ [al-A'raf: 66], and ﴿We do not see you except as a human being like us﴾ [Hud: 27]. And here it is with the *wa*. So what is the difference between them?

We say: the one without *wa* is on the assumption of a questioner who said: "What did his people say?" and it was answered: "Such and such." As for the one with *wa*, it is a conjunction of what they said to what he said, and its meaning is that in this event there gathered this true statement and this false statement.

As for the doubts of the people, there are two:

The first is their saying: ﴿This is none but a human being like you. He eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾, and the explanation of this doubt has already passed in the first story. His saying: ﴿of what you drink﴾, that is: of your drink; or it is elided from it because what precedes it indicates it, which is His saying: ﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves, then you would indeed be losers.﴾ So they made following the messenger a loss, but they did not make worshipping idols a loss. That is: if you have given him obedience without there being any benefit for you in return, then that is the loss.

The second: they criticized the soundness of the gathering (*hashr*) and the resurrection (*nashr*), and then they criticized his prophethood because of his bringing that. As for their criticism of the soundness of the gathering, it is their saying: ﴿Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ — meaning, you will be returned alive for recompense. Then they did not limit themselves to this degree, until they combined with it a great astonishment, which is their saying: ﴿Far, far is what you are promised!﴾ Then they reinforced the doubt with their saying: ﴿There is only our life of this world: we die and we live﴾. They did not mean by their saying "we die and we live" a single person, but rather they meant that some die and some live, and that there is no return and no gathering. Therefore they said: ﴿and we will not be resurrected.﴾ When they had finished criticizing the soundness of the gathering, they built upon it a criticism of his prophethood. They said: since he has brought this falsehood, he has invented a lie against Allah. Then, when they had established the doubt that criticized his prophethood, they said: ﴿and we are not going to believe him﴾, because the people were like followers to them.

Know that Allah, exalted is He, did not answer these two doubts, because their corruption is evident. As for the first doubt, its weakness has already been explained. As for the second, they considered the gathering improbable, and the gathering is not improbable, for two reasons.

The first: since He, glorified is He, is able over all possibilities and knows all knowables, it is necessary that He be able to gather and resurrect.

The second: if there were no return, then the subjugation of the strong over the weak in this world would be injustice, and this is not fitting for the Wise, as He established, glorified is He, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15].

Here are some issues:

**First issue:** *Inna* is repeated (*innakum*) for emphasis, and the separation between the first and the second by the adverbial phrase made it good. *Mukhrajun* ("brought forth") is the predicate of the first. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and you were dust and bones, brought forth."

**Second issue:** *Hayhat* ("far") is read with *fath* and *kasr*, all with and without tanwin, and with sukun following the pause form.

Its original form is: "*in al-hayatu illa hayatuna al-dunya*" (there is no life but our life of this world). Then *hiya* was placed in the position of *al-hayat* ("life") because the predicate indicates it. From this is the saying of the poet:
"She is the soul; whatever you load upon her, she bears."
The meaning is: there is no life but this life. And because the negating *in* entered upon *hiya*, which has the meaning of "life" and indicates the genus, it negated it, and so it matched *la* ("no"), which negates what follows it as a negation of the genus.

Second: the Blast is the earthquake, according to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both.

Third: the Blast is the very punishment and death, as is said of one who dies: "He was called and he answered." This is from al-Hasan.

Fourth: it is the annihilating punishment. The poet said:

**The first question:** The verb *arsala* ("to send") should take *ila* ("to"), like its counterparts *wajjaha* ("to direct"), *anfadha* ("to dispatch") and *ba'atha* ("to send forth"). Why, then, is it construed in the Qur'an sometimes with *ila* and sometimes with *fi* ("in"), as in His saying: ﴿Thus We sent you to a community﴾ [al-Ra'd: 30], ﴿We did not send into any town﴾ [al-A'raf: 94], ﴿So We sent among them a messenger﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 32], meaning among 'Ad, and in another place: ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud﴾ [al-A'raf: 65]?

The answer: it was not construed with *fi* in the same way it was construed with *ila*. Rather, the community or the town was made the place of the sending. On this meaning *ba'atha* came in His saying: ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised in every town a warner﴾ [al-Furqan: 51].

**The second question:** Is it correct what some of them said, that His saying: ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾ is not connected to the first statement, and that he only said it to them after they had denied him, and had rejected him after the proof had been established against them? Then at that point he said to them, warning them about what they were engaged in: ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾ [meaning] this way, for fear of the punishment with which I have warned you?

The answer: it is possible that it is connected to the first statement, in that he saw them turning away from the worship of Allah and occupied with the worship of idols, so he called them to the worship of Allah and warned them of punishment because of their devotion to the worship of idols.

Then know that Allah, exalted is He, related the attributes of those people and related their speech. As for the attributes, they are three, and they are the worst of attributes:
- The first is disbelief in the Creator, glorified is He, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿who disbelieved﴾.
- The second is disbelief in the Day of Resurrection, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and denied the meeting of the Hereafter﴾.
- The third is immersion in love of this world and its desires, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and to whom We had granted luxury in the life of this world﴾, that is: We made them prosperous.

If it is said: Allah mentioned the saying of the people of Hud in response to him in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Hud without a *wa* (conjunction): ﴿The chiefs of those who disbelieved among his people said: "Indeed, we see you in folly"﴾ [al-A'raf: 66], and ﴿We do not see you except as a human being like us﴾ [Hud: 27]. And here it is with the *wa*. So what is the difference between them?

We say: the one without *wa* is on the assumption of a questioner who said: "What did his people say?" and it was answered: "Such and such." As for the one with *wa*, it is a conjunction of what they said to what he said, and its meaning is that in this event there gathered this true statement and this false statement.

As for the doubts of the people, there are two:

The first is their saying: ﴿This is none but a human being like you. He eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾, and the explanation of this doubt has already passed in the first story. His saying: ﴿of what you drink﴾, that is: of your drink; or it is elided from it because what precedes it indicates it, which is His saying: ﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves, then you would indeed be losers.﴾ So they made following the messenger a loss, but they did not make worshipping idols a loss. That is: if you have given him obedience without there being any benefit for you in return, then that is the loss.

The second: they criticized the soundness of the gathering (*hashr*) and the resurrection (*nashr*), and then they criticized his prophethood because of his bringing that. As for their criticism of the soundness of the gathering, it is their saying: ﴿Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?﴾ — meaning, you will be returned alive for recompense. Then they did not limit themselves to this degree, until they combined with it a great astonishment, which is their saying: ﴿Far, far is what you are promised!﴾ Then they reinforced the doubt with their saying: ﴿There is only our life of this world: we die and we live﴾. They did not mean by their saying "we die and we live" a single person, but rather they meant that some die and some live, and that there is no return and no gathering. Therefore they said: ﴿and we will not be resurrected.﴾ When they had finished criticizing the soundness of the gathering, they built upon it a criticism of his prophethood. They said: since he has brought this falsehood, he has invented a lie against Allah. Then, when they had established the doubt that criticized his prophethood, they said: ﴿and we are not going to believe him﴾, because the people were like followers to them.

Know that Allah, exalted is He, did not answer these two doubts, because their corruption is evident. As for the first doubt, its weakness has already been explained. As for the second, they considered the gathering improbable, and the gathering is not improbable, for two reasons.

The first: since He, glorified is He, is able over all possibilities and knows all knowables, it is necessary that He be able to gather and resurrect.

The second: if there were no return, then the subjugation of the strong over the weak in this world would be injustice, and this is not fitting for the Wise, as He established, glorified is He, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15].

Here are some issues:

**First issue:** *Inna* is repeated (*innakum*) for emphasis, and the separation between the first and the second by the adverbial phrase made it good. *Mukhrajun* ("brought forth") is the predicate of the first. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and you were dust and bones, brought forth."

**Second issue:** *Hayhat* ("far") is read with *fath* and *kasr*, all with and without tanwin, and with sukun following the pause form.

**Third issue:** In His saying: ﴿There is only our life of this world﴾, *hiya* is a pronoun whose referent is not known except through what follows it as an explanation. Its original form is: "*in al-hayatu illa hayatuna al-dunya*" (there is no life but our life of this world). Then *hiya* was placed in the position of *al-hayat* ("life") because the predicate indicates it. From this is the saying of the poet:
"She is the soul; whatever you load upon her, she bears."
The meaning is: there is no life but this life. And because the negating *in* entered upon *hiya*, which has the meaning of "life" and indicates the genus, it negated it, and so it matched *la* ("no"), which negates what follows it as a negation of the genus.

Know that when that messenger despaired of acceptance from the eminent and the humble, he turned to his Lord and said: ﴿My Lord, support me, for they have denied me.﴾ Its explanation has already passed. Allah answered him in what he asked, and said: ﴿In a little while they will surely become regretful.﴾ The closest view is that what is meant is that the signs of their destruction would appear to them; at that point regret and remorse for not accepting would arise in them, and the time would be the time of the faith of despair, so they would not benefit from the regret. Allah, exalted is He, explained the destruction He sent down upon them with His saying: ﴿So the Blast seized them in truth.﴾ And they mentioned several views about the Blast:

First: Gabriel, peace be upon him, cried out at them, and the cry was so great that they died at it.

Second: the Blast is the earthquake, according to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both.

Third: the Blast is the very punishment and death, as is said of one who dies: "He was called and he answered." This is from al-Hasan.

Fourth: it is the annihilating punishment. The poet said:

(Page 87)

"Time cried out at the family of Barmak with a cry; they fell prostrate on their chins from its severity."

The first view is the better, because it is the literal meaning.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿in truth﴾, its meaning is that He destroyed them with justice, from your saying: "So-and-so judges with truth," when he is just in his judgments. Al-Mufaddal said: "in truth" means: with what cannot be repelled, like His saying: ﴿And the agony of death came in truth﴾ [Qaf: 19].

As for His saying: ﴿So We made them debris﴾, *ghuthaʾ* is the debris carried by the torrent of what has decayed and turned black of leaves and sticks, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He made it dark-brown debris﴾ [al-A'la: 5].

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So away with the wrongdoing people!﴾, there are two issues in it:

**First issue:** His saying *bu'dan* ("away"), *suhqan* ("destruction"), *dumran* ("ruin") and the like are verbal nouns placed in the position of their verbs, and they are among the verbal nouns about which Sibawayh said they are put in the accusative by verbs whose appearance is not used. The meaning of *bu'dan* is "they perished," that is: they were destroyed. It is said: *ba'ada ba'dan* and *ba'adan*, with *fath* on the *'ayn*, like *rashada rushdan* and *rashadan*, with *fath* on the *shin*. And Allah knows best.

**Second issue:** His saying: ﴿So away﴾ is in the position of a curse, which is distancing from good. Allah mentioned this as a way of contempt and humiliation for them. And since the punishment had already come down upon them, this indicates that what will befall them in the Hereafter of distance from bliss and reward is greater than what has befallen them now, so that this may be a lesson for those who come after them.
