The Third Story

﴿Then We produced after them other generations.﴾ ﴿No nation can outstrip its appointed term, nor can they delay it.﴾ ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession. Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him, so We made them follow one another, and We made them into tales. So away with a people who do not believe!﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We produced after them other generations.﴾ ﴿No nation can outstrip its appointed term, nor can they delay it.﴾ ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession. Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him, so We made them follow one another, and We made them into tales. So away with a people who do not believe!﴾

Know that He, glorified is He, relates stories in the Qur'an sometimes in detail, as has passed, and sometimes in summary, as here. It has been said that what is meant is the story of Lut, Shu'ayb, Ayyub and Yusuf, peace be upon them.

As for His saying, ﴿Then We produced after them other generations.﴾, the meaning is that He did not leave the abodes empty of accountable people whom He produced and brought to the limit of responsibility, until they took the place of those who were before them in cultivating the world.

As for His saying, ﴿No nation can outstrip its appointed term, nor can they delay it.﴾, the word "term" here may mean the terms of their lives and their being charged, and it may mean the terms of their death and destruction. Although the most apparent meaning of "term" when used absolutely is the time of death, He explains that every nation has written terms in life and death, which can neither be advanced nor postponed, thereby alerting that He knows things before they exist, so nothing comes into being except in accordance with His knowledge. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, when the term of Allah comes, it is not delayed, if you only knew.﴾ [Nuh: 4]. Here there are two issues:

The first issue: Our companions said: this verse indicates that the one who is killed dies at his term, for if he were killed before his term, the term would have been advanced or delayed, and this text contradicts that.

The second issue: al-Ka'bi said: the meaning of His saying, ﴿No nation can outstrip...﴾ is that they cannot go ahead of the time appointed for their punishment if they do not believe, nor can they lag behind it, and He does not annihilate them except when He knows of them that they will only increase in obstinacy, that they will not beget a believer, and that there is no benefit in their remaining for others and no harm to anyone in their destruction. This is like the saying of Nuh, peace be upon him: ﴿If You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will beget only wicked disbelievers.﴾ [Nuh: 27].

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession.﴾, the meaning is that just as We produced them one after another, messengers were sent to them on this same pattern. Ibn Kathir read "tatra" with tanwin, and the rest without tanwin. This is the choice of most of the linguists, because it is (fa'la) from al-mutawatirah, which is successive following, and fa'la is not given tanwin, like "da'wa" and "taqwa", and the "ta" is a substitute for a "waw", for it is derived from "watr", which is singular. al-Wahidi said: "tatra", on both readings, is a verbal noun or a noun placed in the position of a circumstantial accusative, because the meaning is "successive".

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him.﴾, He means that in denying their prophets they followed the course of those mentioned earlier who were destroyed by drowning and by the Cry. Therefore He said: ﴿So We made them follow one another﴾, that is, in destruction.

﴿And We made them into tales﴾ may mean the plural of "hadith", and from this come the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The meaning is that He, glorified is He, carried their destruction to such a degree that they became mere tales, so no trace or sign of them is seen, and nothing remains of them except the account that is recounted and taken as a lesson.

It is also possible that it is the plural of "uhdutha", like "udhuka" and "u'juba", which is what people speak of for amusement and wonder.

Then He said: ﴿So away with a people who do not believe!﴾, in the form of supplication, reproach and rebuke, and by this it indicates that just as they were destroyed swiftly, their destruction by punishment later, forever, is awaited, and that is a severe threat.

**The Fourth Story: The Story of Musa (peace be upon him)**

﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs. But they were arrogant, for they were a haughty people﴾ ﴿and said, "Shall we believe in two mortals like us, whose people serve us?"﴾ ﴿So they denied them, and became among those who were destroyed﴾ ﴿And We gave Musa the Scripture, so that they might be guided﴾

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs. But they were arrogant, for they were a haughty people﴾ ﴿and said, "Shall we believe in two mortals like us, whose people serve us?"﴾ ﴿So they denied them, and became among those who were destroyed﴾ ﴿And We gave Musa the Scripture, so that they might be guided﴾.

The scholars differed concerning "the signs" (al-ayat). Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: they are the nine signs: the staff, the hand, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the splitting of the sea, the years of drought, and the shortage of fruits. Al-Hasan said that His saying, ﴿with Our signs﴾, means: with Our religion. He argued that if "the signs" meant the miracles, then "the clear authority" would also mean the miracle, and so it would be the conjoining of a thing with itself. The first view is closer to the truth, because when the word "signs" is mentioned in connection with messengers, what is meant by it is the miracles. As for the argument they put forward, the answer to it is given in several ways.

The first: "the clear authority" may refer to the most noble of his miracles, which is the staff, since many miracles are connected with it: its transformation into a serpent, its swallowing of what the magicians had faked, the splitting of the sea, the gushing of springs from the rock when he struck it with it, its serving as a guard, a candle, a fruitful tree, a bucket and a rope. Because the staff alone possessed these virtues, it was singled out for mention, as in His saying: ﴿and Jibril and Mikail﴾.

The second: "the signs" may refer to those miracles themselves, and "the clear authority" to the manner in which they demonstrate truthfulness. For although these miracles shared with the signs of the other prophets the quality of being signs, they differed from them in the strength of their demonstration of the strength of Musa, peace be upon him.

The third: "the clear authority" may refer to Musa's, peace be upon him, overpowering of them through reasoning, in proving the existence of the Creator and establishing prophethood, and that they did not give him any consideration or weight.

Know that the verse indicates that the miracles of Musa, peace be upon him, were also the miracles of Harun, peace be upon him, and that just as prophethood was shared between them, so too were the miracles. Then, Exalted is He, related the description of Pharaoh and his people, and then mentioned their doubt. As for their description, it consists of two matters. The first: arrogance and disdain. The second: that they were a haughty people, that is, of high standing in worldly affairs; it may also mean being powerful through their numbers and strength. As for their doubt, it is their saying: ﴿Shall we believe in two mortals like us, whose people serve us?﴾ The author of the *al-Kashshaf* said: "He did not say 'two like us' (mithlayna), as He said: ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them﴾ [al-Nisa 4:140], and He did not say 'like them' in the plural (amthalahum), and He said: ﴿You are the best nation﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:110], and He did not say 'best of nations' (akhyar ummah). All of this is because brevity is more beloved to the Arabs than verbosity." The doubt is founded upon two matters. The first: that they are of the human race, and the answer to this has already been given. The second: that the people of Musa and Harun were like servants and slaves to them. Abu ʿUbayda said: "The Arabs call everyone who submits to a king 'one who serves him'." It may also be said that he (Pharaoh) claimed divinity, and so he claimed that the people were his servants, and that their obedience to him was worship in the true sense. Then Exalted is He explained that when this doubt occurred to them, they openly declared their denial, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿So they denied them﴾.

Since that denial was like the cause of their being among those who were destroyed, He therefore connected it to that with the particle of consequence (fa), saying: they were among those whom Allah had decreed should be drowned. For the drowning did not occur immediately after the denial; what occurred immediately after the denial was Allah's Exalted decree that they be so, at the appropriate time.

As for His saying: ﴿And We gave Musa the Scripture, so that they might be guided﴾, al-Qadi said: its meaning is that He, Exalted is He, singled out Musa, peace be upon him, with the Scripture, which is the Torah, not because of that denial, but so that they might be guided by it. Then, when they persisted in disbelief despite the great clarity, they became deserving of destruction. The author of the *al-Kashshaf* objected to this, saying: "It is not permissible for the pronoun in (la'allahum) to refer to Pharaoh and his chiefs, because the Torah was given to the Children of Israel only after the drowning of Pharaoh and his chiefs, as is shown by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Musa the Scripture after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾ [al-Qasas 28:43]. Rather, the correct meaning is: 'And We gave Musa the Scripture so that they (the Children of Israel) might act upon its laws and its admonitions.' Thus Musa is mentioned, and what is meant is the family of Musa, just as it is said 'Hashim' and 'Thaqif' and what is meant is their people."

**The Fourth Story: The Story of Musa (peace be upon him)**

﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs. But they were arrogant, for they were a haughty people﴾ ﴿and said, "Shall we believe in two mortals like us, whose people serve us?"﴾ ﴿So they denied them, and became among those who were destroyed﴾ ﴿And We gave Musa the Scripture, so that they might be guided﴾

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs. But they were arrogant, for they were a haughty people﴾ ﴿and said, "Shall we believe in two mortals like us, whose people serve us?"﴾ ﴿So they denied them, and became among those who were destroyed﴾ ﴿And We gave Musa the Scripture, so that they might be guided﴾.

The scholars differed concerning "the signs" (al-ayat). Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: they are the nine signs: the staff, the hand, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the splitting of the sea, the years of drought, and the shortage of fruits. Al-Hasan said that His saying, ﴿with Our signs﴾, means: with Our religion. He argued that if "the signs" meant the miracles, then "the clear authority" would also mean the miracle, and so it would be the conjoining of a thing with itself. The first view is closer to the truth, because when the word "signs" is mentioned in connection with messengers, what is meant by it is the miracles. As for the argument they put forward, the answer to it is given in several ways.

The first: "the clear authority" may refer to the most noble of his miracles, which is the staff, since many miracles are connected with it: its transformation into a serpent, its swallowing of what the magicians had faked, the splitting of the sea, the gushing of springs from the rock when he struck it with it, its serving as a guard, a candle, a fruitful tree, a bucket and a rope. Because the staff alone possessed these virtues, it was singled out for mention, as in His saying: ﴿and Jibril and Mikail﴾.

The second: "the signs" may refer to those miracles themselves, and "the clear authority" to the manner in which they demonstrate truthfulness. For although these miracles shared with the signs of the other prophets the quality of being signs, they differed from them in the strength of their demonstration of the strength of Musa, peace be upon him.

The third: "the clear authority" may refer to Musa's, peace be upon him, overpowering of them through reasoning, in proving the existence of the Creator and establishing prophethood, and that they did not give him any consideration or weight.

Know that the verse indicates that the miracles of Musa, peace be upon him, were also the miracles of Harun, peace be upon him, and that just as prophethood was shared between them, so too were the miracles. Then, Exalted is He, related the description of Pharaoh and his people, and then mentioned their doubt. As for their description, it consists of two matters. The first: arrogance and disdain. The second: that they were a haughty people, that is, of high standing in worldly affairs; it may also mean being powerful through their numbers and strength. As for their doubt, it is their saying: ﴿Shall we believe in two mortals like us, whose people serve us?﴾ The author of the *al-Kashshaf* said: "He did not say 'two like us' (mithlayna), as He said: ﴿Indeed, you would then be like them﴾ [al-Nisa 4:140], and He did not say 'like them' in the plural (amthalahum), and He said: ﴿You are the best nation﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:110], and He did not say 'best of nations' (akhyar ummah). All of this is because brevity is more beloved to the Arabs than verbosity." The doubt is founded upon two matters. The first: that they are of the human race, and the answer to this has already been given. The second: that the people of Musa and Harun were like servants and slaves to them. Abu ʿUbayda said: "The Arabs call everyone who submits to a king 'one who serves him'." It may also be said that he (Pharaoh) claimed divinity, and so he claimed that the people were his servants, and that their obedience to him was worship in the true sense. Then Exalted is He explained that when this doubt occurred to them, they openly declared their denial, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿So they denied them﴾.

Since that denial was like the cause of their being among those who were destroyed, He therefore connected it to that with the particle of consequence (fa), saying: they were among those whom Allah had decreed should be drowned. For the drowning did not occur immediately after the denial; what occurred immediately after the denial was Allah's Exalted decree that they be so, at the appropriate time.

As for His saying: ﴿And We gave Musa the Scripture, so that they might be guided﴾, al-Qadi said: its meaning is that He, Exalted is He, singled out Musa, peace be upon him, with the Scripture, which is the Torah, not because of that denial, but so that they might be guided by it. Then, when they persisted in disbelief despite the great clarity, they became deserving of destruction. Thus Musa is mentioned, and what is meant is the family of Musa, just as it is said 'Hashim' and 'Thaqif' and what is meant is their people."

**The Fifth Story: The Story of Jesus and Mary, peace be upon them both**

﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign, and We sheltered them on a high ground, a place of settlement and flowing water.﴾

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign, and We sheltered them on a high ground, a place of settlement and flowing water.﴾

Know that the son of Mary is Jesus, peace be upon him. God, may He be exalted, made him a sign by creating him without a male, by making him speak in the cradle while still a small infant, and by bringing about through his hands the healing of the blind and the leprous and the raising of the dead. As for Mary, God, may He be exalted, made her a sign because she conceived him without a male. Al-Hasan said: Mary spoke in her childhood just as Jesus, peace be upon him, spoke, and this is her saying: ﴿It is from God. Indeed, God provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:37]. She was never made to suckle a breast. Al-Qadi said: If that is established, it is a miracle (mu'jizah) for Zechariah, peace be upon him, since she was not a prophetess. We say: al-Qadi only said this because in his view the *irhas* (a preparatory sign preceding a prophethood, lit. "foundation-laying") is not permissible, and the miracles of the saints (*karamat al-awliya'*) are not permissible. In our view both are permissible, so there is no need for what he said. The closer view is that He made them both a sign by the very birth itself, since he was born without a male and she bore him without a male. Thus they both shared in this wondrous matter that breaks the normal course of things. What indicates that this interpretation is preferable are two points.

The first: He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾, because the very miraculous quality appeared in the two of them, not that it appeared through their hands. This is preferable to reading it as referring to the signs that appeared through his hands, such as raising the dead. This is because the birth concerned him and her together, and so it is a sign in both of them. Likewise, his speaking in the cradle, and the other signs, appeared through his hands, not that he himself was the sign.

The second: He, may He be exalted, said "a sign" (*ayah*) and did not say "two signs." Interpreting this word as referring to a matter that is complete only by the two of them together is preferable, and that is the matter of the birth, not the miracles which Jesus, peace be upon him, performed independently.

As for His statement, ﴿and We sheltered them on a high ground, a place of settlement﴾, that is: We made their dwelling the *rabwah* (high ground). *Al-rabwah* and *al-rabawah*, with their two *r*-vowels, are the three vowel forms, and it means elevated land. Then Qatadah and Abu al-Aliyah said: it is Iliya', the land of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is al-Ramlah. Al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd said: it is in Egypt. Most of the scholars said: it is Damascus. Muqatil and al-Dahhak said: it is the Ghouta of Damascus. *Al-qarar* is the place of settled rest in every level, spread-out land. From Qatadah: it has fruits and water, meaning that its inhabitants settle there because of the fruits. *Al-ma'in* is the water that is apparent and flows on the surface of the earth. He, may He be glorified, thus drew attention to the completeness of His blessings upon them through this concise wording.

Then there are two opinions regarding *al-ma'in*. The first: it is a *maf'ul* (passive form), since by its being apparent it is perceived by the eye, from *'anahu*, meaning when one perceives it with one's eye. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: if you wish, you may make it a *fa'il* (form of the pattern *fa'il*) from *al-ma'un*, and its origin is from *al-ma'n*. *Al-ma'un* is a *fa'ul* form derived from it. Abu 'Ali said: *al-ma'in* is the easy thing that yields and does not resist, and *al-ma'un* is what is easy for its giver.

Then they said: the reason for the sheltering was that she fled with her son Jesus to the high ground and remained there for twelve years. Her cousin Yusuf took them away, and then she returned to her people after their king had died. Here ends the stories, and Allah knows best.

[Page 91]

**Allah the Exalted said:** ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds. Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do.﴾ ﴿And indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me.﴾ ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves into sects, each faction rejoicing in what it has.﴾ ﴿So leave them in their confusion until a time.﴾ ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children ﴾ ﴿is for hastening good things for them? Rather, they do not perceive.﴾

Know that the apparent meaning of His words ﴿O messengers﴾ is an address to the messengers. This is not possible, because the messengers were sent at different times and in different eras, so how can this address be directed to all of them? Because of this difficulty, the scholars differed in interpreting it in several ways.

The first: the meaning is to inform that every messenger, in his own time, was addressed with this message and was enjoined with it, so that the listener may believe that a command addressed to all the messengers and enjoined upon them all is worthy of being taken up and acted upon.

The second: the intended one is our Prophet (ﷺ), because this was mentioned after the accounts of the messengers had ended. It is expressed in the plural form, as one says to a single person: "O people, stop your harm to me." A similar example is ﴿those to whom the people said﴾ (Al 'Imran: 173), and he was Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud. It is as if He, glorified is He, when He addressed Muhammad (ﷺ) with this, made clear that if all the messengers were present and gathered, they would have been addressed with nothing other than this, so that our Messenger would know that this burden is not upon him alone, but is binding upon all the prophets, peace be upon them.

The third, which is the view of Muhammad ibn Jarir (al-Tabari), is that the intended one is 'Isa (peace be upon him), because this was mentioned only after the mention of a place that combines food and drink, and because it is narrated that 'Isa (peace be upon him) used to eat from the spinning of his mother. However, the first view is closer, because it better fits the wording of the verse. Also, it is narrated from Umm 'Abd Allah, the sister of Shaddad ibn Aws, that she sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a bowl of milk in the intense heat at the time of his breaking his fast, while he was fasting. The Messenger returned it to her and said: "From where do you have this?" She said: "From a sheep of mine." Then he returned it and said: "From where is this sheep?" She said: "I bought it with my own wealth." So he took it. Then she came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, why did you return it?" He, peace be upon him, said: "With this the messengers were commanded not to eat except what is good, and not to act except righteously."

As for His words ﴿of the good things﴾, there are two views.

The first: it means the lawful (ḥalāl). It was also said: the good provisions are lawful, pure, and sustaining. The lawful is that in which Allah is not disobeyed; the pure is that in which Allah is not forgotten; and the sustaining is that which keeps the soul alive and protects the intellect.

The second: it means what is agreeable and pleasant of food and fruits. Thus, the Exalted made clear that although prophethood and what He obligated them to, namely upholding its rights, may be heavy upon them, He has nevertheless permitted them to eat the good things, just as He permitted them to others. Know that just as He, glorified is He, said to the messengers: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾, He said to the believers: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things that We have provided for you﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 172). Know also that placing His words ﴿eat of the good things﴾ before His words ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ is like an indication that righteous action must always be preceded by eating what is lawful. As for His words ﴿Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾, it is a warning against contravening what He commanded them. If this is a warning to the messengers despite their high rank, then it is all the more appropriate that it be a warning to others.

As for His words ﴿And indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me﴾, we have explained it in Surat al-Anbiya', and it contains two issues.

The first issue: the meaning is that just as it is obligatory for them to agree on eating what is lawful and on righteous deeds, so too they agree on monotheism (tawhid) and on guarding against disobedience to Allah the Exalted. If it is said: since their legislations differ, how can their religion be one? We say: what is meant by religion is that about which they do not differ, namely knowledge of the essence of Allah the Exalted and His attributes. As for the legislations, differing in them is not called a difference in religion. Just as it is said of menstruating and purified women that their religion is one, even though their obligations differ, so it is here. This is confirmed by His words ﴿and I am your Lord, so fear Me﴾, as if He thereby alerted that the religion of all

[Page 92]

is one in what concerns the knowledge of Allah the Exalted and guarding against His disobedience, so the legislations have no bearing on this, even though they differ in other matters.

The second issue: it is read as ﴿wa-inna﴾ with a kasra (inna), as a fresh start, and ﴿inna﴾ with the meaning of "because" (li-anna), and ﴿in﴾ is the light form of the heavy one, and ﴿ummatukum﴾ is in the nominative case with it.

As for His words ﴿so they divided their affair among themselves﴾, the meaning is that the communities of the prophets, peace be upon them, divided their affair among themselves. The phrase ﴿they divided﴾ carries the sense of emphasis on the severity of their disagreement. By ﴿their affair﴾ is meant what pertains to the religion.

As for His words ﴿zuburan﴾, it is read as "zuburan," the plural of "zabur," meaning books that differ, that is, they made their religion into religions. And "zubaran" means pieces, borrowed from the fragments (zubar) of silver and iron. And "zubran" with a light ba', like "rusl" in "rusul." Al-Kalbi, Muqatil and al-Dahhak said: it refers to the polytheists of Makkah, the Magians, the Jews and the Christians.

As for His words ﴿each faction rejoicing in what it has﴾, its meaning is that each group among them is pleased with what it has adopted as its religion for itself, admiring it, considering itself to be the one who is right and successful, and that others are the falsifiers and losers. When Allah the Exalted mentioned the division of these people in their religion, He followed it with a threat and said: ﴿So leave them in their confusion until a time.﴾ The address is to our Prophet (ﷺ): he says, leave these disbelievers in their ignorance. The word "ghamra" means water that covers a person's stature, so it is as if what they are in of ignorance and bewilderment has become an overwhelming flood covering their intellects. It is reported from 'Ali (peace be upon him): "in their floods until a time." Scholars mentioned several views concerning "until a time."

The first: until the time of death.

The second: until the time of seeing (the reality).

The third: until the time of punishment. The custom in such speech is that it is mentioned, and what is meant by it is the state accompanied by regret and remorse. This occurs when Allah makes them aware of the falsehood of what they were upon and makes them aware of the evil of their final outcome. It also occurs at the reckoning in the Hereafter, and at the punishment of the grave and questioning. So it must be understood as all of these.

Since these people were in great blessings in this world, it was possible that they would think those blessings were like an immediate reward for them for their religions. So the Exalted made clear that the matter is contrary to this, and said: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾ ﴿is for hastening good things for them?﴾ It was read as "yumiddu-hum" and "yusari'u," with ya', and the agent is Allah, glorified is He. There are two views on the meaning.

One of them: this extension is nothing but a gradual leading of them on in sins and drawing them on to an increase in sin, while they think it is hastening towards good things. The word "bal" (rather) is for correction of "do they think," meaning: rather, they are like cattle, having no discernment nor awareness, so that they would reflect on whether this is a gradual leading on or a hastening towards good. This verse is like His words ﴿Let not their wealth impress you﴾ (al-Tawbah: 85). It is narrated from Yazid ibn Maysarah: Allah the Exalted revealed to one of the prophets: "Does My servant rejoice that I extend the world to him, while it is further from him than Me? And does he grieve that I withhold the world from him, while it is nearer to him than Me?" Then he recited: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾. And it is reported from al-Hasan: When 'Umar was brought the bracelet of Kisra, he took it and placed it on the hand of Suraqah, and it reached his shoulder. 'Umar said: "O Allah, You know that Your Prophet (peace be upon him) loved to acquire wealth to spend it in Your way, but You withheld that from him out of wisdom. Then Abu Bakr loved that too. O Allah, let this not be a deception from You towards 'Umar." Then he recited: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾.

The second view: He, glorified is He, gave them these blessings only so that they would be free of mind, able to occupy themselves with the burdens of the truth. So when they turn away from the truth in this state, the proof against them becomes all the stronger. For this reason He said: ﴿Rather, they do not perceive.﴾

Because of this difficulty, the scholars differed in interpreting it in several ways.

The first: the meaning is to inform that every messenger, in his own time, was addressed with this message and was enjoined with it, so that the listener may believe that a command addressed to all the messengers and enjoined upon them all is worthy of being taken up and acted upon.

The second: the intended one is our Prophet (ﷺ), because this was mentioned after the accounts of the messengers had ended. It is expressed in the plural form, as one says to a single person: "O people, stop your harm to me." A similar example is ﴿those to whom the people said﴾ (Al 'Imran: 173), and he was Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud. It is as if He, glorified is He, when He addressed Muhammad (ﷺ) with this, made clear that if all the messengers were present and gathered, they would have been addressed with nothing other than this, so that our Messenger would know that this burden is not upon him alone, but is binding upon all the prophets, peace be upon them.

The third, which is the view of Muhammad ibn Jarir (al-Tabari), is that the intended one is 'Isa (peace be upon him), because this was mentioned only after the mention of a place that combines food and drink, and because it is narrated that 'Isa (peace be upon him) used to eat from the spinning of his mother. However, the first view is closer, because it better fits the wording of the verse. Also, it is narrated from Umm 'Abd Allah, the sister of Shaddad ibn Aws, that she sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a bowl of milk in the intense heat at the time of his breaking his fast, while he was fasting. The Messenger returned it to her and said: "From where do you have this?" She said: "From a sheep of mine." Then he returned it and said: "From where is this sheep?" She said: "I bought it with my own wealth." So he took it. Then she came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, why did you return it?" He, peace be upon him, said: "With this the messengers were commanded not to eat except what is good, and not to act except righteously."

As for His words ﴿of the good things﴾, there are two views.

The first: it means the lawful (ḥalāl). It was also said: the good provisions are lawful, pure, and sustaining. The lawful is that in which Allah is not disobeyed; the pure is that in which Allah is not forgotten; and the sustaining is that which keeps the soul alive and protects the intellect.

The second: it means what is agreeable and pleasant of food and fruits. Thus, the Exalted made clear that although prophethood and what He obligated them to, namely upholding its rights, may be heavy upon them, He has nevertheless permitted them to eat the good things, just as He permitted them to others. Know that just as He, glorified is He, said to the messengers: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾, He said to the believers: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things that We have provided for you﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 172). Know also that placing His words ﴿eat of the good things﴾ before His words ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ is like an indication that righteous action must always be preceded by eating what is lawful. As for His words ﴿Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾, it is a warning against contravening what He commanded them. If this is a warning to the messengers despite their high rank, then it is all the more appropriate that it be a warning to others.

As for His words ﴿And indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me﴾, we have explained it in Surat al-Anbiya', and it contains two issues.

The first issue: the meaning is that just as it is obligatory for them to agree on eating what is lawful and on righteous deeds, so too they agree on monotheism (tawhid) and on guarding against disobedience to Allah the Exalted. If it is said: since their legislations differ, how can their religion be one? We say: what is meant by religion is that about which they do not differ, namely knowledge of the essence of Allah the Exalted and His attributes. As for the legislations, differing in them is not called a difference in religion. Just as it is said of menstruating and purified women that their religion is one, even though their obligations differ, so it is here. This is confirmed by His words ﴿and I am your Lord, so fear Me﴾, as if He thereby alerted that the religion of all

[Page 92]

is one in what concerns the knowledge of Allah the Exalted and guarding against His disobedience, so the legislations have no bearing on this, even though they differ in other matters.

The second issue: it is read as ﴿wa-inna﴾ with a kasra (inna), as a fresh start, and ﴿inna﴾ with the meaning of "because" (li-anna), and ﴿in﴾ is the light form of the heavy one, and ﴿ummatukum﴾ is in the nominative case with it.

As for His words ﴿so they divided their affair among themselves﴾, the meaning is that the communities of the prophets, peace be upon them, divided their affair among themselves. The phrase ﴿they divided﴾ carries the sense of emphasis on the severity of their disagreement. By ﴿their affair﴾ is meant what pertains to the religion.

As for His words ﴿zuburan﴾, it is read as "zuburan," the plural of "zabur," meaning books that differ, that is, they made their religion into religions. And "zubaran" means pieces, borrowed from the fragments (zubar) of silver and iron. And "zubran" with a light ba', like "rusl" in "rusul." Al-Kalbi, Muqatil and al-Dahhak said: it refers to the polytheists of Makkah, the Magians, the Jews and the Christians.

As for His words ﴿each faction rejoicing in what it has﴾, its meaning is that each group among them is pleased with what it has adopted as its religion for itself, admiring it, considering itself to be the one who is right and successful, and that others are the falsifiers and losers. When Allah the Exalted mentioned the division of these people in their religion, He followed it with a threat and said: ﴿So leave them in their confusion until a time.﴾ The address is to our Prophet (ﷺ): he says, leave these disbelievers in their ignorance. The word "ghamra" means water that covers a person's stature, so it is as if what they are in of ignorance and bewilderment has become an overwhelming flood covering their intellects. It is reported from 'Ali (peace be upon him): "in their floods until a time." Scholars mentioned several views concerning "until a time."

The first: until the time of death.

The second: until the time of seeing (the reality).

The third: until the time of punishment. The custom in such speech is that it is mentioned, and what is meant by it is the state accompanied by regret and remorse. This occurs when Allah makes them aware of the falsehood of what they were upon and makes them aware of the evil of their final outcome. It also occurs at the reckoning in the Hereafter, and at the punishment of the grave and questioning. So it must be understood as all of these.

Since these people were in great blessings in this world, it was possible that they would think those blessings were like an immediate reward for them for their religions. So the Exalted made clear that the matter is contrary to this, and said: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾ ﴿is for hastening good things for them?﴾ It was read as "yumiddu-hum" and "yusari'u," with ya', and the agent is Allah, glorified is He. There are two views on the meaning.

One of them: this extension is nothing but a gradual leading of them on in sins and drawing them on to an increase in sin, while they think it is hastening towards good things. The word "bal" (rather) is for correction of "do they think," meaning: rather, they are like cattle, having no discernment nor awareness, so that they would reflect on whether this is a gradual leading on or a hastening towards good. This verse is like His words ﴿Let not their wealth impress you﴾ (al-Tawbah: 85). It is narrated from Yazid ibn Maysarah: Allah the Exalted revealed to one of the prophets: "Does My servant rejoice that I extend the world to him, while it is further from him than Me? And does he grieve that I withhold the world from him, while it is nearer to him than Me?" Then he recited: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾. And it is reported from al-Hasan: When 'Umar was brought the bracelet of Kisra, he took it and placed it on the hand of Suraqah, and it reached his shoulder. 'Umar said: "O Allah, You know that Your Prophet (peace be upon him) loved to acquire wealth to spend it in Your way, but You withheld that from him out of wisdom. Then Abu Bakr loved that too. O Allah, let this not be a deception from You towards 'Umar." Then he recited: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾.

The second view: He, glorified is He, gave them these blessings only so that they would be free of mind, able to occupy themselves with the burdens of the truth. So when they turn away from the truth in this state, the proof against them becomes all the stronger. For this reason He said: ﴿Rather, they do not perceive.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 23, verse 57–61:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who are apprehensive out of fear of their Lord﴾ ﴿and those who believe in the signs of their Lord﴾ ﴿and those who do not associate anything with their Lord﴾ ﴿and those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful, because they are returning to their Lord﴾ ﴿It is they who hasten to good deeds, and they are foremost in them﴾.

Know that when He, may He be exalted, censured those mentioned earlier with His saying: ﴿Do they think that We extend to them wealth and children﴾ ﴿We hasten for them in good things?﴾ and then said: ﴿Nay, they do not perceive﴾, He afterwards described the attributes of those who hasten to good deeds and perceive that. They are four:

The first attribute: His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are apprehensive out of fear of their Lord﴾. Ishfaq (apprehension, deep concern) includes khashya (fear) together with an additional tenderness and weakness. Some said: He combined the two for emphasis. Others took khashya to mean punishment, and the meaning is "those who are apprehensive of the punishment of their Lord"; this is the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Others took ishfaq to mean its effect, which is persistence in obedience, and the meaning is "those who are constant in obedience to Him out of fear of their Lord, diligent in seeking His good pleasure." The verified view is that whoever reaches in khashya the limit of ishfaq, which is the perfection of khashya, is at the utmost fear of the wrath of Allah in this world and of His punishment in the next, and so is at the utmost avoidance of sins.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿and those who believe in the signs of their Lord﴾. Know that the signs of Allah, may He be exalted, are the created things that indicate His existence. Belief in them is affirming them. If the affirmation is of their existence, that is known by necessity, and the one who holds this affirmation does not deserve praise. If it is of their being signs and proofs of the existence of the Creator, that is something that cannot be reached except through reflection and thought, and its possessor must become one who knows the existence of the Creator and His attributes. When knowledge is attained in the heart, the outward affirmation by the tongue follows, and that is faith (iman).

The third attribute: His saying: ﴿and those who do not associate anything with their Lord﴾. What is meant is not belief in tawhid and the negation of partners to Allah, for that is included in His saying: ﴿and those who believe in the signs of their Lord﴾. Rather, what is meant is the negation of hidden shirk (ash-shirk al-khafi), which is that one is sincere in worship, not undertaking it except for the sake of the Face of Allah, may He be exalted, and seeking His good pleasure. And Allah knows best.

The fourth attribute: His saying: ﴿and those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾. Its meaning: they give what they have given. Thereby every right that must be given is included, whether it is of the right of Allah, may He be exalted, such as zakat, expiation (kaffarah) and others, or of the rights of the children of Adam, such as deposits, debts, and kinds of fairness and justice. He showed that this benefits only if they do it while their hearts are fearful, because whoever undertakes worship while fearful of his shortcoming and failure, through deficiency or otherwise, will, because of that fear, strive hard to render it its due in performance. ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, saying: "[Regarding] ﴿those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾, is it the one who commits adultery, drinks wine, and steals, and yet fears Allah, may He be exalted?" The Prophet ﷺ, upon him be prayer and peace, said: "No, O daughter of al-Siddiq, but it is the man who prays, fasts and gives charity, and yet fears Allah, may He be exalted."

Know that the arrangement of these attributes is at the peak of excellence, because the first attribute indicates the presence of intense fear which necessitates avoiding what is not fitting; the second attribute indicates abandoning showing off (riya') in acts of obedience; and the third attribute indicates that one who combines these three attributes performs acts of obedience together with fear and apprehension of falling short, and that is the ultimate station of the siddiqin (the truthful ones). May Allah, glorified is He, grant us to reach it.

If it is said: Do you say that His saying ﴿and their hearts are fearful﴾ refers to ﴿give﴾, or refers to all the qualities mentioned before? We say: Rather, the better view is that it refers to all of them, because giving is not more deserving of that than other deeds, since what is meant is that one performs that while apprehensive of his shortcoming, so that he is exceeding in fulfilling its right. As for reading ﴿those who bring what they bring﴾ (wa-alladhina ya'tuna ma ataw), the statement regarding it is clearer, since what is meant thereby is: whatever they bring and do of abstaining from disobedience and undertaking faith and deeds, they undertake it with fear. Then He, glorified is He, explained the cause of that fear, which is their knowledge that they are "returning to their Lord," that is, for recompense, accountability, the unrolling of the scrolls, and the tracing of deeds, and that there regret will not benefit, so there is nothing but the decisive judgment from the Owner of the dominion. Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned these attributes of the sincere believers, He said after them: ﴿It is they who hasten to good deeds﴾, and regarding it there are two aspects.

One: that what is meant is that they desire acts of obedience with the utmost desire, so they hasten to them lest they pass their time, and lest they be lost to them without being cut short.

The second: that they hasten in this world to various kinds of benefit and forms of honor, as He said: ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 148], and ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 27], because when good things are hastened for them, they have hastened to attain them and gained them quickly. This second aspect is more fitting in correspondence with the preceding verse, because it affirms for the believers what was negated for the disbelievers. And it has been read as "yusri'una fi al-khayrat" (they hasten quickly to good things).

As for His saying: ﴿and they are foremost in them﴾, the meaning is: those who perform precedence for their sake, or who precede people for their sake; or ﴿and they are foremost in them﴾, that is, they attain them before the Hereafter, since they were hastened for them in this world. It is also permissible that it be a predicate after a predicate. The meaning would be: "they are for it" as one says "you are for it and it is for you," then He said "foremost" (sabiqun), i.e., "and they are foremost."

Ishfaq (apprehension, deep concern) includes khashya (fear) together with an additional tenderness and weakness. Some said: He combined the two for emphasis. Others took khashya to mean punishment, and the meaning is "those who are apprehensive of the punishment of their Lord"; this is the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Others took ishfaq to mean its effect, which is persistence in obedience, and the meaning is "those who are constant in obedience to Him out of fear of their Lord, diligent in seeking His good pleasure." The verified view is that whoever reaches in khashya the limit of ishfaq, which is the perfection of khashya, is at the utmost fear of the wrath of Allah in this world and of His punishment in the next, and so is at the utmost avoidance of sins.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿and those who believe in the signs of their Lord﴾. Know that the signs of Allah, may He be exalted, are the created things that indicate His existence. Belief in them is affirming them. If the affirmation is of their existence, that is known by necessity, and the one who holds this affirmation does not deserve praise. If it is of their being signs and proofs of the existence of the Creator, that is something that cannot be reached except through reflection and thought, and its possessor must become one who knows the existence of the Creator and His attributes. When knowledge is attained in the heart, the outward affirmation by the tongue follows, and that is faith (iman).

The third attribute: His saying: ﴿and those who do not associate anything with their Lord﴾. What is meant is not belief in tawhid and the negation of partners to Allah, for that is included in His saying: ﴿and those who believe in the signs of their Lord﴾. Rather, what is meant is the negation of hidden shirk (ash-shirk al-khafi), which is that one is sincere in worship, not undertaking it except for the sake of the Face of Allah, may He be exalted, and seeking His good pleasure. And Allah knows best.

The fourth attribute: His saying: ﴿and those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾. Its meaning: they give what they have given. Thereby every right that must be given is included, whether it is of the right of Allah, may He be exalted, such as zakat, expiation (kaffarah) and others, or of the rights of the children of Adam, such as deposits, debts, and kinds of fairness and justice. He showed that this benefits only if they do it while their hearts are fearful, because whoever undertakes worship while fearful of his shortcoming and failure, through deficiency or otherwise, will, because of that fear, strive hard to render it its due in performance. ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, saying: "[Regarding] ﴿those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾, is it the one who commits adultery, drinks wine, and steals, and yet fears Allah, may He be exalted?" The Prophet ﷺ, upon him be prayer and peace, said: "No, O daughter of al-Siddiq, but it is the man who prays, fasts and gives charity, and yet fears Allah, may He be exalted."

Know that the arrangement of these attributes is at the peak of excellence, because the first attribute indicates the presence of intense fear which necessitates avoiding what is not fitting; the second attribute indicates abandoning showing off (riya') in acts of obedience; and the third attribute indicates that one who combines these three attributes performs acts of obedience together with fear and apprehension of falling short, and that is the ultimate station of the siddiqin (the truthful ones). May Allah, glorified is He, grant us to reach it.

If it is said: Do you say that His saying ﴿and their hearts are fearful﴾ refers to ﴿give﴾, or refers to all the qualities mentioned before? We say: Rather, the better view is that it refers to all of them, because giving is not more deserving of that than other deeds, since what is meant is that one performs that while apprehensive of his shortcoming, so that he is exceeding in fulfilling its right. As for reading ﴿those who bring what they bring﴾ (wa-alladhina ya'tuna ma ataw), the statement regarding it is clearer, since what is meant thereby is: whatever they bring and do of abstaining from disobedience and undertaking faith and deeds, they undertake it with fear. Then He, glorified is He, explained the cause of that fear, which is their knowledge that they are "returning to their Lord," that is, for recompense, accountability, the unrolling of the scrolls, and the tracing of deeds, and that there regret will not benefit, so there is nothing but the decisive judgment from the Owner of the dominion. Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned these attributes of the sincere believers, He said after them: ﴿It is they who hasten to good deeds﴾, and regarding it there are two aspects.

One: that what is meant is that they desire acts of obedience with the utmost desire, so they hasten to them lest they pass their time, and lest they be lost to them without being cut short.

The second: that they hasten in this world to various kinds of benefit and forms of honor, as He said: ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 148], and ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 27], because when good things are hastened for them, they have hastened to attain them and gained them quickly. And it has been read as "yusri'una fi al-khayrat" (they hasten quickly to good things).

It is also permissible that it be a predicate after a predicate. The meaning would be: "they are for it" as one says "you are for it and it is for you," then He said "foremost" (sabiqun), i.e., "and they are foremost."

[Page 95]

The Exalted says: ﴿And We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity, and with Us is a Record that speaks with the truth, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this, and they have deeds other than that which they are doing.﴾ ﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones with the punishment, behold, they cry out for help.﴾ ﴿Do not cry out for help today; indeed, you will not be helped by Us.﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, mentioned the manner of the deeds of the sincere believers, He mentioned two rulings concerning the deeds of His servants.

[Page 96]

The first is His saying: ﴿And We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity.﴾ Regarding *al-wus'* (capacity), there are two opinions. One is that it is *al-ṭāqa* (ability), reported from al-Mufaḍḍal. The second is that it is less than ability, which is the view of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school of theology), Muqatil, al-Ḍaḥḥak and al-Kalbi. They argued for this by saying that *al-wus'* is so named because the action is spacious for him; it is not difficult or constricting. Thus He made clear that those sincere ones were not obligated to more than what they did. Muqatil said: "Whoever cannot pray standing, let him pray sitting; and whoever cannot pray sitting, let him gesture with a nod, for We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity." The Mu'tazila used this verse to deny *taklīf mā lā yuṭāq* (obligation to what is beyond one's power), and the discussion of this has already preceded.

The second is His saying: ﴿And with Us is a Record that speaks with the truth, and they will not be wronged.﴾ Its parallel is His saying: ﴿This is Our Book, which speaks against you with the truth﴾ [al-Jathiya: 29], and His saying: ﴿It leaves out nothing small or great but has enumerated it﴾ [al-Kahf: 49].

Know that He, exalted is He, likened the Book to one from whom speech proceeds, for the Book does not speak, but it makes clear what is in it, just as an eloquent speaker makes clear and speaks when he is truthful. If it is said: "Those to whom that Book is presented either attribute falsehood to Allah, the Exalted, or permit it for Him. If they attribute it to Him, they will believe Him in everything He says, whether or not the Book exists. If they permit it for Him, they will not trust that Book, because they permit that He, glorified is He, wrote in it the opposite of what occurred. So in both cases there is no benefit in that Book." We say: Allah does what He wills, and it is not far-fetched that this is a benefit for the accountable ones among the angels.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And they will not be wronged,﴾ its parallel is His saying: ﴿They will find what they did present, and your Lord wrongs no one﴾ [al-Kahf: 49]. The Mu'tazila said: Wronging is either by increasing the punishment, or by decreasing the reward, or by punishing for what one did not know, or by imposing on them what they cannot bear. So the verse indicates that the servant creates his own act; otherwise, punishing him for it would be wronging. It also indicates that He, glorified is He, does not impose what is beyond one's capacity. The answer is: when He obligated Abu Lahab to believe, and belief requires affirming Allah, the Exalted, in everything He reports, and among what He reported is that Abu Lahab will not believe, then He obligated him to believe that he will not believe. Therefore, everything you mentioned applies to you.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this,﴾ there are two opinions. One is that it refers to the disbelievers, those to whom His saying ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾ is fitting, and it is not fitting for the believers. The meaning is: in confusion about this which We have made clear in the Qur'an, or about this Book that speaks with the truth, or about this which is the description of the fearful ones. ﴿And they have﴾ means: for these disbelievers there are deeds other than that; that is, deeds besides that, meaning besides their ignorance and disbelief. Then some said: He meant their deeds at present. Others said: rather He meant the future, and this is closer, because His saying ﴿they are doing them﴾ is closer to the future. He said ﴿they are doing them﴾ because they are recorded in the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, in His judgment, and in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ*), so it is necessary that they do them in order to enter the Fire by them, because of the wretchedness that Allah has decreed for them.

The second opinion, which is the choice of Abu Muslim, is that these verses are attributes of the fearful ones. It is as if He, glorified is He, said after describing them: ﴿And We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity,﴾ and its end is what these fearful ones have brought. ﴿And with Us is a Record﴾ that preserves their deeds ﴿that speaks with the truth, and they will not be wronged﴾; rather, We fully repay them the reward of all their deeds. ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾ is also a description of them as bewildered; it is as if He said: and they, along with that fear and dread, are like those bewildered about whether their deeds will be accepted or rejected. ﴿And they have deeds other than that﴾ means: they also have supererogatory acts and forms of righteousness besides what they are upon, either deeds they have already done in the past or deeds they will do in the future. Then He, glorified is He, returned with His saying:

[Page 96]

﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones with the punishment﴾ to the description of the disbelievers.

Know that the view of Abu Muslim is preferable, because when it is possible to refer the speech to what is connected to it, which is the mention of the fearful ones, it is better than referring it to what is far from it. Especially since a person may be encouraged to do good by being reminded that his deeds are preserved, just as he may be warned by that against evil. A person may also be described, because of the intensity of his thinking about the matter of his Hereafter, as having a heart in confusion, meaning that thought about the acceptance or rejection of his deed has taken hold of him, and about whether he has fulfilled it as required or fallen short. If it is asked: what is meant by His saying ﴿about this﴾, and what does "this" refer to? We say: it refers to their fear and dread, while both of these dominate their hearts.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when We seize their affluent ones with the punishment,﴾ the author of *al-Kashshaf* said: this "until" (*ḥattā*) is one after which a sentence begins, and the sentence is the conditional clause.

Know that there is no doubt that the pronoun in "their affluent ones" refers to those disbelievers previously mentioned, because punishment is fitting only for them. Regarding this punishment there are two views.

One is that by the punishment He meant what befell them on the day of Badr.

The second is that it is the punishment of the Hereafter. Then He, glorified is He, explained that when the affluent among them are struck by the punishment, they cry out; that is, their voices rise in pleading and wailing because of the severity of what they are in. It will be said to them, as a rebuke: ﴿Do not cry out today; indeed, you will not be helped by Us,﴾ so nothing will be repelled from you of what He intends to bring upon you. By this, He, glorified is He, indicated that on the Day of Resurrection they will reach this degree of regret and remorse, and this serves as a motivation for them in this world to abandon disbelief and to hasten to faith and obedience, for they now benefit from it.

[Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 23, verses 66–72]

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿My verses were recited to you, but you turned back on your heels.﴾ ﴿Being arrogant about it, talking nonsense at night, and reviling.﴾ ﴿Have they not pondered the word, or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾ ﴿Or have they not recognized their Messenger, so that they deny him?﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has madness"? Rather, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.﴾ ﴿Had the truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Rather, We have brought them their reminder, but they turn away from their reminder.﴾ ﴿Or do you ask them for payment? But the payment of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers.﴾

Know that when He, glory be to Him, had previously shown that He does not help those disbelievers, He followed this with the reason for it, which is that whenever the verses of Allah were recited to them, they did three things.

The first: they were turning back on their heels (yankisun), and this is a proverb used of one who distances himself from the truth entirely. This is His saying: ﴿so you were turning back on your heels﴾, meaning: you fled from those verses and from the one who recites them, as the one who turns back (al-nakis) goes backward on his heels.

The second: His saying: ﴿being arrogant about it﴾. To what does the pronoun in "bihi" (about it) refer? There are several views.

The first: it refers to the Ancient House (al-Bayt al-'Atiq) or the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram). They used to say: "No one will prevail over us, for we are the people of the Haram." What makes this pronoun-reference acceptable is their well-known arrogance concerning the House, even though they had no glory except that they were its custodians and its keepers.

The second: what is meant is arrogance about this turning back and distancing.

The third: the preposition "bi" (about) is connected to "samiran" (talking at night), meaning they talk nonsense at night about the Qur'an and disparage it. This is the third thing they do when the Qur'an is recited to them. They used to gather around the House at night and converse (yasmurun). Most of their night-talk was about the Qur'an, calling it sorcery and poetry, and reviling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). And "yahjurun" (talking nonsense / reviling): "al-samir" is like "al-hadir" in its use for a group. It was also read as "samaran," and "samiran tahjurun" is from "ahjara" in his speech, meaning he uttered obscenity. "Al-hajr" with a fatha means nonsense (hadhayan), and "al-hujr" with a damma means obscenity (al-fuhsh). Or it is from "hajjara," which is an intensive form of "hajara," meaning he talked nonsense.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, described their condition, He responded to them by showing that their undertaking of these acts must be due to one of four things.

The first: that they do not reflect upon the evidence of its (the Qur'an's) validity, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Do they not contemplate the Qur'an?﴾ [An-Nisa' 4:82]. He showed that the word, which is the Qur'an, was known to them, and they had been enabled to reflect upon it, since it was distinct from the speech of the Arabs in eloquence and free from contradiction throughout its long duration, and since it alerts them to what they are obliged to know concerning the knowledge of the Creator and the knowledge of His oneness. So why do they not reflect upon it, so that they might abandon falsehood and return to the truth?

The second: that they believe the coming of messengers to be something contrary to custom, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾. This is because they knew through mass transmission (tawatur) that messengers used to come successively to nations, and miracles appeared at their hands. Nations were divided between one who believed and was saved, and one who denied and was destroyed by a punishment of annihilation (isti'sal). Did this not move them to affirm the Messenger?

The third: that they did not know of his religiousness and goodness of character before he claimed prophethood, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿or they did not recognize their Messenger, so they deny him﴾. By this He alerted them that they had known of him, before he claimed the message, that he was at the utmost in trustworthiness and truthfulness, and in the extreme of avoiding lying and blameworthy character. So how could they deny him after their word had agreed on calling him "the Trustworthy"?

The fourth: that they believe him to be mad, so they say: what led him to claim the message was his madness. And this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿or do they say, "He has madness"?﴾. This also is evidently corrupt, because they knew by necessity that he was the most intelligent of people, and how could a madman bring the like of what he brought of decisive proofs and complete laws? Indeed, among those who hated him, peace be upon him, was one who called him that. And there are two views concerning it.

One of them: they attributed this to him because he was eager for their submission to him, and that was among the most remote things in their view, so they attributed madness to him for that reason.

The second: they said that to create confusion among their common folk, so that they would not submit to him, and they presented it in a manner of belittling him. Then, after He, glory be to Him, enumerated these possibilities and alerted to their corruption, He said: ﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth﴾, because they clung to imitation (taqlid), and because they knew that if they acknowledged Muhammad (ﷺ), their positions would be removed and their leaderships would be disrupted. Therefore they disliked him. If it is said: His saying "most of them" indicates that a few of them do not dislike the truth, we say: among them there was one who abandoned faith out of pride, fearing reproach from his people, and that they would say: "He abandoned the religion of his fathers," not out of aversion to the truth, as is related about Abu Talib.

Then He, glory be to Him, showed that the truth does not follow desire, but rather it is obligatory upon the responsible person to cast aside desire and follow the truth. So He, glory be to Him, showed that following desire leads to great corruption, and He said: ﴿Had the truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted﴾. And there are several views concerning its interpretation.

The first: the people used to see that the truth lies in taking gods alongside Allah, the Exalted. But if that were valid, corruption would have occurred in the heavens and the earth, according to what we have established in the argument of mutual hindrance (dalil al-tamanu') in His saying: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would have been corrupted﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 21:22].

The second: their desires regarding the worship of idols and denying Muhammad (ﷺ) are the source of corruption, while the truth is Islam. So if Islam followed their saying, Allah would know that corruptions would occur as long as this world remains, and that would necessitate the ruin and annihilation of the world.

The third: their opinions were contradictory, so if the truth followed their desires, contradiction would occur and the order of the world would be disrupted. From al-Qaffal.

As for His saying: ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾, it has been said: it is the Qur'an and the proofs. And it has been said: rather, it is their honor and their pride in the Messenger. Both views are close, because in the coming of the Messenger there is the explanation of the proofs, and in the coming of the proofs there is the explanation of the Messenger, so each of them is joined with the other. It has also been said: the "reminder" is admonition and warning. And it has been said: it is what they used to wish for, saying: ﴿If we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been sincere servants of Allah﴾ [As-Saffat 37:168–169]. It was also read as "bidhikrahum" (their reminder, with the variant form). Then He, glory be to Him, showed that he, peace and blessings be upon him, does not covet them, so that this would be a cause for aversion, and He said: ﴿Or do you ask them for payment? But the payment of your Lord is better﴾. It was also read as "kharajan" (payment). Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "al-kharj" is what you give voluntarily, and "al-kharaj" is what it is obligatory for you to pay. The preferred view is that "al-kharj" is more specific than "al-kharaj," as in your saying "kharaj al-qaryah" (the land tax of the village) and "kharj al-kurdah" (the payment for the hide). The increase in wording indicates an increase in meaning. For this reason the reading of one who recites ﴿kharjan fa-kharaju rabbika﴾ (kharjan) is good. The meaning is: do you ask them, for guiding them, for a little of the bounty of creatures? Then the abundance of the bounty of creatures is better. By this He alerted that this accusation is far from him, and it is not permissible that they should shun accepting his word on account of it. By these verses He alerted that they are wholly without excuse and that they are overwhelmed by proof from every aspect.

Al-Jubba'i said: The saying of the Exalted, ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾, indicates that none of the servants can match His bounty and provision, nor equal Him in bestowing favors upon His servants. It also indicates that servants may provide for one another, for otherwise it would not be permissible to say: ﴿and He is the best of providers﴾.

Know that when He, glory be to Him, had previously shown that He does not help those disbelievers, He followed this with the reason for it, which is that whenever the verses of Allah were recited to them, they did three things.

The first: they were turning back on their heels (yankisun), and this is a proverb used of one who distances himself from the truth entirely. This is His saying: ﴿so you were turning back on your heels﴾, meaning: you fled from those verses and from the one who recites them, as the one who turns back (al-nakis) goes backward on his heels.

The second: His saying: ﴿being arrogant about it﴾. To what does the pronoun in "bihi" (about it) refer? There are several views.

The first: it refers to the Ancient House (al-Bayt al-'Atiq) or the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram). They used to say: "No one will prevail over us, for we are the people of the Haram." What makes this pronoun-reference acceptable is their well-known arrogance concerning the House, even though they had no glory except that they were its custodians and its keepers.

The second: what is meant is arrogance about this turning back and distancing.

The third: the preposition "bi" (about) is connected to "samiran" (talking at night), meaning they talk nonsense at night about the Qur'an and disparage it. This is the third thing they do when the Qur'an is recited to them. They used to gather around the House at night and converse (yasmurun). Most of their night-talk was about the Qur'an, calling it sorcery and poetry, and reviling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). And "yahjurun" (talking nonsense / reviling): "al-samir" is like "al-hadir" in its use for a group. It was also read as "samaran," and "samiran tahjurun" is from "ahjara" in his speech, meaning he uttered obscenity. "Al-hajr" with a fatha means nonsense (hadhayan), and "al-hujr" with a damma means obscenity (al-fuhsh). Or it is from "hajjara," which is an intensive form of "hajara," meaning he talked nonsense.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, described their condition, He responded to them by showing that their undertaking of these acts must be due to one of four things.

The first: that they do not reflect upon the evidence of its (the Qur'an's) validity, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Do they not contemplate the Qur'an?﴾ [An-Nisa' 4:82]. He showed that the word, which is the Qur'an, was known to them, and they had been enabled to reflect upon it, since it was distinct from the speech of the Arabs in eloquence and free from contradiction throughout its long duration, and since it alerts them to what they are obliged to know concerning the knowledge of the Creator and the knowledge of His oneness. So why do they not reflect upon it, so that they might abandon falsehood and return to the truth?

The second: that they believe the coming of messengers to be something contrary to custom, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾. This is because they knew through mass transmission (tawatur) that messengers used to come successively to nations, and miracles appeared at their hands. Nations were divided between one who believed and was saved, and one who denied and was destroyed by a punishment of annihilation (isti'sal). Did this not move them to affirm the Messenger?

The third: that they did not know of his religiousness and goodness of character before he claimed prophethood, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿or they did not recognize their Messenger, so they deny him﴾. By this He alerted them that they had known of him, before he claimed the message, that he was at the utmost in trustworthiness and truthfulness, and in the extreme of avoiding lying and blameworthy character. So how could they deny him after their word had agreed on calling him "the Trustworthy"?

The fourth: that they believe him to be mad, so they say: what led him to claim the message was his madness. And this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿or do they say, "He has madness"?﴾. This also is evidently corrupt, because they knew by necessity that he was the most intelligent of people, and how could a madman bring the like of what he brought of decisive proofs and complete laws? Indeed, among those who hated him, peace be upon him, was one who called him that. And there are two views concerning it.

One of them: they attributed this to him because he was eager for their submission to him, and that was among the most remote things in their view, so they attributed madness to him for that reason.

The second: they said that to create confusion among their common folk, so that they would not submit to him, and they presented it in a manner of belittling him. Then, after He, glory be to Him, enumerated these possibilities and alerted to their corruption, He said: ﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth﴾, because they clung to imitation (taqlid), and because they knew that if they acknowledged Muhammad (ﷺ), their positions would be removed and their leaderships would be disrupted. Therefore they disliked him. If it is said: His saying "most of them" indicates that a few of them do not dislike the truth, we say: among them there was one who abandoned faith out of pride, fearing reproach from his people, and that they would say: "He abandoned the religion of his fathers," not out of aversion to the truth, as is related about Abu Talib.

Then He, glory be to Him, showed that the truth does not follow desire, but rather it is obligatory upon the responsible person to cast aside desire and follow the truth. So He, glory be to Him, showed that following desire leads to great corruption, and He said: ﴿Had the truth followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted﴾. And there are several views concerning its interpretation.

The first: the people used to see that the truth lies in taking gods alongside Allah, the Exalted. But if that were valid, corruption would have occurred in the heavens and the earth, according to what we have established in the argument of mutual hindrance (dalil al-tamanu') in His saying: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would have been corrupted﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 21:22].

The second: their desires regarding the worship of idols and denying Muhammad (ﷺ) are the source of corruption, while the truth is Islam. So if Islam followed their saying, Allah would know that corruptions would occur as long as this world remains, and that would necessitate the ruin and annihilation of the world.

The third: their opinions were contradictory, so if the truth followed their desires, contradiction would occur and the order of the world would be disrupted. From al-Qaffal.

As for His saying: ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾, it has been said: it is the Qur'an and the proofs. And it has been said: rather, it is their honor and their pride in the Messenger. Both views are close, because in the coming of the Messenger there is the explanation of the proofs, and in the coming of the proofs there is the explanation of the Messenger, so each of them is joined with the other. It has also been said: the "reminder" is admonition and warning. It was also read as "bidhikrahum" (their reminder, with the variant form). Then He, glory be to Him, showed that he, peace and blessings be upon him, does not covet them, so that this would be a cause for aversion, and He said: ﴿Or do you ask them for payment? But the payment of your Lord is better﴾. It was also read as "kharajan" (payment).
