**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 23, verses 76–80:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate.﴾ ﴿Until, when We opened upon them a gate of severe punishment, behold, they were in despair therein.﴾ ﴿And it is He who produced for you hearing, sight, and hearts; little are you grateful.﴾ ﴿And it is He who multiplied you upon the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿And it is He who gives life and causes death, and His is the alternation of night and day. Will you not then reason?﴾

The scholars differed concerning His saying, ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment﴾, in several respects.

The first: that when Thumamah ibn Uthal al-Hanafi embraced Islam and went to al-Yamamah, he prevented the grain supplies (al-mirah) from reaching the people of Makkah, so Allah seized them with years of famine, until they ate hides and carrion. Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Do you not claim that you were sent as a mercy to the worlds? Yet you have killed the fathers with the sword and the sons with hunger. So pray to Allah that He lift this drought from us." He prayed, the drought was lifted from them, and Allah revealed this verse. The meaning is: We seized them with hunger, yet they did not obey.

The second: it is what befell them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture. That is, this, despite its severity, did not move them to faith. This is from al-Asamm.

The third: the intended meaning is those among the earlier nations who were punished, ﴿yet they did not humble themselves﴾, that is, the idolaters of the Arabs, before their Lord. This is from al-Hasan.

The fourth: the severity of this world is closer to the one bound by obligation than the severity of the Hereafter. So if the severity of this world does not affect them, then the severity of the Hereafter likewise will not. This indicates that if ﴿they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

As for His saying, ﴿Until, when We opened upon them a gate of severe punishment﴾, there are two views concerning it.

One: until, when We opened upon them the gate of hunger, which is harsher than killing and capture.

The second: when they are punished with the Fire of Jahannam, then they will be in despair, like His saying: ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will be in despair﴾ [al-Rum: 12], and ﴿Its punishment will not be lightened for them, and they will be in it in despair﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 75]. Al-Iblas (ibla's) is despair of every good. It has also been said: it is stillness together with grief.

Here there are questions.

The first question: what is the morphological pattern (wazn) of *istakana*? The answer: it is *istaf'ala*, from *al-kawn* (being); that is, he passed from one state of being to another, just as it is said *istahala* when one passes from one condition to another. It is also permissible that it be *iftaʿala*, from *al-sukun* (stillness), with the fatha of its ʿayn lengthened.

The second question: why does *istakanu* come in the past tense while *yatadarrauna* comes in the present tense? The answer: because the meaning is, We tested them, and after the trial We found from them no humbling. It is not the custom of these people to supplicate until the gate of severe punishment is opened upon them. It is also read *fattahna* (with the doubled letter).

The third question: conjunction (ʿatf) is not good except with a connection of kind, so what is the relation between His saying, ﴿And it is He who produced for you hearing and sight﴾, and what came before it? The answer: it is as if He, Glorified is He, when He had explained the extent to which those disbelievers persisted in turning away from hearing the proofs

[page 100]

and seeing the lessons and reflecting on the realities, addressed the believers: "And it is He who gave you these things and made you aware of them," as an alert that whoever does not use these organs for what they were created for is like one who lacks them, just as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Their hearing did not avail them, nor their sight, nor their hearts, against anything, since they used to deny the signs of Allah﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 26]. This is an alert that the deprivation of those disbelievers and the attainment of these believers is only from Allah.

Know that He, Glorified is He, explained the magnitude of His blessings in several respects.

The first: by giving hearing, sight, and hearts, and He singled out these three for mention because proof depends upon them. Then He explained that few of them are thankful. Abu Muslim said: It is not meant that they have some gratitude, even if little. Rather, it is like saying of the ungrateful one who denies the blessing: "How little is so-and-so's gratitude."

The second: His saying, ﴿And it is He who multiplied you upon the earth﴾. It has been said in tafsir: "He created you." Abu Muslim said: It may also mean He spread you upon it as offspring, some of you from others, until you multiplied, like His saying: ﴿The offspring of those We carried with Nuh﴾ [al-Isra': 3]. So we say: He is the one who made you multiply upon the earth, and He will gather you on the Day of Resurrection to an abode in which none judges besides Him. So their gathering to that place is called a gathering "to Him," not in the sense of a place.

The third: His saying, ﴿And it is He who gives life and causes death﴾, meaning: the blessing of life, although it is among the greatest blessings, is cut off, and although He, Glorified is He, bestows it, the purpose of it is the transition to the abode of reward.

The fourth: His saying, ﴿And His is the alternation of night and day﴾. The aspect of blessing in this is known. Then He, Glorified is He, warned against neglecting reflection upon these matters, saying: ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾, because this is an indication of rebuke and threat. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 23, verses 81–90:**

God's saying: ﴿Nay, but they said the like of what the former ones said.﴾ ﴿They said: "When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised again?"﴾ ﴿"We and our forefathers were indeed promised this before. This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾

Know that when He, glory be to Him, had explained the argument regarding the proofs of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), He followed it with mention of the ma'ad (the return and resurrection). So He said: ﴿Nay, but they said the like of what the former ones said﴾, in denying the resurrection despite the clarity of the proofs. By this He indicated that they denied it only by blind imitation (taqlid) of the ancients, and this shows the corruption of the view that relies on taqlid. Then He related their doubt from two aspects.

The first is their saying: ﴿When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised again?﴾ This is well known.

The second is their saying: ﴿We and our forefathers were indeed promised this before.﴾ It is as if they said: this promise, just as it was made by him (upon him be blessings and peace), had been made long ago by the prophets, yet it was not found to occur despite the long passage of time. So they thought that the restoration would take place in the abode of this world. Then they said: since it is so, ﴿this is nothing but the fables of the ancients.﴾ The word asatir is the plural of uslur, and uslur is the plural of satr (line); that is, what the ancients wrote, having no reality. The plural usṭura (usṭūra) is more appropriate.

God's saying: ﴿Say: "To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?"﴾ ﴿They will say: "To God." Say: "Will you not then remember?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?"﴾ ﴿They will say: "To God." Say: "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ ﴿Say: "In whose hand is the dominion of everything, who gives protection while none can be protected against Him, if you know?"﴾ ﴿They will say: "To God." Say: "How then are you deluded?"﴾ ﴿Nay, We have brought them the truth, and indeed they are liars.﴾

Know that it is possible that the purpose of these verses is a refutation of those who deny the restoration, and it is possible that the purpose is a refutation of the idol-worshippers. This is because the people acknowledged God, Exalted, yet they said: "We worship the idols so that they may bring us near to God in nearness." Then He, glory be to Him, argued against them with three matters.

The first is His saying: ﴿Say: "To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it?"﴾ The aspect of inference from it regarding restoration is that since He, Exalted, is the Creator of the earth and of the living beings in it, and the Creator of their life, their power, and other things, it is necessary that He be able to restore them after He has annihilated them. The aspect of inference from it regarding the negation of idol-worship is that the worship of the One who created you, created the earth and everything in it of blessings, is the one that is obligatory, not the worship of what neither harms nor benefits. His saying ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ means an encouragement to reflect, so that they may know the falsity of what they are upon.

The second is His saying: ﴿Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?﴾ The aspect of inference for both matters is as has preceded. He said ﴿Will you not then fear Him?﴾ as an alert that the averting of God's punishment is not attained except by abandoning the worship of idols and acknowledging the possibility of restoration.

The third is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Say: "In whose hand is the dominion of everything?"﴾

Know that when He, glory be to Him, first mentioned the earth and then the heaven second, He generalized the ruling here, saying: "in whose hand is the malakut (sovereignty) of everything." The malakut includes both mulk (dominion) and milk (possession), by way of emphasis. His saying ﴿who gives protection while none can be protected against Him﴾: it is said "ajartu fulanan 'ala fulan" (I granted fulan protection against fulan) when you rescue him from him and prevent him. That is, He gives relief to whomever He wills from whomever He wills, and no one gives relief to anyone from Him.

As for His saying, Exalted: ﴿How then are you deluded?﴾, the meaning is: how are you deceived away from His tawhid and obedience to Him? The deceiver is Satan and desire. Then He made clear by His saying: ﴿Nay, We have brought them the truth﴾ that He had thoroughly argued against them with these verses and others, and yet they are liars. This is like a threat and warning. It has been read as "ataytuhum" and "ataytahum," with a damma and with a fatha.

Here there are questions.

The first question: In the first answer, "qul lillahi" (Say: "To God") is read only with the lam, while in the last two "Allahu" (God) is read without the lam in the codices of the people of the Two Sanctuaries (Mecca and Medina), Kufa, and Syria, and with the lam in the codices of the people of Basra. ﴿Say, "My Lord, if You should show me that which they are promised, / My Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people. / And indeed, We are able to show you what We promise them. / Repel evil by that which is best; We are most knowing of what they describe."﴾

**His saying, Exalted is He:** ﴿Allah has not taken any son, and there was not with Him any deity. Otherwise, each deity would have taken away what it created, and some of them would have overcome others. Exalted is Allah above what they describe. / Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, so exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿Say, "My Lord, if You should show me that which they are promised, / My Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people. / And indeed, We are able to show you what We promise them. / Repel evil by that which is best; We are most knowing of what they describe."﴾

Know that He, glorified is He, asserted two matters. The first is His saying: ﴿Allah has not taken any son.﴾ This is in the manner of an alert that this is from the saying of these disbelievers, for a group of them used to say, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." The second is His saying: ﴿And there was not with Him any deity,﴾ which is their claim of taking idols as deities. It is possible that He intended by it the refutation of the saying of the Christians and the Dualists (al-Thanawiyya). Then, He, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the decisive proof by His saying: ﴿Otherwise, each deity would have taken away what it created, and some of them would have overcome others.﴾ The meaning is that each one of the deities would have been independent with the creation it created and would have acted alone with it, and you would have seen the dominion of each one of them distinct from the dominion of the other, and some of them would have prevailed over others, just as you see the condition of the kings of the world: their realms are distinct and they overpower one another. Since you do not see any trace of distinction in the realms or of overpowering, then know that there is one God in whose hand is the dominion of everything.

If it is said: "*Idhan* (then/otherwise) only enters upon a statement that is a conditional and a response. How then did His saying *la-dhahaba* (would have taken away) occur as a conditional and a response, when no condition preceded it and no question from a questioner?" We say: the condition is omitted, and its estimate is "and if there had been with Him deities." It was omitted because of the indication of His saying: ﴿And there was not with Him any deity﴾ upon it. Then He, glorified is He, declared Himself free of their saying by His saying: ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they describe,﴾ namely, the attribution of a son and a partner.

As for His saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed,﴾ it was read in the genitive (*jarr*) as an adjective of Allah, and in the nominative (*raf'*) as the predicate of an omitted subject. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, is the one specialized in knowledge of the unseen and the witnessed. Others, even if they know the witnessed, will not know the unseen along with it, and the witnessed that He knows is not completed in benefit except together with knowledge of the unseen. This is like a threat to them, and therefore He said: ﴿so exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ Then He, glorified is He, commanded him to devote himself to Him and to call upon Him by His saying: ﴿My Lord, if You should show me that which they are promised, / My Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people.﴾

The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: *ma* and the *nun* (in *turayanni*) are emphatic particles. That is: "If it must be that You show me what You threaten them with of punishment, whether in this world or in the Hereafter, then do not make me a companion to them, nor punish me with their punishment." If it is said: "How is it permissible for Allah to place His infallible Prophet with the wrongdoers, so that he asks that He not place him with them?" We say: it is permissible for a servant to ask his Lord for what he knows He will do, and to seek refuge in Him from what he knows He will not do, in order to manifest servitude and humility before his Lord. How excellent is the saying of al-Hasan concerning the saying of al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr): "I have been put in charge of you, though I am not the best of you," although he knew that he was the best of them, but the believer diminishes himself. He mentioned "My Lord" twice: once before the condition and once before the response, for the sake of intensifying supplication.

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, We are able to show you what We promise them,﴾ there are two opinions concerning it. One of them: they used to deny the promise of punishment and mock it, so it was said to them that Allah is able to fulfill what He promised. It may refer to a punishment in this world, delayed until the days of him, peace be upon him, and therefore some said it concerns the people of rebellion (*ahl al-baghy*), and others said it concerns the disbelievers who were fought after the Messenger (ﷺ). The second opinion: the intended meaning is the punishment of the Hereafter.

[Page 103]

As for His saying: ﴿Repel evil by that which is best; We are most knowing of what they describe,﴾ the meaning is that the better course for him, peace be upon him, is to deal with the disbelievers in this manner. He was commanded to bear what comes from them of denial and various kinds of harm, and to repel it with beautiful speech, such as greeting and presenting proofs in the best manner. He (Allah) explained to him that He is more knowing of their condition than he, peace be upon him, is, and that since He has not cut off His blessings from them, it is fitting that he, peace be upon him, should be constant in this way. As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, We are able to show you what We promise them,﴾ there are two opinions concerning it. One of them: they used to deny the promise of punishment and mock it, so it was said to them that Allah is able to fulfill what He promised. It may refer to a punishment in this world, delayed until the days of him, peace be upon him, and therefore some said it concerns the people of rebellion (*ahl al-baghy*), and others said it concerns the disbelievers who were fought after the Messenger (ﷺ). The second opinion: the intended meaning is the punishment of the Hereafter.

[Page 103]

As for His saying: ﴿Repel evil by that which is best; We are most knowing of what they describe,﴾ the meaning is that the better course for him, peace be upon him, is to deal with the disbelievers in this manner. He was commanded to bear what comes from them of denial and various kinds of harm, and to repel it with beautiful speech, such as greeting and presenting proofs in the best manner. He (Allah) explained to him that He is more knowing of their condition than he, peace be upon him, is, and that since He has not cut off His blessings from them, it is fitting that he, peace be upon him, should be constant in this way. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: His saying ﴿Repel evil by that which is best﴾ is more eloquent than saying "repel evil with good," because of what it contains of preference. The meaning is to pardon their offense and to respond to it with as much kindness as possible, so that when pardon and kindness are combined, and full effort is exerted in it, it becomes a doubled good deed against the evil. It was said: this verse is abrogated (*mansukha*, i.e., its ruling replaced) by the verse of the sword. It was also said: it is *muhkama* (definitive, not abrogated), because conciliation (*al-mudara*) is encouraged so long as it does not lead to a loss in religion or in dignity.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 23, verses 97–100:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whispers of the devils,"﴾ ﴿and I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me."﴾ ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "My Lord, send me back,"﴾ ﴿"that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind." No! It is only a word he is saying, and before them is a barrier until the day they are resurrected.﴾

Know that He, glorified is He, when He taught His Messenger with His saying, ﴿Repel evil with that which is better,﴾ followed it with what enables him to do so, which is seeking refuge in Allah from two matters. One of them is from the whispers (hamazat) of the devils. The hamazat is the plural of hamzah, which means pushing and strong stirring, like hazz and azz. From it comes mihmaz (the goad) of the rider of horses. The hamazat of the devil is his plotting through whispering. This happens from him toward the Messenger in two ways.

The first is through whispering, and the second is by sending his enemies to harm him. The same applies to the believers, because the devil plots against them in these two ways. It is known that whoever turns to Allah, exalted is He, and asks Him to protect him from the devil, must be mindful and alert in what he does and what he leaves undone. So this very turning to Allah, exalted is He, becomes a call to adhere to obedience and a restraint from disobedience. Al-Hasan said: "After opening the prayer, he (peace be upon him) would say: 'There is no god but Allah,' three times; 'Allah is the Greatest,' three times; 'O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the whispers of the devils, their hamz, their nafth, and their nafkh.' It was asked, 'O Messenger of Allah, what is their hamz?' He said: 'The seizure of death that takes the son of Adam,' meaning the madness that seizes the son of Adam. It was asked, 'What is their nafth?' He said: 'Poetry.' It was asked, 'What is their nafkh?' He said: 'Arrogance.'"

The second matter is His saying: ﴿and I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me.﴾ On this there are two views.

The first is that they be present with him during the recitation of the Qur'an, so that he remains mindful and his forgetfulness decreases.

Others said: Rather, he sought refuge in Allah from their very presence, because it is their presence that calls to their whispering, just as a person says, "I seek refuge in Allah from your enmity, indeed I seek refuge in Allah from meeting you." It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that a man complained to him of sleeplessness he was experiencing, and he said: "When you want to sleep, say: 'I seek refuge in Allah and in the perfect words of Allah from His anger and His punishment, and from the evil of His servants, and from the whispers of the devils, and that they be present with me.'"

*[Page 104]*

As for His saying: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them﴾, there are several issues here.

**First issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "Until" (hatta) is connected to "they describe" (yasifun), meaning: they continue in their evil speech until this time. The verse is an interjection placed between them as a parenthetical clause, and the emphasis is on overlooking them, while seeking Allah's help against the devil so that he does not make him slip from forbearance. And Allah knows best.

**Second issue:** They differed concerning His saying: ﴿until, when death comes to one of them﴾. The majority hold that it refers to the disbelievers. Al-Dahhak said: "I was sitting with Ibn 'Abbas, and he said: 'Whoever does not pay zakat and does not perform Hajj asks for a return at the time of death.' One man said: 'Only the disbelievers ask that.' Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: 'I will recite to you a Qur'anic verse about it: ﴿And spend from what We have provided you before death comes to one of you, and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me to a near term so I could give charity..."﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10].'" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When death is present to a person, everything that prevented him from his rights is gathered before him, and at that point he says: 'My Lord, send me back, that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind.'"

The closer view is the first one: when the believer knows his station in Paradise, then when he witnesses it, he does not wish for anything more than it. Otherwise, the one with the least reward would be grieved by the loss of what others have attained of a station. As for what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, mentioned, namely His saying, ﴿And spend from what We have provided you before death comes to one of you﴾, it is a report about the state of life in this world, not about the state of reward, so it does not necessitate what we have mentioned.

**Third issue:** They differed about the time of the request for return. The majority hold that he asks at the moment of direct witnessing, because at that point he is compelled to know Allah, exalted is He, and that he had been disobedient. He becomes forced to the realization that he will not commit evil, since Allah informs him that if he were to attempt it, he would be prevented from it. One who is in this state becomes like one restrained from vices by this compulsion. At that point he asks for return and says: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ ﴿that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind.﴾ Others said: Rather, he says this when he witnesses the Fire in the Hereafter. Perhaps this speaker left the apparent meaning of this verse because Allah, exalted is He, informed in His Book about the people of the Fire in the Hereafter that they ask for a return. But this does not prevent them from asking for return at the moment of witnessing, and Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "My Lord, send me back"﴾, so He linked their saying to the time of death's presence, which is the moment of direct witnessing. Therefore there is no reason to abandon this apparent meaning.

**Fourth issue:** They differed concerning His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Send me back﴾. Who is meant by it? Some said: the angels who take the souls, and they are a group, so He mentioned it in the plural form. Others said: Rather, what is meant is Allah, exalted is He, because His saying "my Lord" (rabbi) is equivalent to saying "O my Lord." The plural was used to magnify, just as the great one addresses with his own words, saying "we did and we made." The poet said:

*"If you wish, I will forbid women other than you..."*

Whoever holds the first view makes the mention of the Lord an oath, as if at the moment of witnessing he said: "By the right of the Lord, send me back."

Here there are some questions:

**First question:** How do they ask for return when they know the truth of the religion by necessity, and it is part of the religion that there is no return? The answer: Even if that is so, it is not impossible that they ask Him, because seeking help with this kind of request is good even if one knows it will not happen. As for his wanting a return, that is also not impossible, in the manner of one who wishes for something.

**Second question:** What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿that I may do righteousness﴾? Is it permissible to ask for return with doubt? The answer: "Perhaps" (la'alla) is not meant to express doubt, since at that time he is exerting full effort in resolving to obey, if he is granted what he asked for. Rather, he is like one who has fallen short regarding his own rights and knows the bad outcome of that shortfall, so he says: "Enable me to make amends; perhaps I will make amends." He says this word while being certain that he will make amends. It is also possible that when they do not know a future matter, they use language that is designed for hope and supposition rather than certainty. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

**Third question:** What is meant by His saying: "in what I have left behind"? The answer: Some said: "in the wealth I left behind," so that upon return he would discharge Allah's right from it. What is understood from His saying "left behind" is the estate. Others said: Rather, what is meant is "I will do righteousness in what I fell short of," so this includes bodily and financial acts of worship and rights. This is the closer view. It is as if they wished for return in order to correct what they had corrupted and to obey in everything in which they had disobeyed.

**Fourth question:** What is meant by His saying: "No!" (kalla)? The answer: There are two views. The first is that it serves as their answer, a refusal of what they requested, just as one says to someone seeking a distant matter: "Far-fetched!" It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) said to 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "When a believer witnesses the angels, they say: 'Shall we return you to the abode of this world?' He says: 'To the abode of worries and sorrows? No, rather, I come to Allah.' As for the disbeliever, it is said to him: 'Shall we return you?' He says: 'Send me back!' It is said to him: 'To what would you wish to return: to gathering wealth, or planting orchards, or building structures, or digging rivers?' He says: 'that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind.' Then the Almighty says: 'No!'" The second is that it may be a report that they say this, and that this report is true, as if He said: "Truly, it is a word that he is the one saying."

As for His saying: ﴿it is only a word he is saying﴾, there are two views.

The first: he does not leave it alone and does not remain silent about it, because of the grief that overwhelms him.

The second: he is the only one who says it, and he is not answered in it, and it is not heard from him.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and before them is a barrier until the day they are resurrected.﴾ The barrier (barzakh) is the obstacle and the preventer, like His saying about the two seas: ﴿between them is a barrier they do not transgress﴾ [al-Rahman: 20]. That is, these people have come to a state that prevents recovery, a barrier against reunion, and that is death. The meaning is not that they will return on the Day of Resurrection. Rather, this is a complete despair, since it is known that there is no return on the Day of Resurrection except to the Hereafter.

Rather, he is like one who has fallen short regarding his own rights and knows the bad outcome of that shortfall, so he says: "Enable me to make amends; perhaps I will make amends." He says this word while being certain that he will make amends. It is also possible that when they do not know a future matter, they use language that is designed for hope and supposition rather than certainty. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

**Third question:** What is meant by His saying: "in what I have left behind"? The answer: Some said: "in the wealth I left behind," so that upon return he would discharge Allah's right from it. What is understood from His saying "left behind" is the estate. Others said: Rather, what is meant is "I will do righteousness in what I fell short of," so this includes bodily and financial acts of worship and rights. This is the closer view. It is as if they wished for return in order to correct what they had corrupted and to obey in everything in which they had disobeyed.

**Fourth question:** What is meant by His saying: "No!" (kalla)? The answer: There are two views. The first is that it serves as their answer, a refusal of what they requested, just as one says to someone seeking a distant matter: "Far-fetched!" It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) said to 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "When a believer witnesses the angels, they say: 'Shall we return you to the abode of this world?' He says: 'To the abode of worries and sorrows? No, rather, I come to Allah.' As for the disbeliever, it is said to him: 'Shall we return you?' He says: 'Send me back!' It is said to him: 'To what would you wish to return: to gathering wealth, or planting orchards, or building structures, or digging rivers?' He says: 'that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind.' Then the Almighty says: 'No!'" The second is that it may be a report that they say this, and that this report is true, as if He said: "Truly, it is a word that he is the one saying."

As for His saying: ﴿it is only a word he is saying﴾, there are two views.

The first: he does not leave it alone and does not remain silent about it, because of the grief that overwhelms him.

The second: he is the only one who says it, and he is not answered in it, and it is not heard from him.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and before them is a barrier until the day they are resurrected.﴾ The barrier (barzakh) is the obstacle and the preventer, like His saying about the two seas: ﴿between them is a barrier they do not transgress﴾ [al-Rahman: 20]. That is, these people have come to a state that prevents recovery, a barrier against reunion, and that is death. The meaning is not that they will return on the Day of Resurrection. Rather, this is a complete despair, since it is known that there is no return on the Day of Resurrection except to the Hereafter.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 23, verses 97–100:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whispers of the devils,"﴾ ﴿and I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me."﴾ ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "My Lord, send me back,"﴾ ﴿"that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind." No! It is only a word he is saying, and before them is a barrier until the day they are resurrected.﴾

Know that He, glorified is He, when He taught His Messenger with His saying, ﴿Repel evil with that which is better,﴾ followed it with what enables him to do so, which is seeking refuge in Allah from two matters. One of them is from the whispers (hamazat) of the devils. The hamazat is the plural of hamzah, which means pushing and strong stirring, like hazz and azz. From it comes mihmaz (the goad) of the rider of horses. The hamazat of the devil is his plotting through whispering. This happens from him toward the Messenger in two ways.

The first is through whispering, and the second is by sending his enemies to harm him. The same applies to the believers, because the devil plots against them in these two ways. It is known that whoever turns to Allah, exalted is He, and asks Him to protect him from the devil, must be mindful and alert in what he does and what he leaves undone. So this very turning to Allah, exalted is He, becomes a call to adhere to obedience and a restraint from disobedience. Al-Hasan said: "After opening the prayer, he (peace be upon him) would say: 'There is no god but Allah,' three times; 'Allah is the Greatest,' three times; 'O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the whispers of the devils, their hamz, their nafth, and their nafkh.' It was asked, 'O Messenger of Allah, what is their hamz?' He said: 'The seizure of death that takes the son of Adam,' meaning the madness that seizes the son of Adam. It was asked, 'What is their nafth?' He said: 'Poetry.' It was asked, 'What is their nafkh?' He said: 'Arrogance.'"

The second matter is His saying: ﴿and I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me.﴾ On this there are two views.

The first is that they be present with him during the recitation of the Qur'an, so that he remains mindful and his forgetfulness decreases.

Others said: Rather, he sought refuge in Allah from their very presence, because it is their presence that calls to their whispering, just as a person says, "I seek refuge in Allah from your enmity, indeed I seek refuge in Allah from meeting you." It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that a man complained to him of sleeplessness he was experiencing, and he said: "When you want to sleep, say: 'I seek refuge in Allah and in the perfect words of Allah from His anger and His punishment, and from the evil of His servants, and from the whispers of the devils, and that they be present with me.'"

As for His saying: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of them﴾, there are several issues here.

**First issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "Until" (hatta) is connected to "they describe" (yasifun), meaning: they continue in their evil speech until this time. The verse is an interjection placed between them as a parenthetical clause, and the emphasis is on overlooking them, while seeking Allah's help against the devil so that he does not make him slip from forbearance. And Allah knows best.

**Second issue:** They differed concerning His saying: ﴿until, when death comes to one of them﴾. The majority hold that it refers to the disbelievers. Al-Dahhak said: "I was sitting with Ibn 'Abbas, and he said: 'Whoever does not pay zakat and does not perform Hajj asks for a return at the time of death.' One man said: 'Only the disbelievers ask that.' Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: 'I will recite to you a Qur'anic verse about it: ﴿And spend from what We have provided you before death comes to one of you, and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me to a near term so I could give charity..."﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10].'" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When death is present to a person, everything that prevented him from his rights is gathered before him, and at that point he says: 'My Lord, send me back, that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind.'"

The closer view is the first one: when the believer knows his station in Paradise, then when he witnesses it, he does not wish for anything more than it. Otherwise, the one with the least reward would be grieved by the loss of what others have attained of a station. As for what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, mentioned, namely His saying, ﴿And spend from what We have provided you before death comes to one of you﴾, it is a report about the state of life in this world, not about the state of reward, so it does not necessitate what we have mentioned.

**Third issue:** They differed about the time of the request for return. The majority hold that he asks at the moment of direct witnessing, because at that point he is compelled to know Allah, exalted is He, and that he had been disobedient. He becomes forced to the realization that he will not commit evil, since Allah informs him that if he were to attempt it, he would be prevented from it. One who is in this state becomes like one restrained from vices by this compulsion. At that point he asks for return and says: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ ﴿that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind.﴾ Others said: Rather, he says this when he witnesses the Fire in the Hereafter. But this does not prevent them from asking for return at the moment of witnessing, and Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "My Lord, send me back"﴾, so He linked their saying to the time of death's presence, which is the moment of direct witnessing. Therefore there is no reason to abandon this apparent meaning.

The plural was used to magnify, just as the great one addresses with his own words, saying "we did and we made." The poet said:

*"If you wish, I will forbid women other than you..."*

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 23, verses 101–105:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that day, nor will they ask one another. Then whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful. And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves, abiding in Hell. The Fire will scorch their faces, and they will be grimacing therein. Were not My verses recited to you, and did you not deny them?﴾

Know that when He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And before them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected﴾, He mentioned the states of that Day, saying: ﴿And when the Trumpet is blown﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: the Trumpet (al-Sur) is an instrument into which, when blown, a great sound appears, which Allah the Exalted made a sign of the ruin of the world and of the restoration of the dead. It has been related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that it is a horn that is blown into.

The second: the intended meaning of al-Sur is the collection of forms (al-suwar), and the meaning is: when the spirits are blown into the forms. This is the view of al-Hasan, who used to recite it with a fatha on the waw (al-Suwar). Both the fatha and the kasra (al-Sur and al-Sur) are reported from Abu Razin, and it is evidence for those who explained al-Sur as the plural of sura (form).

The third: the blowing into the Trumpet is a metaphor (isti'ara), and what is meant by it is resurrection and gathering. But the first is preferable because of the report. In His saying: ﴿Then it will be blown into a second time﴾ [Az-Zumar: 68] there is an indication that what is meant is not the blowing of the spirit and the giving of life, because that is not repeated.

As for His saying: ﴿There will be no kinship among them that day, nor will they ask one another﴾, it is known that when He resurrects them, kinship remains, since the resurrected are children and parents. So the intended meaning cannot be the literal negation of lineage; rather what is meant is the negation of its ruling (hukm). That is in several respects.

The first: it is part of the right of kinship that it brings about compassion and mercy, as is said in this world: "I ask you by Allah and by the bond of kinship to do such-and-such." He, glory be to Him, negated this, since every one of the people of the Fire is preoccupied with himself, and that prevents him from turning to kinship. The same is the case in this world, for when a man falls into a great affliction of pains he forgets his child and his parent.

The second: it is part of the right of kinship that boasting through it occurs in this world, and that some ask others about the manner of one another's lineage. In the Hereafter they will have no leisure for that.

The third: that it be taken as a metaphor for intense fear, for each person is preoccupied with himself, away from his sons, his brother, and his clan who shelter him. How then (would he be concerned) with other matters? Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "On the Day of Resurrection the male and female slave will be seized before the witnesses, and a caller will call out: 'Behold, this is so-and-so; whoever has a right over him, let him come to claim his right.' Then the woman will rejoice at that time if a right is established for her over her mother, her sister, her father, her brother, her son, or her husband." ﴿There will be no kinship among them that day, nor will they ask one another.﴾

And from Qatada: "There is nothing more hateful to a person on the Day of Resurrection than to see someone he knows, for fear that some claim against him will be established." Then he recited: ﴿On the Day a man will flee from his brother﴾ ﴿and his mother and his father﴾ [Abasa: 34–35]. And from al-Sha'bi, who said: Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "O Messenger of Allah, will we not recognize one another on the Day of Resurrection? I hear Allah the Exalted saying: ﴿There will be no kinship among them that day, nor will they ask one another.﴾" So he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "There are three stations in which every soul will be distracted: when each person is given his book, at the scales, and on the bridge of Hell."

Some of the heretics (al-mulhida) criticized, saying: His saying ﴿nor will they ask one another﴾ and His saying ﴿And no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾ [Al-Ma'arij: 10] contradict His saying ﴿And some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾ [As-Saffat: 50] and His saying ﴿They will recognize one another﴾ [Yunus: 45]. The answer to this is in several respects.

The first: the Day of Resurrection has a duration of fifty thousand years, and so it contains different times and states. They will recognize one another and ask one another during some of them, and they will be bewildered during others because of the intensity of terror.

The second: when the Trumpet is blown once, they are occupied with themselves, away from asking; but when it is blown a second time, some of them turn to others and say: ﴿O woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place? This is what the Most Merciful promised﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52].

The third: the intended meaning is: they will not ask one another about the rights of kinship.

The fourth: His saying ﴿nor will they ask one another﴾ is a description of the disbelievers, because of the intensity of their fear.

[Page 107]

As for His saying ﴿And some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾ [As-Saffat: 50], it is a description of the people of Paradise when they enter it. Know that He, glory be to Him, has clarified that after the blowing of the Trumpet there will be the reckoning, and the explanation of the states of the blessed and the wretched. It has been said: When He, glory be to Him, made clear that in the Hereafter there is nothing but the heaviness and lightness of the scales, it must be that every accountable person is either among the people of Paradise and the people of success, or among the people of the Fire. Thereby the view is refuted that among them are those who do not deserve reward or punishment, or those for whom reward and punishment are equal.

Then He, glory be to Him, explained the state of the blessed in His saying: ﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful.﴾ Concerning the scales there are several opinions.

The first: it is a metaphor for justice (al-'adl).

The second: the scales are the good deeds. Whoever brings what has weight and worth is the one who wins and prevails, and whoever brings what has no weight, like His saying the Exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty man thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾ [An-Nur: 39], then he is one who abides in Hell.

Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "The mawazin (scales) is the plural of mawzun, which means the things weighed of deeds, that is, the righteous deeds which have weight and value with Allah the Exalted, from His saying: ﴿So We will not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al-Kahf: 105], meaning, no value."

The third: it is a scale that has a tongue and two pans, in which good deeds are weighed in their most beautiful form and bad deeds in their ugliest form. Whoever's good deeds are heavy is driven to Paradise, and whoever's bad deeds are heavy is driven to the Fire. The complete discussion of this topic has already been given in surah al-Anbiya, upon them be peace.

As for the wretched, Allah the Exalted described them with four attributes:

The first: that they have lost themselves. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "They were cheated of them, in that their dwellings became those of the believers." It has also been said: their benefit from themselves was prevented because they are in punishment.

The second: His saying ﴿abiding in Hell﴾, and its indication of the eternal abiding of the disbelievers in the Fire is clear. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "'Abiding in Hell' is either a substitute (badal) for 'they have lost themselves', or a predicate after a predicate for 'those', or the predicate of an omitted subject."

The third: His saying ﴿The Fire will scorch their faces﴾. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "That is, it will strike and consume their flesh and skins." Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-laft (scorching) and al-nafkh (blowing) are the same, except that al-laft has a stronger effect."

The fourth: His saying ﴿and they will be grimacing therein﴾. Al-kulűh (grimacing) is that the two lips shrink and draw away from the teeth, as you see roasted heads. It has been related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The Fire will roast him, so his upper lip will shrink until it reaches the middle of his head, and his lower lip will hang down until it reaches his navel." And it has been recited as kalihun.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, explained their punishment, He related what will be said to them at that time as rebuke and reproach, which is His saying the Exalted: ﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾ Then you used to deny them despite their clarity, so you have rightly become deserving of what you are in of painful punishment.

The Mu'tazila (a theological school) said: The verse indicates that they fell into that punishment only because of their evil deeds, and if the actions of servants were by the creation of Allah the Exalted, that would not be valid. The answer: the one able to obey and disobey, if disobedience proceeds from him without any preponderant cause at all, then its proceeding from him is accidental, not voluntary, so he does not deserve punishment. And if it is by a preponderant cause, then that preponderant cause is not his act, otherwise an infinite regress (tasalsul) would follow. In that case, the proceeding of that obedience from him would be compelled, not voluntary, so he does not deserve reward.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 23, verses 101–105:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that day, nor will they ask one another. Then whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful. Were not My verses recited to you, and did you not deny them?﴾

Know that when He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And before them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected﴾, He mentioned the states of that Day, saying: ﴿And when the Trumpet is blown﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: the Trumpet (al-Sur) is an instrument into which, when blown, a great sound appears, which Allah the Exalted made a sign of the ruin of the world and of the restoration of the dead. It has been related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that it is a horn that is blown into.

The second: the intended meaning of al-Sur is the collection of forms (al-suwar), and the meaning is: when the spirits are blown into the forms. This is the view of al-Hasan, who used to recite it with a fatha on the waw (al-Suwar). Both the fatha and the kasra (al-Sur and al-Sur) are reported from Abu Razin, and it is evidence for those who explained al-Sur as the plural of sura (form).

The third: the blowing into the Trumpet is a metaphor (isti'ara), and what is meant by it is resurrection and gathering. But the first is preferable because of the report. In His saying: ﴿Then it will be blown into a second time﴾ [Az-Zumar: 68] there is an indication that what is meant is not the blowing of the spirit and the giving of life, because that is not repeated.

As for His saying: ﴿There will be no kinship among them that day, nor will they ask one another﴾, it is known that when He resurrects them, kinship remains, since the resurrected are children and parents. So the intended meaning cannot be the literal negation of lineage; rather what is meant is the negation of its ruling (hukm). That is in several respects.

The first: it is part of the right of kinship that it brings about compassion and mercy, as is said in this world: "I ask you by Allah and by the bond of kinship to do such-and-such." He, glory be to Him, negated this, since every one of the people of the Fire is preoccupied with himself, and that prevents him from turning to kinship. The same is the case in this world, for when a man falls into a great affliction of pains he forgets his child and his parent.

The second: it is part of the right of kinship that boasting through it occurs in this world, and that some ask others about the manner of one another's lineage. In the Hereafter they will have no leisure for that.

The third: that it be taken as a metaphor for intense fear, for each person is preoccupied with himself, away from his sons, his brother, and his clan who shelter him. How then (would he be concerned) with other matters? Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "On the Day of Resurrection the male and female slave will be seized before the witnesses, and a caller will call out: 'Behold, this is so-and-so; whoever has a right over him, let him come to claim his right.' The complete discussion of this topic has already been given in surah al-Anbiya, upon them be peace.

As for the wretched, Allah the Exalted described them with four attributes:

The first: that they have lost themselves. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "They were cheated of them, in that their dwellings became those of the believers." It has also been said: their benefit from themselves was prevented because they are in punishment.

The second: His saying ﴿abiding in Hell﴾, and its indication of the eternal abiding of the disbelievers in the Fire is clear. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "'Abiding in Hell' is either a substitute (badal) for 'they have lost themselves', or a predicate after a predicate for 'those', or the predicate of an omitted subject."

The third: His saying ﴿The Fire will scorch their faces﴾. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "That is, it will strike and consume their flesh and skins." Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-laft (scorching) and al-nafkh (blowing) are the same, except that al-laft has a stronger effect."

The fourth: His saying ﴿and they will be grimacing therein﴾. Al-kulűh (grimacing) is that the two lips shrink and draw away from the teeth, as you see roasted heads. It has been related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The Fire will roast him, so his upper lip will shrink until it reaches the middle of his head, and his lower lip will hang down until it reaches his navel." And it has been recited as kalihun.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, explained their punishment, He related what will be said to them at that time as rebuke and reproach, which is His saying the Exalted: ﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾ Then you used to deny them despite their clarity, so you have rightly become deserving of what you are in of painful punishment.

The Mu'tazila (a theological school) said: The verse indicates that they fell into that punishment only because of their evil deeds, and if the actions of servants were by the creation of Allah the Exalted, that would not be valid. The answer: the one able to obey and disobey, if disobedience proceeds from him without any preponderant cause at all, then its proceeding from him is accidental, not voluntary, so he does not deserve punishment. And if it is by a preponderant cause, then that preponderant cause is not his act, otherwise an infinite regress (tasalsul) would follow. In that case, the proceeding of that obedience from him would be compelled, not voluntary, so he does not deserve reward.

He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿Did not My verses get recited to you, and did you not deny them?﴾ Then they mentioned something that serves as a reply to this, and it has two aspects.

The first is their saying: ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overpowered us, and we were a people who went astray.﴾ On this there are two issues.

The first issue: The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) said: "*Ghalabat 'alaynā*" means "it possessed us," from your saying "so-and-so overpowered me over such-and-such," meaning he took it from you. "*Al-shiqwa*" means the evil outcome. It has been read as *shiqwatunā* with a *fatḥa* and with a *kasra* on the *shīn* in both cases. Abu Muslim said: *al-shiqwa* is from *al-shaqā'* (wretchedness), like *jirya al-mā'* (the flow of water). The verbal noun is *al-jary* (flowing), but the form *fi'la* may also occur with the meaning of a state or condition. One says *jilsa ḥasana* (a good sitting), *rikba* and *qi'da*, and these refer to a manner or posture. One also says *'āsha fulān 'īshatan ṭayyiba* (so-and-so lived a good life) and *māta mītatan karīma* (died a noble death). This is the condition and manner. Accordingly, what is meant by *al-shiqwa* is the state of wretchedness.

The second issue: Al-Jubba'i said: What is meant is that our pursuit of forbidden pleasures and our eagerness for ugly deeds led us to this wretchedness, so the name of the cause (*al-musabbab*) was applied to the cause (*al-sabab*). This is not an excuse on their part, since they know that they have no excuse in it. Rather, it is an acknowledgment that God's proof stands against them for their evil conduct.

We say: You have taken *al-shiqwa* to mean the pursuit of those forbidden pleasures. The pursuit of those pleasures either came about through their choice or not through their choice. If it came about through their choice, then that choice is originated (*muḥdath*). If it is self-sufficient without an efficient cause, then why should this not be the case for all originated things? In that case the door to establishing the Creator would be closed to you. If it requires an originator, then its originator is either the servant or God, the Exalted. If it is the servant, that is false for several reasons:

The first: The servant's power is capable of both the act and its omission. If the issuing of that volition from it depends on another determinant, the discussion returns to that determinant and an infinite regress (*tasalsul*) follows. If it does not depend on a determinant, then you have allowed that one of the two equal possibilities is preferred over the other without a determinant, and that closes the door to establishing the Creator.

The second: The servant does not know the quantity or the manner of those acts, and one who is ignorant of a thing cannot be its originator. Otherwise the indication of precision and perfection of design would be invalidated as a proof of knowledge.

The second point: No one in this world chooses ignorance. Rather, one intends only to acquire knowledge. The disbeliever intended only to acquire knowledge. If the one who brings about his act is himself, then only what he intended to bring about should occur. But he intended only knowledge, so how did ignorance come about? Thus it is established that the one who brings about the motives and incitements is God, the Exalted. Then, if the motive drives toward good, it is happiness, and if it drives toward evil, it is wretchedness.

The second aspect of their answer is their saying: ﴿and we were a people who went astray.﴾ If this straying, which they made like a cause for their undertaking denial, were itself that very denial, it would follow that something is explained by itself. Since that is invalid, there remains only that this straying is an expression of something else upon which their action followed, and that is nothing but the creation of the incitement to straying.

Then, when the people put forward these two excuses, He, glorified be He, said to them: ﴿Be driven off into it, and do not speak to Me.﴾ This is the clear statement of our position that debating with God, the Exalted, is not permissible, rather "He is not questioned about what He does."

The judge (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: His saying ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overpowered us﴾ indicates that they have no excuse except acknowledgment. If their disbelief were from His creation and by His will, and they knew that, they would be more fitting to mention it and closer to an excuse. We say: We have made clear that what they mentioned is nothing but that, but they admit that they have no excuse, so inevitably He said to them: ﴿Be driven off into it, and do not speak to Me.﴾

As for His saying: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out from it, and if we return, then we are indeed wrongdoers,﴾ the meaning is: bring us out from this abode to the abode of the world, and if we return to evil deeds, then we are wrongdoers. If it is asked: How is it permissible for them to ask this when they know that their punishment is everlasting? We say: It is possible that they forget this in states of severe torment, so they ask for a return. It is also possible that, while knowing this, they ask for it seeking relief and respite.

As for His saying: ﴿Be driven off into it,﴾ the meaning is: be humiliated in it and be restrained, as dogs are restrained when they are driven off. One says *khasa'a al-kalb* and *khasa'a bi-nafsih* (the dog was driven away, and it drove itself away).

As for His saying: ﴿and do not speak to Me,﴾ this is not a prohibition, because there is no obligation in the Hereafter. Rather, what is meant is: do not speak to Me about lifting the punishment, for it will not be lifted or lightened. It has been said: this is the last word they speak, after which there is no speech except *al-shahīq* (groaning) and *al-zafīr* (roaring), and barking like the barking of dogs. They are neither understood nor do they understand.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: They have six supplications. When they enter the Fire, they say for a thousand years: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us﴾ [al-Sajda: 12], and they are answered: ﴿The word from Me has been fulfilled﴾ [al-Sajda: 13]. Then they call out for a second thousand years: ﴿Our Lord, You made us die twice and gave us life twice﴾ [Ghafir: 11], and they are answered: ﴿That is because when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved﴾ [Ghafir: 12]. Then they call out for a third thousand years: ﴿O Malik, let your Lord decree upon us﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 77], and they are answered: ﴿Indeed you will remain﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 77]. Then they call out for a fourth thousand years: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out,﴾ and they are answered: ﴿Did you not swear before that there would be no decline for you?﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]. Then they call out for a fifth thousand years: ﴿Bring us out, and we will do righteous deeds﴾ [Fatir: 37], and they are answered: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough?﴾ [Fatir: 37]. Then they call out for a sixth thousand years: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99], and they are answered: ﴿Be driven off into it.﴾

Then He, glorified and exalted, explained that their grief concerns a matter connected with the believers, and that is His saying: ﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants who said: Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful.﴾ ﴿But you took them in derision﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 110]. He described one of the reasons for which they were punished and removed far from good, which is how they treated the believers.

In Ubayy's codex it reads *annahu kāna farīq* with a *fatḥa* (on *anna*), in the sense of *li-annahu* (because). Nafi' and the people of Medina and the people of Kufa, through 'Asim, read *sukhriyyan* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn* throughout the Qur'an, while the rest read it with a *kasra* here, and in Sad. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: they are two dialects, like *durriyy* and *dirriyy*. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the *kasra* means mockery in speech, and the *ḍamma* means ridicule.

Muqatil said: The leaders of Quraysh, such as Abu Jahl, 'Utba and Ubayy ibn Khalaf, used to mock the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and laugh at the poor among them, such as Bilal, Khabbab, 'Ammar and Suhayb. The meaning is: you took them as objects of ridicule, until your preoccupation with them in that manner made you forget My remembrance. He emphasized this with His saying: ﴿and you used to laugh at them.﴾

Then He, glorified be He, explained what calls for their regret and anguish, by describing what He recompensed those believers with. He said: ﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for what they endured; indeed, they are the triumphant.﴾ Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *innahum* with a *kasra*, and the rest with a *fatḥa*. The *kasra* is a resumption (*isti'naf*), meaning: they have succeeded, since they were patient, so they were rewarded with the best reward for their patience. The *fatḥa* is in the position of the second object of *jaza* (to reward), and it is also possible that it is in the accusative by deleting the preposition, meaning: I rewarded them with abundant reward, because they are the triumphant.

He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿Did not My verses get recited to you, and did you not deny them?﴾ Then they mentioned something that serves as a reply to this, and it has two aspects.

The first is their saying: ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overpowered us, and we were a people who went astray.﴾ On this there are two issues.

The first issue: The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) said: "*Ghalabat 'alaynā*" means "it possessed us," from your saying "so-and-so overpowered me over such-and-such," meaning he took it from you. "*Al-shiqwa*" means the evil outcome. It has been read as *shiqwatunā* with a *fatḥa* and with a *kasra* on the *shīn* in both cases. Abu Muslim said: *al-shiqwa* is from *al-shaqā'* (wretchedness), like *jirya al-mā'* (the flow of water). The verbal noun is *al-jary* (flowing), but the form *fi'la* may also occur with the meaning of a state or condition. One says *jilsa ḥasana* (a good sitting), *rikba* and *qi'da*, and these refer to a manner or posture. One also says *'āsha fulān 'īshatan ṭayyiba* (so-and-so lived a good life) and *māta mītatan karīma* (died a noble death). This is the condition and manner. Accordingly, what is meant by *al-shiqwa* is the state of wretchedness.

The second issue: Al-Jubba'i said: What is meant is that our pursuit of forbidden pleasures and our eagerness for ugly deeds led us to this wretchedness, so the name of the cause (*al-musabbab*) was applied to the cause (*al-sabab*). This is not an excuse on their part, since they know that they have no excuse in it. Rather, it is an acknowledgment that God's proof stands against them for their evil conduct.

We say: You have taken *al-shiqwa* to mean the pursuit of those forbidden pleasures. The pursuit of those pleasures either came about through their choice or not through their choice. If it came about through their choice, then that choice is originated (*muḥdath*). If it is self-sufficient without an efficient cause, then why should this not be the case for all originated things? In that case the door to establishing the Creator would be closed to you. If it requires an originator, then its originator is either the servant or God, the Exalted. If it is the servant, that is false for several reasons:

The first: The servant's power is capable of both the act and its omission. If the issuing of that volition from it depends on another determinant, the discussion returns to that determinant and an infinite regress (*tasalsul*) follows. If it does not depend on a determinant, then you have allowed that one of the two equal possibilities is preferred over the other without a determinant, and that closes the door to establishing the Creator.

The second: The servant does not know the quantity or the manner of those acts, and one who is ignorant of a thing cannot be its originator. Otherwise the indication of precision and perfection of design would be invalidated as a proof of knowledge.

The second point: No one in this world chooses ignorance. Rather, one intends only to acquire knowledge. The disbeliever intended only to acquire knowledge. If the one who brings about his act is himself, then only what he intended to bring about should occur. But he intended only knowledge, so how did ignorance come about? Thus it is established that the one who brings about the motives and incitements is God, the Exalted. Then, if the motive drives toward good, it is happiness, and if it drives toward evil, it is wretchedness.

The second aspect of their answer is their saying: ﴿and we were a people who went astray.﴾ If this straying, which they made like a cause for their undertaking denial, were itself that very denial, it would follow that something is explained by itself. Since that is invalid, there remains only that this straying is an expression of something else upon which their action followed, and that is nothing but the creation of the incitement to straying.

Then, when the people put forward these two excuses, He, glorified be He, said to them: ﴿Be driven off into it, and do not speak to Me.﴾ This is the clear statement of our position that debating with God, the Exalted, is not permissible, rather "He is not questioned about what He does."

The judge (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: His saying ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overpowered us﴾ indicates that they have no excuse except acknowledgment. If their disbelief were from His creation and by His will, and they knew that, they would be more fitting to mention it and closer to an excuse. We say: We have made clear that what they mentioned is nothing but that, but they admit that they have no excuse, so inevitably He said to them: ﴿Be driven off into it, and do not speak to Me.﴾

As for His saying: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out from it, and if we return, then we are indeed wrongdoers,﴾ the meaning is: bring us out from this abode to the abode of the world, and if we return to evil deeds, then we are wrongdoers. If it is asked: How is it permissible for them to ask this when they know that their punishment is everlasting? We say: It is possible that they forget this in states of severe torment, so they ask for a return. It is also possible that, while knowing this, they ask for it seeking relief and respite.

As for His saying: ﴿Be driven off into it,﴾ the meaning is: be humiliated in it and be restrained, as dogs are restrained when they are driven off. One says *khasa'a al-kalb* and *khasa'a bi-nafsih* (the dog was driven away, and it drove itself away).

As for His saying: ﴿and do not speak to Me,﴾ this is not a prohibition, because there is no obligation in the Hereafter. Rather, what is meant is: do not speak to Me about lifting the punishment, for it will not be lifted or lightened. It has been said: this is the last word they speak, after which there is no speech except *al-shahīq* (groaning) and *al-zafīr* (roaring), and barking like the barking of dogs. They are neither understood nor do they understand.

Muqatil said: The leaders of Quraysh, such as Abu Jahl, 'Utba and Ubayy ibn Khalaf, used to mock the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and laugh at the poor among them, such as Bilal, Khabbab, 'Ammar and Suhayb. The meaning is: you took them as objects of ridicule, until your preoccupation with them in that manner made you forget My remembrance. He emphasized this with His saying: ﴿and you used to laugh at them.﴾

Then He, glorified be He, explained what calls for their regret and anguish, by describing what He recompensed those believers with. He said: ﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for what they endured; indeed, they are the triumphant.﴾ Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *innahum* with a *kasra*, and the rest with a *fatḥa*. The *kasra* is a resumption (*isti'naf*), meaning: they have succeeded, since they were patient, so they were rewarded with the best reward for their patience. The *fatḥa* is in the position of the second object of *jaza* (to reward), and it is also possible that it is in the accusative by deleting the preposition, meaning: I rewarded them with abundant reward, because they are the triumphant.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 23, verses 112–116:**

﴿He will say, "How many years did you remain on earth?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "We remained a day or part of a day, so ask those who count."﴾ ﴿He will say, "You remained only a little, if only you had known."﴾ ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ ﴿So exalted is Allah, the True King; there is no god but He, Lord of the Noble Throne.﴾

Know that in this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The author of *al-Kashshaf* said that in the codices of the people of Kufa it is read as "*qala*" (He said), where the pronoun refers to Allah, or to the angels who were commanded to ask them. In the codices of the people of the two Holy Cities (Makkah and Madinah), Basra and Syria, it is read as "*qul*" (Say!), where the pronoun refers to the angel, or to some of the leaders of the people of the Fire.

The second issue: The purpose of this question is rebuke and reproach. They used to deny that there would be any staying (*lubth*) in the Hereafter at all, and they did not count any staying except in the abode of this world. They assumed that after death there is perpetual annihilation with no resurrection. So when they were in the Fire and were certain that it was everlasting, and that they would remain in it forever, He asked them, ﴿How many years did you remain on earth?﴾ as a reminder to them that what they had assumed to be long-lasting is short compared to what they had denied. Thus they would feel regret over what they had believed in the world, now that they knew the opposite. So the purpose is not the question itself, but what we have mentioned. If it is said: How can it be correct for them to answer, ﴿We remained a day or part of a day﴾ when the people of the Fire do not lie? We say: Perhaps they forgot this because of the multitude of terrors they were in. They acknowledged this forgetting when they said, ﴿so ask those who count.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: What they were in of punishment between the two blasts made them forget. It was also said: Their words, ﴿We remained a day or part of a day,﴾ mean to minimize and belittle their staying in comparison with what they had undergone and experienced of painful punishment. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: They differed about which staying the question was about. Some of them said: Their staying is their living in the world, and the meaning is that they were given respite so that they could be empowered with knowledge and action. So they answered that the length of their staying was small, on the basis that Allah had informed them that this world is a little enjoyment and that the Hereafter is the abode of permanence. The one who holds this view argued for his position by saying that they used to claim that there is no life other than this one. So when Allah gave them life in the Fire and they were punished, they were asked about that as a rebuke, because it is closer to reproach. Others said: Rather, the intended staying is the staying in the state of death. They based their view on two matters. The first: His saying "*fi al-ard*" (on earth) indicates being in the grave, and whoever is alive is more likely to be said to be "on the earth." This is weak, because of His saying: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 56]. The second: His saying, ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will swear that they stayed no more than an hour﴾ [al-Rum: 55], then Allah, glorified is He, clarified that they lied in that, and He reported the words of the believers: ﴿You have indeed remained within the Book of Allah until the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Rum: 56].

The fourth issue: Whoever denied the punishment of the grave argued from this verse, saying: His saying, ﴿How many years did you remain on earth?﴾ includes the time of their being alive above the earth and the time of their being dead in the belly of the earth. So if they had been punished in the grave, they would have known that the duration of their stay in the earth was long, and they would not have said, ﴿We remained a day or part of a day.﴾ The answer is in two respects.

The first: The answer must correspond to the question. They were asked about a death after which there is no life except in the Hereafter, and that does not happen except after the punishment of the grave.

The second: It is possible that they were asked about the length of the staying that they had all shared, so that it does not include the earlier death of some of them before others. Thus it is valid that their answer was ﴿We remained a day or part of a day﴾ in our own estimation.

As for His saying, ﴿so ask those who count,﴾ there are several interpretations.

One: By them is meant the guardian angels (*al-hafazah*), who used to record the deeds and the times of life, and who would count the times of death, the going forth of those who went before and the lateness of those who came after. This is the meaning of the statement of 'Ikrimah: "*fa-sal al-'addin*" (ask those who count), i.e., those who count.

Two: Ask the angels who count the days and hours of the world.

Three: The meaning is: Ask whoever knows the number of that, for we have forgotten it.

Four: It is read "*al-'adin*" with a light pronunciation (without the doubled *ya*), meaning the wrongdoers (*al-zalamah*), for they say the same as what we have said.

Five: It is read "*al-'adiyyin*," meaning the ancient long-lived ones, for they consider it short, so how about those who came after them?

As for His saying, ﴿You remained only a little﴾: the meaning is that they said, ﴿We remained a day or part of a day,﴾ in the sense that we remained in the world only a little. It is as if it was said to them: You have spoken truly, you remained in it only a little, except that it has ended and passed away. So it becomes clear that the purpose of this question is to make known how few the days of the world are in comparison with the days of the Hereafter.

As for His saying, ﴿if only you had known,﴾ in this interpretation He clarified that He meant: it is little if you had known resurrection and gathering, but since you denied that, you considered it long.

Then He clarified what is greater in rebuke with His saying: ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ There are two issues in this:

The first issue: The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "*'abathan*" (without purpose) is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), meaning playing around, like His saying: ﴿playing﴾ [al-Anbiya: 16]. Or it is an object, meaning: We did not create you for play.

The second issue: When He, glorified is He, explained the attributes of the Resurrection, He concluded the discussion of it by establishing evidence for its existence. That evidence is that if there were no Resurrection, the obedient would not be distinguished from the disobedient, nor the truthful from the heretic, and in that case the creation of this world would be purposeless. As for returning to Allah, the intended meaning is to a place where there is no owner and no judge except Him, not a movement from one place to another, because that is impossible for Allah, exalted is He. Then He, exalted is He, declared Himself free of purposelessness with His saying: ﴿So exalted is Allah, the True King﴾. "*Al-Malik*" (the King) is the one who owns things, whose dominion and power do not perish or cease. As for "*al-Haqq*" (the True), it is the one to whom dominion is due, because everything is from Him and returns to Him; He is the Established One who does not cease, and whose dominion does not cease. He clarified that there is no god besides Him, and that whatever else there is will end in annihilation, and what perishes cannot be a god. He clarified that He, exalted is He, is ﴿Lord of the Noble Throne.﴾ Abu Muslim said: "The Throne here means the heavens with what is in them of the Throne around which the angels circle, and it is permissible that by it is meant the great dominion." Most scholars said: The intended meaning is the Throne literally, and He described it as "noble" because mercy descends from it, as do goodness and blessing, and because it is attributed to the Most Noble of the noble, just as one says, "a noble house" when its inhabitants are noble. It is also read "*al-Karim*" with a nominative ending (*raf'*), and similar to it is His saying: ﴿Lord of the Throne, the Glorious﴾.
