The fourth issue: Whoever denied the punishment of the grave argued from this verse, saying: His saying, ﴿How many years did you remain on earth?﴾ includes the time of their being alive above the earth and the time of their being dead in the belly of the earth. So if they had been punished in the grave, they would have known that the duration of their stay in the earth was long, and they would not have said, ﴿We remained a day or part of a day.﴾ The answer is in two respects.

The first: The answer must correspond to the question. They were asked about a death after which there is no life except in the Hereafter, and that does not happen except after the punishment of the grave.

The second: It is possible that they were asked about the length of the staying that they had all shared, so that it does not include the earlier death of some of them before others. Thus it is valid that their answer was ﴿We remained a day or part of a day﴾ in our own estimation.

As for His saying, ﴿so ask those who count,﴾ there are several interpretations.

One: By them is meant the guardian angels (*al-hafazah*), who used to record the deeds and the times of life, and who would count the times of death, the going forth of those who went before and the lateness of those who came after. This is the meaning of the statement of 'Ikrimah: "*fa-sal al-'addin*" (ask those who count), i.e., those who count.

Two: Ask the angels who count the days and hours of the world.

Three: The meaning is: Ask whoever knows the number of that, for we have forgotten it.

Four: It is read "*al-'adin*" with a light pronunciation (without the doubled *ya*), meaning the wrongdoers (*al-zalamah*), for they say the same as what we have said.

Five: It is read "*al-'adiyyin*," meaning the ancient long-lived ones, for they consider it short, so how about those who came after them?

As for His saying, ﴿You remained only a little﴾: the meaning is that they said, ﴿We remained a day or part of a day,﴾ in the sense that we remained in the world only a little. It is as if it was said to them: You have spoken truly, you remained in it only a little, except that it has ended and passed away. So it becomes clear that the purpose of this question is to make known how few the days of the world are in comparison with the days of the Hereafter.

As for His saying, ﴿if only you had known,﴾ in this interpretation He clarified that He meant: it is little if you had known resurrection and gathering, but since you denied that, you considered it long.

Then He clarified what is greater in rebuke with His saying: ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ There are two issues in this:

The first issue: The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "*'abathan*" (without purpose) is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), meaning playing around, like His saying: ﴿playing﴾ [al-Anbiya: 16]. Or it is an object, meaning: We did not create you for play.

The second issue: When He, glorified is He, explained the attributes of the Resurrection, He concluded the discussion of it by establishing evidence for its existence. That evidence is that if there were no Resurrection, the obedient would not be distinguished from the disobedient, nor the truthful from the heretic, and in that case the creation of this world would be purposeless. As for returning to Allah, the intended meaning is to a place where there is no owner and no judge except Him, not a movement from one place to another, because that is impossible for Allah, exalted is He. Then He, exalted is He, declared Himself free of purposelessness with His saying: ﴿So exalted is Allah, the True King﴾. "*Al-Malik*" (the King) is the one who owns things, whose dominion and power do not perish or cease. As for "*al-Haqq*" (the True), it is the one to whom dominion is due, because everything is from Him and returns to Him; He is the Established One who does not cease, and whose dominion does not cease. He clarified that there is no god besides Him, and that whatever else there is will end in annihilation, and what perishes cannot be a god. He clarified that He, exalted is He, is ﴿Lord of the Noble Throne.﴾ Abu Muslim said: "The Throne here means the heavens with what is in them of the Throne around which the angels circle, and it is permissible that by it is meant the great dominion." Most scholars said: The intended meaning is the Throne literally, and He described it as "noble" because mercy descends from it, as do goodness and blessing, and because it is attributed to the Most Noble of the noble, just as one says, "a noble house" when its inhabitants are noble. It is also read "*al-Karim*" with a nominative ending (*raf'*), and similar to it is His saying: ﴿Lord of the Throne, the Glorious﴾.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 23, verses 112–116:**

Know that in this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The author of *al-Kashshaf* said that in the codices of the people of Kufa it is read as "*qala*" (He said), where the pronoun refers to Allah, or to the angels who were commanded to ask them. In the codices of the people of the two Holy Cities (Makkah and Madinah), Basra and Syria, it is read as "*qul*" (Say!), where the pronoun refers to the angel, or to some of the leaders of the people of the Fire.

The second issue: The purpose of this question is rebuke and reproach. They used to deny that there would be any staying (*lubth*) in the Hereafter at all, and they did not count any staying except in the abode of this world. They assumed that after death there is perpetual annihilation with no resurrection. So when they were in the Fire and were certain that it was everlasting, and that they would remain in it forever, He asked them, ﴿How many years did you remain on earth?﴾ as a reminder to them that what they had assumed to be long-lasting is short compared to what they had denied. Thus they would feel regret over what they had believed in the world, now that they knew the opposite. So the purpose is not the question itself, but what we have mentioned. If it is said: How can it be correct for them to answer, ﴿We remained a day or part of a day﴾ when the people of the Fire do not lie? We say: Perhaps they forgot this because of the multitude of terrors they were in. They acknowledged this forgetting when they said, ﴿so ask those who count.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: What they were in of punishment between the two blasts made them forget. It was also said: Their words, ﴿We remained a day or part of a day,﴾ mean to minimize and belittle their staying in comparison with what they had undergone and experienced of painful punishment. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 23, verses 117–118:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever invokes along with Allah another god, for which he has no proof—then his account is only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.﴾ ﴿And say, "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, made clear that He is the true King, there is no god but Him, He followed this by saying that whoever claims another god has claimed falsehood without any proof for them concerning it. By this He drew attention to the fact that everything for which there is no proof is not permissible to affirm, and this necessitates the soundness of reasoning (nazar) and the invalidity of blind imitation (taqlid). Then He mentioned that whoever says this, his recompense is the great punishment, by His saying: ﴿then his account is only with his Lord﴾. It is as if He said: his punishment reaches to a point where no one can reckon it except Allah, exalted is He. It has been read (إنّه لا يُفلح) with a fatha on the hamza (أنّه لا يُفلح), and its meaning is: his account is the non-attainment of success. He made the opening of the surah ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1] and its closing ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾. So how far apart are the opening and the closing!

Then the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to say: "My Lord, forgive and have mercy," and to praise Him by saying that He is the best of the merciful. The explanation that He, glorified is He, is the best of the merciful has already passed. If it is said: how does this closing connect with what precedes it? We say: because when He, glorified is He, explained the states of the disbelievers in their ignorance in this world and their punishment in the Hereafter, He commanded (the Prophet) to turn exclusively to Allah, exalted is He, and to take refuge in the signs of His forgiveness and mercy, for these two are the ones that protect from every calamity and fear. It is also narrated that the beginning and the end of the surah "Qad aflaha" are from the treasures of the Throne: whoever acts upon three verses from its beginning and takes admonition from four from its end, has been saved and has succeeded. And Allah knows best what is correct, and to Him is the return and the final place. All praise is for Allah alone, and His blessings be upon the best of His creation, our master Muhammad, and his family, companions, wives, and progeny, the people of his household.
